OVricas.-73, King-street, Manchester. DEPOSIT AND MORTGAGE FUNDS. The Directors of The Manchester Trust Limited, recognis- ing the need of other facilities than those already afforded for the investment of money by way of deposit, have decided to give special attention to this class of business, and have taken suitable premises at Ne. 73, King-st., Manchester, for the purpose. They have accordingly arranged the system of security set forth in the followinir. _

One of the principal features of the system they have devised Is the establishment by trust deed of Specific Trust Funds, whereby, independently of the credit and resourc s of the Manchester Trust itself, with its 6uberibed capital of £500,000 and reserves, securities at least equal to the amount of the deposits must always be held absolutely cLarged as security to the depositors. The security thus obtained Is of an absolute character, and constitutes for the depositor an insured and guaranteed in- vestment, both as to capital and income, free f rum all market fluctuations and vicissitudes. _ _
The depo&itor in each fund will be secured— (Firstly).—By a first charge upon the securities lodged in the fund. (Secondly).—By the guarantee of the Manchester Trust Limited. _

One of these funds will comprise mortgage securities only. Investors In mortgage securities, instead of seeking for separate properties, upon which to lend their capital on , mortgage, may deposit their money in this fund. The ad- vantages to be obtained are —Freedom from individual risk, any incidental failure of security bring spread over a large aggregate of moil gages. and, in addition, the guarantee of the mortgage by the Manchester Trust Limited, both as to principal aid interest. This guarantee, at the present time, lathe business of Mortgage Insurance Companies, but the necessity for it will be obviated by this much more convenient System. When the money has to be returned there is no un- certainty, trouble, or delay in repayment. Borrowers also will find numerous advantages, more partic- ularly in the fact that the private necessities of lenders will not interfere with the permanency of the mortgage. The gmn. ral aim of the Manchester Trust Limited in making these arrangements is to provide or the wants of the numer- ous investors of moderate as well as of largo amounts of savings aocummulated beyond the limits of the savings banks and of investors who like to have their capital at occasional command, and who object to have it absolutely locked up and out of their cmtrol for indefinite pens 5.

THE TRUST FUND SYSTEM.

The Manchester Trust Limited will receive on deposit large or small slims (not under £10). For sums of £5O or over the Trust will issue certificates in the registered name ot the depositor. These will be trans- ferable by special transfer form ancl can be sold and transferred at any time, like Consols, bonds, or shares. Deposits may be for fixed terms, at fixed rates of interest, or the Trust will issue certificates, With coupons for the in- terest attached payable half-yearly, which may be arranged for special dates. These notes will be repayable any half- year on seven days' notice, Large sums of over £l,OOO may, if desired, be treated as a special trust fund, to which spectic securities may be allocated. For earns under £so(or over that amount if desired for the convenience of the depositors) pass books will be issued. re- payment being made either at fixed dates or on seven days' notice.

COUNTY OF CHESTER. CONTAGIOUS DISEASES (ANIMALS) ACTS, 1878 and 1886. FOOT-AND-MOUTH DISEASE. CHESHIRE (FOOT-AND-MOUTH DISEASE) MOVE- MENT ORDER OF 1892 AND THE CHESHIRE MARKETS AND FAIRS (FOOT-AND-MOUTH DIS-

EASE) ORDER OF 1892. NOI ICE IS HEREBY GIVEN, that in consequence of Outbreaks of Foot-and-Mouth Disease within the District of the Local Authority of the County of Chester, the Board of Agriculture by an Order taking effect from and immediately after the 17th day of March, 1892, have ordered as follows, viz. :

div.head: MOVEMENT OF ANIMALS.
div.p: MOVEMENT OF ANIMALS.

No cattle, sheep, goats, or swine shall be moved out of the District described in the Schedule to this Order with- out a license granted by an Inspector of the Board of Agriculture, or by a person appointed for the purpose by the Board, which license will only be granted where the Board, after inquiry, are satisfied that exceptional cir- cumstances render the movement necessary or expedient. Provided that nothing in this Order shall be deemed to apply to the movement of animals by railway through the said District from a place outside the said District to another place outside the said District without un- trucking within the said District.
SCHEDULE.
DISTRICT TO vvrifa-iiiig-ORDER APPLIES.

A District comprising the County of Chester, and also comprising the boroughs of Birkenhead, Chester, Con- gleton, Crewe, Hyde, Macclesfield, Stalybridge, and Stockport. AND NOTICE IS HEREBY ALSO GIVEN, that as a further consequence of such outbreaks of Foot-and- Mouth Disease, the Board of Agriculture by another Order taking effect from and immediately after the 17th day of March, 1892, have ordered as follows, viz. : PUBLIC AND PRIVATE SALES. No public or private sale of cattle, sheep, or swine, fat or store, shall be held in any of the Districts of Local Authorities mentioned in the Schedule to this Order, ex- cept as expressly authorised by this Order. PUBLIC SALES OF FAT CATTLE, SHEEP, OR SWINE, BY LICENCE OF LOCAL AUTHORITY.

(a.) A public sale of fat cattle, or fat sheep, or fat swine may be held with a licence of the Local Authority, on the following conditions (namely) : (i ) Cattle, sheep, and swine exposed at the public sale so licensed shall, after their arrival thereat, and before theyare removed therefrom, be marked by and at the expense of the owner, consignee, or other person exposing them, as follows : Certtle.—By the clipping of a broad arrow, about five inches long, on the left hind quarter of each of the cattle. Sheep and Swine.—By the painting er the stamping of the letter M, about six inches long, on the left side of each of the sheep or swine with the following composition, namely :—Resin, five parts ; oil of turpentine, two parts; and blue or red ochre, one part ; melted and used warm ; or with some other adhesive composition of a blue or red colour. (ii.) Every head of cattle, and every sheep, and every pig that is exposed at the public sale so licensed, whether it is sold thereat or not, shall be slaughtered within six days after the day on which the sale is held. (iii.) Cattle, sheep, and swine exposed at the public sale so licensed shall not afterwards be exposed at any other public sale. (b.) A license of a Local Authority for a public sale of fat cattle, sheep, or swine under this Article shall be signed by the clerk of the Local Authority, by special direction of the Local Authority, and shall give notice of the conditions contained in this Article by specifying the same as conditions on which the license is granted, and may impose such further conditions, if any, as the Local Authority think expedient, and shall be granted to the person entitled to hold the sale (as owner of a market or an autioneer, or otherwise), and shall specify the place where the sale is to be held, and may authorise the holding of periodieal sales on stated days, but may be renewed from time to time, and shall be published in such manner as the Local Authority consider best fitted to insure publicity for the same. (c.) If the Boai dof Agriculture are of opinion, with respect to any license of a Local Authority for a public sale of tat cattle, sheep, or swine under this Article, that the holding of the public sale thereby licensed is inex- pedient, or that the license is objectionable in any par- ticular, and direct the revocation thereof, the same shall thereupon cease to operate. PUBLIC OR PRIVATE SALE. FAT OR STORE, WITHOUT LICENSE OF LOCAL AUTHORITY.

A public or private sale -of ; head .of cattle, or of a sheep, or of a pig, or of cattle, sheep, or swine, fat or store, may be held without a license of the Local Autho- rity, in any case where the sale is held in accordance with the following conditions (namely) : _ . .

(i.) That the ale is held ori a fartii or premises not in a Foot-and-Mouth Disease-infected Place: (ii.) That no animal on the farm or premises is affected with foot-and-mouth disease : (iii.) That the animal or each animal exposed at the sale has been on the farm or premises not less than
Ecrie.e-ii-clear days immediately before the day on which the sale is held. SALES BY LICENCE OF THE BOARD OF AGRICUL- TURE.

Without prejudice to the foregoing provisions and in addition thereto, a public or privatelsale of cattle, sheep, or swine, fat or store, may be held in any circumstances, with a licence of the Board ef Agriculture. OFFENCES.

(a) If a public or private sale of cattle, sheep, or svrinc, fat or store, is held in contravention of this Order or of the conditions of a licence of a Local Authority or of the Board of Agriculture thereunder, the person hold- ing the sale and the occupier of the place, or farm, or premises where the sale is held, and the owner or con- signee of each animal exposed thereat, and the person exposing the same thereat, and the auctioneer, if any, or other person conducting the sale, and the person, if any, taking entrance money or other payment for admission thereto, and the purchaser thereat of any animal, such last-mentioned person, or such purchaser knowing the sale to be held in contravention as aforesaid, shall, each according to, and in respect of his own acts and defaults. be deemed guilty of an offence against the Act of 1878. (b) If a head of cattle, or a sheep, or a pig is not marked as required by this Order, the owner, consignee, or other person exposing the same, and the person for the time being in charge thereof, and the purchaser thereof, and the person holding the sale, and the auc- tioneer, if any, or other person conducting the sale, shall each according to and in respect of his own acts and defaults, be deemed guilty of an offence against the Act of 1878. (c) If any person, with a view to unlawfully evade or defeat the operation of this Order, by clipping or wash- ing, or in any other manner takes out, effaces, or obliter- ates, or attempts to take out, efface, or obliterate any mark clipped, painted, or stamped, on any cattle, sheep, or swine, as required by this Order, the person doing the same, and the person causing, directing, or permitting the same to be done, and the owner of the animal, and the person for the time being in charge thereof, shall, each according to and in respect of his own acts and defaults, be deemed guilty of an offence against the Act of 1878. (d) If a head of cattle, or a sheep, or a pig, is not slaughtered as required by this Order, the person failing to cause the same to be so slaughtered shall be deemed guilty of an offence against the Act of 1878.
INTERPRETATION.
:n this Order—
_.. ...... ........ The Act of 1878 means the Contagious Diseases (Ani.

mats) Act, 1878: Fat cattle or fat sheep, ot fat swine, means cattle,sheep, or swine intended for slaughter : Store cattle, or store sheep, or store swine, means cattle, sheep, or swine, other than fat cattle, or fat sheep, or fat swine: Public sale includes a market or fair, and any sale, whether conducted by auction or not, which is open to the public, whether on payment of entrance money or other payment or not, whether it is held in a pub- lic place or not, and whether animals of different owners are exposed thereat or not; and includes also an exhibition: . .

Private sale means any sale other than a public sale: Expose means expose for sale or in any manner put up or offer for sale, or exhibited at an exhibition: Farm or premises includes two or more adjoining farms or premises in the same occupation: Other terms have the same meaning as in the Animals Order of 1886.

DwELLEns on dangerous coasts have many strange wreck-collections. WHEN a man hasn't a "red," he gets so blue that everything looks black. Is there anything that could be run on "tick" and give satisfaction? Yes, a time-piece. Ie you wish to communicate with the finny tribes of the sea, first drop them a line. "Wa don't find the times so very hard," said a hackman. "We all do a driving business." WHERE you can't find a good looking-glass you Will scarcely find a good-looking lass either. THE members of the Jokers' Club are supplied With butter made from the cream of their jokes. A BOSTON barber would like to get possession of the hone with which the water's edge is sharpened. VOLTAIRE said that he never regretted going to law but twice. Onoe when he lost the suit, and once when he won it. A GARDEN hoe, or a rake or spade, always raises a blister on a buy's hands, hut a ball club never does. THERE are twin sisters in Coenecticut that can't be told apart, and zo they have to be told every- thing together. AN enterprising sign painter says he would pay liberally for the bribh that the "signs of the times" are painted with. A roixricAL economist says "the best wives are cheapest." Yet every good man who ha a a good wife looks upon her as "a little dear." A NArUnALIST says that this season's crop of mosquitoes wiil he about the same as the last, only this year's crop mill carry the jig saws, no as to cut bias. A STAN being accused of extravagance .leclared that the accusation was unjust, "for," said he, "I am very careful to live within the means of my creditors." THERE is said to be an old lady in Boston one hundred and seven years old, who does not wear spectacles, and whose sight is just as good as ever was. She was barn blind. As a man came to the station just as the train was steaming out, a friend on the platform of a car called out: "You didn't run fast enough." "Oh, yes, I did, but I didn't start soon enough 1" was the reply. AN Oakland (Cal.) paper has been sued for libel , by a widow for speaking of her deceased husband as having "gone to a happier home." "WHAT shsll I write about ?" inquired the would-be poet, entering the editorial sanctum. "You had better right about face," replied the editor, pointing to the door. B'TRANGER— 'I left my umbrella here last night. Where is it 2" Shopkeeper —"I don't know." "Why, you said I could leave it here." " Yes ; ! but I didn't say you'd find it here when you came back." WHAT is that big iron thing full of holes ?" I 4' Locomotive boiler," said Tom. Laura looked thoughtful. After a moment's silence she asked: "Why do they boil locomotives ?" Tom looked amazed. "To make them tender," he said slowly. A TRAVELLER on a Hudson river steamer was making way at dinner with a large pudding near him, when a waiter stepped up and told him it was a part of the dessert. "I don't,care," said the traveller; eat it U it was an entire wilder- ness." "WELL, sonny," said a doting uncle to his little nephew, who had been absent all day fishing— "well, sonny, did you catch a good many fish ?" CHATS WITH A GREY GULL. HOW BEECHAM'S PILLS ARE MADE. BY JOHN PARKINSON.

The other week we made some reference to the feeding of the sea gulls at Southport,We have since received a number of letters giving an account of imaginary chats with one of these birds. They were not written for publication ;and are perhaps all the better for that; for the talk is free and racy, as will be seen from the following selections : That grey gull was still standing on one leg beneath my window, when I returned from dinner. I tapped at the sill to see if it would notice me at all. It seemed so completely absorbed that I was doubtful about its hearing the tap, but it immedi- ately looked up, and didn't seem at all displease.' at being disturbed. " You seem in a brown study," I said. The grey gull shook out its feathers slowly, and then settled down again on the leg which had been resting, and 1 half closing its left eye seemed to say, ‘" Yes, I was musing a bit about things." " What things," I said? " Oh, Parnell and Mr. Gladstone, and the Salva- 'lion Army, and the Congregational Union, etc." " Indeed," said I, "do you take much interest in them ? " " Well,' said the grey gull, " one has to pass the time somehow, and when I am tired of billing and cooing, and feeding, and splashing about and riding on the waves, I sometimes amuse myself by watch- ing the antics of you bigger gulls." "And what do you think about us ?" said 1? " Well," said the grey gull, " I think you are an unco squad' and mostly fools." "Humph !" I grunted, "and pray what do you think of Burns and Carlyle ?" "Burns." said the grey gull, "was a man whose failings didn't 'lean to virtue's side,' in the sense commonly attached to the words, but neither was he. as he described himself, a man with passions wild and strong.' He could not run in harness, lie had neither education nor cant enough to spoil his nature, which prevented him living thy rule, grave, tideless, bloodless, calm and cool.' But he loved the wee modest crimson-tipped flower.' The wounded hare touched his heart. He could sym- pathise with the mouse ids plough disturbed, 'Oppressed with grief, oppressed with care ' he was made to mourn,' but he never became so absorbed in his own misfortune as to forget to sympathise with the misery of any living creature. Carlyle was a different sort of man altogether. Much learning "filled him with self conceit, and regard for others was lost in his own self-importance." "But you will allow," I said, "that Carlyle was a moral man, while ncsone would claim so much for Burns."

The grey gull seemed to make several efforts to vomit. On regaining its composure, it said, "You must excuse ,tMe. The mention of that word moral' creates an uncontrollable sensation of nausea in my gizzard. Nine-tenths of those who use the word so glibly have no definite idea at- tached to it. It is mere fashionable cant to intro- duce it constantly into one's talk, and is intended by the unco guid ' and 'rigidly righteous' to im- ply that they themselves are highly superior people, and never, or at least, hardly over, do any- thing they shouldn't. Now, what do you under- stand by morality ?" "I am afraid," said I, "my acquaintance with morality is so distant and limited, that I can't say much about it, but I remember a definition of it I came across the other day—namely,morality is that which tends for the good of mankind." "I don't think that definition bad at all," said the grey gull, "but I think it has a very small accept- ance. At any rate,your species are daily and hourly doing things which ar,) inimical to the public wel- fare, but which no one ever seems to regard as immoral."

"You will excuse me," said I, interrupting, "but it is my tea time, and I must leave you." "Oh certainly," said the grey gun, "but I'll come round and have another chat with you some day," and it spread its wings and flew away to a flock of its mates, away off. * * if

Well caught !" exclaimed Ito the grey gull this morning, as be snatched a young fish out of the briny, which he had espied at a distance of thirty or forty feet above the water, and had dropped upon " like shot," and swallowed 'like lightning." Good busi- ness ! You did it as if '` to the manner born." _ . _

"Not bad at all—the fish I mean," said the grey gull. "The catching is nothing. The dexterity necessary, like ray feathers, came naturally, and is neither merit nor demerit of mine, lam a gull, and have the characteristics of a gull,for the same reason that Lord Derby is a lord and has the manners of one—my father was a gull. Mentioning Derby re- minds me that he uncovered a statue of John Bright in Manchester the other day. It is a curious thing that you lords of creation always erect statues, and render homage to those amongst you who fleeced you most—those whom we should delight to kill you delight to honour. If a man has plundered only a limited number of his weaker brethren, and to the extent of only a few thousands a year, you erect one statue to his memory. If he has robbed you wholesale, you increase the number of statues in proportion. An archbishop may have a couple ; a great warrior half-a-dozen, and an empe- ror half-a-score. Our species never erect any statues. If ever we do, it will not be in honour of those who plunder us, you bet. We may be fools, but there is a limit to our folly. When parasites attempt, as they frequently do, to fasten themselves upon us, wa simply kill them at once. The disposi- tion to lick the knife that draws our blood is un- known to tis, and, I hope, always will be. If some pretentious gull called itself a lord, and claimed the sole right of possession over three or four hun- dred square wiles of the sea, do you think we should tolerate it?" _ .
"And I don't see how it could enforce its claim," said I. _

"No fortunately for us we know nothing of the resources of civilisation of which you are so proud. Its organised means of tyranny and plunder are be- yond us—and no loss I think. To maintain that dominion' that pretentious gull would have to fight the rest of us individually, and en masse, and I well know what the end must be. Instead of that gull eating shrimp, shrimps would eat it." " And serve it right too," say 1. "John Bright," said the grey gull, " has been very much over-estimated. The politics of the Man- chester school, of which he was one of the chief apostles, were prompted mainly by commercial greed. The introduction of Free Trade was an Eldorado to cotton spinners and manufacturers. Their wealth increased by leaps and bounds, but they never manifested any particular desire to let their wealth-producing workpeople share in their prodigious gains. Wages in those days were low. The health conditions of the factories and sheds were anything but what they should be. And the housing of the people was such as is tolerated no- where now. But these things did not enter into the consideration of the Manchester school. Indeed when measures were brought into the House of Commons to improve the condition of things' their great opponents were the Manchester school of politicians, and first and foremost amongst them all was John Bright."
Bang went; rifle on the shore at this moment, and off went the grey gull,for though it loves gossip, it loves life still more. (To be continued.) • MAKING A PROFIT OUT OF SMOKE.

In an article in "The Smoke Fiend," "The Review of Reviews" says:—lt would really seem as if at last we were going to be rid of our great enemy, for we read that another inventor, Mr. Mond, of Messrs. Brunner, Mond, and Co., has invented a process by which smoke is not merely done away with, but converted into a source of profit. Mr. Mond burns his coal with artificial draught, and, conveying the gases into a chamber, he washes them with water spray. which causes every particle of soot to be deposited, and at the same time condenses and recovers the ammonia (a product of nitrogen and hydrogen) as well as the sulphurous fumes. To do this, however, and yet to get an equal efficiency of steam raising power, he has to burn 125 tons of coal in the place of 100 tons, and for every 125 tons of coal burned he recovers four tons of sulphate of ammonia. The fuel, if cheap (say ss. a ton), will cost £3l, and the sulphate of ammonia, at £l2 a ton, is worth £4B. If such results as these can be obtained the doom of smoke is sealed. _

That is, of course, true; but there is no neeessity of pitching our hopes so high. It is obvious that if sulphate of ammonia were produced on anything approaching to that scale, it would very soon cease to command the price which it now* fetches in the market. Still, even if the whole of the product of the combustion were not worth more than the .cost of the coal consumed, that might still appreciably diminish the coal bill. Whenever a manufacturer had a smoky chimney he would be regarded as a fool who had more money than brains, and self in- terest will effect what public spirit has utterly failed to do,

A very interesting illustrated pamphlet has been issued by Mr. Thomas Beecham, describing an ' M.P.'s visit to the pill manufactory at St. lielens. ' We extract the following:— From the engine-room we turned into the room in which the secrets of the establishment are kept : the masonic or " mixing-room." Here are weighed out and mixed the ingredients of which the Pill is composed, and from this it goes into the grinding room where the mass is reduced to fine powder by two heavy rollers which pursue the even tenour of their way in a large hopper. Like the mills of the gods, it grinds exceeding fine the mass of drugs which is mixed and sent up a hoist to the making- room at the top of the building, where it is turned into the consistency of dough. Pieces of this brown ' mass are put into a press, from which it is ejected I in twelve long narrow strips, which are cut into lengths of about a foot. The strips are laid in another machine, the double cylinders of which, by some mysterious evolution, cut them into proper shape and send them out id the form of Pills,at the rate of 15,000 per minute.

"And that is the Pill of commerce?" I asked,pick- ing up one of the boluses I had seen made. "I ana afraid," said my chaperone, "they would hardly pass muster in that condition ; there is a good deal to be done with them yet. They are quite as efficacious now as they will be later on, but we could not turn them out as they are." Then he ex- plained to me that as the Pills came from the se- cond machine they pass through a perforated metal revolver, so that all of a smaller than the regulation size fall through. It is next necesgary that those in any degree larger should be also removed. They are next placed on a smooth table and every imper- fect globule carefully removed by the boy-atten- dants. Not content with this,the accepted ones are then placed in another machine which empties them on a slightly-declined mechanical contrivance. Then our past particular pill producer has the pills placed into rounding machines, a combination of cogs and eccentrics, and any bolus which is not mathemati- cally perfect has its roundness so destroyed that it does not roll down the decline without a wobbling motion, which the trained eye of the youngsters soon detects, when the offending pill has to go through the whole process again until it passes muster. And now what comes next ?"

"They are put into those trays and left to dry." "Are there Pills in any of those trays ?" I en- enquired, pointing to piled-up rows of trays which extended along both sides of the wall. "Every one of them is full." " Full of Pills ?" I enquired incredulously. "Full of Pills," said Mr. Beecham in an amused tone.

"Then in the name of goodness," I exclaimed, "how many are there?" " What weight of Pills have we in the room to- day ?" he enquired of the foteman. "Eight tons and a half, sir," was the reply. "And how many Pills would that make ?" I asked. "I don't know, sir, but there are 85 dozen boxes in every stone." Out came my pencil and, by the aid of the multi- plication table and a piece of paper, I found that there were no fewer than seventy-seven million, six hundred and eighty-four thousand, two hundred Pills heinggot ready for shipment,and the machines were still in full blast!
"NEVER MIND THE MAN IN THE MOON." Don't worry your brain about the man in the moon, but study the man in your own suit of clothes.

If every individual person took the best possible care of himself, institutions of charity would soon go out of fashion. There's a good deal of sense in the saying that " Charity begins at home." When a man has got to swim or drown, he will at least make a laudable effort to swim. Perhaps we coddle ono another too much. As in the army, so in society—we depend individually upon the commander and the multitude. It's a bad thing, because it induces a man to trust to luck and to numbers and not to his own courage and wits. Con- sequently, when trouble comes, it finds us not ready : ignorant how to fight and conquer it. For example, here is our good friend, Mr. John Wil- kinson, of Norbury, Whitehurch, Salop, who not long ago said to an acquaintance.: " Lad I am done for." Why did he think so ? Because the doctors had given him up to die of consumption. Eaough to scare him if he really had consumption. But did he ? Ab, that is the question.

He tells his story thus: "I come," he says, "of a strong healthy family, and up to the spring of 1885 1 was always well. I could lift, run, and jump with any one, and walk thirty miles a day with ease. About April of that year I felt something coming over me which gradually fastened upon me. At first I felt dull, heavy, and tired, with a sinking all-gone sensation at the pit of the stomach, and pain in the side and between the shoulder-blades. My skin grew sallow, and the whites of my eyes were tinged with a yellow colour. I had a foul taste in the mouth, particularly in the morning. My mouth and teeth were covered with a thick slime, and a thin watery fluid came up from my stomach 'into my mouth.' "My appetite failed, and what little food I managed to eat gave me great pain. I had a tight feeling at my chest and round both sides as if I was held in a vice, and I got weaker and weaker and very low in spirits. There seemed to be no life or soul left in me.

" By-and-by I began to have a hacking cough, which made me loss a deal of sleep. Indeed, I could not rest at night on account of it. I would lie awake all night long coughing and spitting. As time went on I became so reduced I could scarcely get about. when I did ven- ture outdoors I had to be constantly stopping to rest, as walked along the lanes, for fear of falling. " I tried all kinds of medicines, and was under the doctor, but without getting relief. In this miserable way I dragged on for six months. All my friends and neighbours thought I was breaking up, and was not long for this world.

"One day a friend of mine Mr. Thomas Bateman,game- keeper, Marbury, seeing me so bad asked me how my complaint came on. I replied: •I am dons for : I shall never get well again, lad.' "Then he said, Don't say that until after you have tried Mother Seigel's Curative Syrup.' And he went on to tell me how this medicine had cured him after he was at death's door, and given up by the doctors as being in a consumption. So, to leave nothing undone, I sent to Whitehurch and bought the remedy. After taking three bottles all pais an sickness left vie; I could at anything, and the cough and the spitting, as well as the pain in the chest, left me, I was a well man. "I tell everybody how Mother Seigel's Syrup saved my life, and you are at liberty te publish my statement in order that any other sufferers may know what to, do.

(Signed) JOIEN WILKINSON, Shoemaker, Norbury, Whitchurch, Salop." The casea of these two men, Bateman and Wilkinson, were almost identical in symptoms and character. Both had indigestion and dyspepsia, both apprehended con- sumption, and both were happily cured by the same medicine. How many others, situated as they were, are there in this country? Hundreds of thousands Ab, the dreary, dreadful days they have to pass through, right on the road to the grave, for unhelped they must , surely die ! .* Are you, who read these lines, one of this suffering multitude? or do you know anyone who belongs to it? We say but a word to you—don't expect to get well through waiting. and vaguely hoping. Study the man in your own snit of clothes. Otherwise act on your own good judgment, and on the reputation of a remedy,which has such evidence to prove its power.

" CAPITAL " (MAT. It is practically settled that Mr, IL M. Stanley is to go out to the Congo in the interest of the Inde- pendent State before the close of the year, and will remain there for a lengthened period.

-- The new journal, "Prizes." claims to be the first in the field with a name for the torthcoming Inter- national Horticultural Exhibition. It proposes to replace that mouthful with the easy title of "The Gardenstafferies." But what of "The Celeries ?" The Mr. Duncombe who has just divorced his wife, i is in reality the Hon. Valentine Buncombe, third son of the Earl of Faversham; and the lady is professionally known as Miss Nelly Leamar, one of the 'sisters who used to warble "Why is the world so gay to-day ? " 'The Dean of Westminster, and Mrs. and Miss Bradley are staying at the Hotel Cap d'Antibes. The Dean has just returned from Egypt, which he has visited for the first time, and which he declares surpasses in interest and impressiveness anything he could have imagined from the descriptions and photographs. The Dean proposes to return to the Deanery, Westminster, very shortly. _

The other day we mentioned that the Trade and Labour Council of the golden city of Ballarat, Australia, had decided to place a portrait of Cardinal Manning in their council chamber. By Monday's mail we learn that a resident of Melbourne had offered the council a large painting of the Cardinal, but it was decided to decline the offer, it being the wish of the council to invite artists generally to compete, "in order to secure for the meeting- chamber a first-class portrait of the great champion of the labouring classes."

The general opinion of those best qualified to judge in the north of England is that the general Election will take place very soon; in all probabi- lity within six weeks, and that it will be sprung suddenly upon us. Whether this opinion be well founded or not, it is clear that those who express it believe it, for in South Yorkshire there is a general movement of preparation. The canvass books are prepared, and in many constituencies are all distri- buted amongst the canvassers, ready to be used at an hour's notice, and the committee-rooms are also engaged.

The Goupil Galleries were crammed. on Saturday afternoon, with a goodly company of guests, who surged too and fro, ti#is way and that, chatting and laughing, and every now and then getting a glimpse of Mr. Whistler's pleasing nocturnes, marines, and figure pieces, for the inspection of which they were primarily gathered together. One lady, well known in theatrical circles, was heard to remark at the top of her voice, that when she was invited to see "the famous Whistler's show," she thought she was going to hear Mrs. Shaw whistle. And so is James McNeill Whistler avenged.

That "picturesqueness "of the House of Lords, to which Mr. Chamberlain so complimentarily referred on Saturday night, may possibly be enhanced in the future by the presence of a peer of color. When the late Earl of Stamford went out to the Cape some years ago he espoused a black domestic, by whom he was in due course presented with a dusky son. Whether that son becomes the future Earl remains to be settled by an action at law, as the late Earl's brother, the Hon. William Grey, claims the title and estates, which are not larze, alleging informality in the deceased Earl's wedding, and consequent illegitimacy of his son.

-- The debate, on Monday, on the second reading of the Small Agricultural Holdings Bill drew forth two speeches of exceptional interest from compara- tively young members of the House, Mr. Henry John Cast, and the Hon. Charles Robert Spencer. Cust, who is the Tory member for the Stamford Division of Lincolnshire, is a young man in his thirty-first year, and is strikingly handsome. He has thick brown hair, and a head which might be a model for a Greek sculptor. He is highly popular in the House, and is reported to be the original of one of the heroes of Miss Broughton's novel, "Dr. Cupid."

Mr. Spencer, who replied from the Front Opposi- tion Bench to Mr. (Just, is the stepbrother and heir presumptive of Bail Spencer, and is one of the Radical Whips. He rarely speaks, but his remarks are always sensible and to the point. Mr. Spencer is well known for the height and matchless white- ness of his collars. He is one of the best-dressed men in Parliament. He is small in stature,but well proportioned. He has somewhat sandy hair scrupu- lously brushed down. Ile took the House by storm when he "Jam not an agricultural labourer." He dexterously covered his retreat by the qualify- ing remark, " I have, however, the honour of knowing many agricultural labourers."

--- I have often speculated (says a writer in the " Dwarf ") upon the ultimate destination of those white kid gloves which are presented to judges and recorders in comthemoration of maiden sessions. I have just acquired a little information about the custom of one popular recorder. When Mr. C. Gill is not holding briefs either at the Law Courts or the Old Bailey,he is presiding over the Quarter Sessions at Chichester, the fine old Sussex cathedral town. He has won several pairs of gloves from the clerk of the peace there,and he certainly does not preserve them in lavender, or deal with them in any such senti- mental manner. He calmly wears them out at the Covent Garden fancy dress balls

Princes and princesses are but human,and the first thing Prince George and Princesses Maude and Vic- toria did on arriving at the Cap Martin,was to rush down through the pine woods to the rocky sea shore to enjoy the fresh breezes from the blue Mediterra- nean. It was noticed, however, that since then, the conduct of the young people has been far more decorous. They drive out in the afternoon, and in the morning the Princesses sit and work or read in a favorite little kiosk in the hotel grounds over- looking the sea. The Prince of Wales, who is said to be a little bored with the strict domesticity ob- served at Cap Martin (within easy telephone of Monte Carlo, by the way), sometimes smokes his cigar there, or walks over to Menton° with Prince George.

Mr. Hefner, the Prince of Wales's courier, is, next to the royalties, by far the most important person- age at the Hotel Cap. He is a small dark-com- plexioned Austrian, with a slight black moustache, and has been the Prince of Wales's body servant for eight years. Most telegrams and letters pass through his hands, and he is the chief medium of communi- cation between the Prince and the outer world. He is stationed all day close to the Prince and Princess of Wales, and is in pretty constant request. Much heartburning and discontent have been creates by the appointment of Sir. J. E. Commerell over the heads of officers senior to him in the set' vice to the post of Admiral of the Fleet, rendered vacant by the death of the late Sir Provo Wallis. The secret of this appointment will be found in the fact that Admiral Commerell is a favourite at Court, having been Groom-in-Waiting to the Queen for five years, and that he is a favourite with Lord Salisbury, baying been Tory member for Southamp- ton from 1885 to 1888, and an obedient supporter of the Coercionist Government. He vacated his seat, which was supposed to be a safe Tory stronghold, on being appointed superintendent of the dockyard at Portsmouth. Southampton was, however, cap- , tured for the Radicals by Mr. Evans. The first ties in the Parliamentary golf handicap are finished. Several of the Lancashire members have come well out of their matches. Quite a number of them entered for the tournament, and so far Mr. Seton-Karr is the only one who has been knocked out. His defeat by Mr. H. Tollemache was quite unexpected. Mr. IL Tollemache is well known in Cheshire as an all-round sportsman, but he is a young golfer, whereas Mr. Seton-Earr, besides hav- ing a long-established name in the sporting world —he is, perhaps with one exception, the best shot in the house—has had years of practice at golf. Sir William Houldsworth and Mr. Shepherd-Cross have, however, done better for Lancashire than the member for St. Helens. Sir William is one of the cleverest players in the tournament, and he is well off with his handicap of sixteen. The first Lord of the Treasury ha a unfortunately been deprived of his game by the congestion of business in the house.

BY 141,LIAS WASSERMAN, Atakor of "Some Fisher Folk," "Judith," "Where the North Wind Blows," &c., tke.
'CHAPTER XXIY. MADAM IS DkdrlED.
For long, Lady Callerley hovered between life aud death; and nothing but the devoted care of tell, combined with her own perfect constitution, could have saved her.

It was strange to see how the strong character IA the fisher girl came out in the crisis. Even Sir Lancelot found himself looking to her now for advice and guidance. Since those very plain words she had spoken to him, he had gained an intense respect for her; and recognised, too, the fact that she understood his wife, Silvia, better • than anyone else had ever done. The agony of the mother bereft of her child— as he witnessed, it in the hour when he tried to Comfort her, and she put him and his consolation aside impatiently abided ever with him, and filled his heart with mingledpity and regret. It showed, too, what a treasure of love he had lost through the simple want of seeing that it was there.
So soon as he recognised that this love, which might have been his, had he cared to accept it, had died'still-bcrn ; he began, with a passion of sorrowful longing, to wish for it back again. . .

He would j-ree-P into the sick room, -Lind watch, the flushed face, and the vacant staring eyes of his wife ; listening patiently for hours together to her ravine: , Daring these times he must have beard many a word that stung him, but if so he made no sign. Whenever he came near, or touched Silvia at all In helping to raise her, a thing which he begged so humbly to assist in, that Bell consented once or twice ; . she would shudder away from him, or scream aloud in terror; until at last he was fain to draw sadly away for fear of doing her harm. When her time was up, the 'nurse left, having "mother engagement; and then Bell ruled supreme jnstead. Once Madam, offered to help, but' the girl looked her calmly in the face., "No, no, Madam ! ' Ye're not gaun to do ma work like ye did Mrs. Posset's !" Madan' started. What did the girl suspect ." How do you mean, Bell? I did' not help the woman, save with advice now and then; and that only. when it was asked for

Sirs. Breamish had wonderful command of tone, and there was not a trace of anxiety in her voice. But Bell noticed that her hand, resting upon the arm of the chair she was sitting on, trembled iuddenly as with ague. .• " Mebbe 'ay, and Mebbe no," said Bell, with obstinate incredulity, "but arm none so sure Lady SilvM'd be the better of any •advice from you. Ye're beat at givin' soothin' draughts to canny bairns, but ma patient's wantin' none o' them. Will ye take a hint, or must I ax Sir Lancelot dbout ":

•Madam seized her by the shoulders as she pre- tended to be leaving the room. . "You'll .not stir from here on any such friers errand I" hissed the lady, through her closed teeth. Even the fisher girl's brave spirit failed her, under the &woe malignity of the expression she saw ,in the handsome face so near her own . •
The mask had fallen, and the CaHarley temper Was written there in full.

"Take care whit you say, Belt Widdrington It is not always safe to brave me in the way you are doing now. lam not BO weak that I could not crush a creature like you if it were worth while. Do you hear me, girl? Don't make it worth while then—you understand?" Bell had recovered her equanimity. "Do yer worst," she replied in a steady voice, "so as ye leave yon bonny wee lady alone.", Madam did not answer. She was walking about the room with long, graceful, feline strides. It was the method she frequently used to calm her- self, and bring her rebellious temper under controL Presently she stopped and spoke again • but Bell noticed that she kept her eyes fixed on the ground, as though fearful they Might contradict her smooth words.

"You provoked me with your foolish suspicion, Bell Withirington, and I grew hot over it! Be- lieve me, I mean no harm to Lady Callerley—why should I? And I think she is fortunate in having such a faithful creature as yourself about her. Do, you not know that we made up our little differences long ago 1" ".Ay, an' another thing too I know, that ye kissed her just afore she was stabbed to the heart. Dinna waste yer time over me, Madam! Ye'll hiver make yer words ring true 'i' ma ears, sound they ever so softly. Let her alone and aw'll let you alone; cause what's done canna be undone ; and the knowledge of it it wauld take more mischief, encl mebbe punish the innocent for th' guilty !" So saying, Bell turned on her heel, leaving Madam standing there, consumed with impotent rage and hatred that could And no relief in action. When Lady Callerley was sufficiently: recovered , to leave her room, her husband carried her into the long room looking over the flower garden; and laid her down'gently into a big chair, from which she could see the snow-covered landscape outside. She shivered as she looked out, and turned quickly to the fire, blazing aria glowing in the big hearth, and filling the room with light and warmth.

"It looks so cold out there—always so cold and big and lonely" she said, with the fretful peevish- ness of a sick child, "do you remember the day we came. It looked like that then—only without the snow, I knew, I was coining to something sad and dreary; it was surely, a presentiment. That was what made me feel so afraid !"

Sir Lancelot sighed. Would nothing now induce her to care for her home—and for her husband? Ile sat down beside her and. took her hand; and even as he did so was acutely conscious of a shud- dering movement of repugnance on her part. "Poor little girl! Poor little Silvia ! Cannot I 60 anything to make you more contented with life, dear? It was selfish of me to tie you. down to such a dull home and husband; but it is no use talking of that now! Tell me if I can do anything to please you ?" A wistful expression crept into the blue eyes raised to his. Only for a moment, though, and then they were turned away impatiently. "Yes, there is something that would make me happier and more contented—only I know that you won't do it !" ' "Silvia, you wrong me. I have promised." "Send for Teddy, then." "Is that all ?" asked Sir Lancelot, laughing. "Toddy shall certainly be forthcoming, if I have to go to town and fetch him myself. But I happen to have news of him to-day, news which makes me fancy he will not object to leave town for a while."

_ "Another scrape?' "Not a very serious one, Silvia, so you need not disturb your mind about it! All the same he will be out of mischief here." Lady Callerley's spirits rose to effervescing point at once. She clapped her hands with delight, and began. planning a hundred schemes for Teddy's amusement and edification. What room he should occupy, what horse he should ride, what places he tinouid be taken to see—all these occupied the affectionate sister very pleasantly for the rest of the day, and kept her from brooding over her loss. Perhaps, too, a hint of Bell's to the effect that Mrs. Breamish would not be sorry to see her cousin's wife sink into a state of chronic invalidism, helped to rouse her. If Madam wished for her death, and there was small doubt in Silvia's mind, spite of that kiss of forgiveness, that such was the case—why, there would be some fun in disappoint. ing such wishes ! Bell was too conscientious to give a hint of the sort without sufficient grounds for it, and Lady Callerley was now entirely swayed by Bell's opinions, and trusted in her completely.

CHAPTER XXV. LOVE AND PRIDE. Low down in the heavens, a cold February sun was shining into a secluded dene, EOM few miles inland from Breamish. Along the bottom of this ravine ran a small hill burn, which ultimately emptied its tiny waters into the larger Yarrop stream. • A more secluded spot could not well be found in the whole of the country side; and perhaps for that reason, Bell Widdrington and Dick Daglish had chosen it for a trysting place; and were walk- ing there under the trees or sitting upon the big boulders that studded the banks. Some 'steep fells were above the dene, and it was away across giese fells that the cottage lay where Dick was noii in hiding. For Dick was at this time under a cloud; and obliged to keep away from Breamish, and all the dear delights of his sweetheart's society, save in some such stolen moments as These. The revenue officers' pursuit of the free-traders ila colaSeUrAo aL a &pare** igeittla

qinekeriecl. 'flerably during the last few days; which oast u4i them the suspicion of foul play. Two,-,otthrOe days previously one of the most efficient ~metribers of the coastguard had dis- appeared in a mysterious manner. It was conjectured amongst his fellows that poor James—the missing member—must have been murdered, although up to the present time no trace of him could be found. He had been of an excessively energetic temper and of incorruptible honesty; which said qualities had brought him into frequent collisien, with the smugglers. Indeed one or two of these were well known to have borne him a grudge. Amongst these Dick Daglish was unfortunately conspiouous for his reputation. Upon one occasion, when a secret storage place was discovered through the keen watchfulness of James, Dick, in a fit of temper, had threatened to wring the neck of the too vigilant exciseman; and this threat having been publicly uttered, told heavily against the smuggler, although it was never meant, and was forgotten as soon as uttered. Except in the way of fair fight in defence of a valu- able cargo, Dick would not have hurt a fly ; being one of the most good natured and kind-heartedmen in. existence, - •,. But this Was notknown 'Save to his friends; and his reputation for reckless daring and audacity as a prominent free-trader and skipper of the Bonny, Bess, caused suspicion to point him out as the, most probable culprit.. It said a great deal for Bell's affection towards him that she condescended to meet him in this secret and, clandestine manner,—she ' who hated everything that savoured of concealment. She was proud of her love, and longed to be able to avow it before all the world. ,The wooing of this strangely matched' and sin- gularly handsome pair did not run very smoothly, or with any great rapidity. It is very. difficult for a woman to accept the bitter truth that the lover, who is for ever m her thoughts, does not, and by nature cannot, take his passion in the same continuous way as she herself does. In all probabilitjr he, while they are to- getherigites himself up ,to it.. the more' com- pletely of the two. Therefore does it seem incred- ible to her that its power should be so fleeting. ' ' She fondly pictures him as dwelling upen her words, her looks her smile's; .at times when in the prose of life he has forgotten the poetry of love. V A thousand other matters he does not mention to her, occupy Ing mind instead. The' old story of the real against the ideal.' • And after, all it is only the natural course of things if women wouldlut•ailmit it. If they reflected they would recognise the, impossibility of its being otherwise. If men went dreaming and mooning about, in place of acting and working, and leaving love to their moments of leisure; it would interfere to a ridiculous extent with the work of the viorld. •! Bell Widdrington was a very sensible girl indeed, but to counterbalance her extra store •of coinmon- , sense, she had all the unreasonableness of a woman in love. ' • ' Oh either, side a' tough fight was raging between love and pride . . • Not unnaturally, Bell declared that if Dick were as much in love with her as his professions gave her to believe, he would accede at once to her wishes ; and, giving up the smuggling, settle down to 'patrimony and fishing life. Instead of this he shilly shallied over the business in a fashion that roused her temper and her pride both.

Now when he was with Bell, Dick forgot every- thing else ; and would even have heard of the wreck of the Bonny Bess with equanimity, so long as he could steal his arm around her firm yet supple waist, and gaze Unchecked into her glorious eyes. But alas, sad as it is to have to acknowlege the fact, there were certainly times,.when,in the wild excitement of running a cargo and of cheating the revenue officers, he forgot eyes and Waist and girl altogether, as completely as though they had never existed.

Without doubt there was a strange fascination about free-tradineri especially to venturous spirits; and Dick succumbed to this fascination time after time; weakly deferring his purpose of giving up the life and settling down to rushing and matrimony until after another voyage. So it came to pass that matters were strained and uncomfortable between the lovers,, and that they were still in the same position of a year before. .

Ye're as cold as a stone, ma lass," said Dick reproachfully, after a lengthened pause in the con- versation, a pause he higl endeavoured to utilise in an osculatory manner, and in which he had suffered repulse, " Night; after night aw've hung about th' big house, hopin' ye might steal out for a word; but no! Ye never took a bit o' notice o', ma signal, though aw whistled till aw was tired, and they must ha' heered.rae indoors. • Mebbe they thowt the spring had come, and ,browt the inavises?" , "Aw couldn't get away fm' Lady Callerlef, even if aw'd been so minded !"
"Darrsay ! But things have changed a bit, ma woman! Once on a time aw'd ha' been first we ye,.Ltidy Callerley or no!" . -

_ No stop that jearous minded nonsense, Dick, or ye and me'll hey a quarrel 1 If there's anybody has a right to complain o' bein' neglected, it's not you. What do aw come and meet ye here for, now th' excise cheps hey made it too hot for ye doom P th' village yonder, if aw dinna care for ye? But if aw was a man and the lass aw went wi had to meet me on the sly, and to give up lots o' things for ma sake, aw wad try and make her happy while she was wi' me 1."
Bell's head was lifted high with a sense of injury, and Dick grew ashamed of his ill temper.

"liw've been bothered and plagued to death this week, Bell, ma canny woman, so ye mun just excuse me bein' a bit short. An' ye are cool, ye know. Come hinny, give us a kiss, and make it up, and aw'll try hard te be patient !" Her cheek looked rich and tempting, and he managed to touch it with his lips,, but she was in no mood for fooling and drew off qulckly. " Aw'm gettin' sick o' this," she exclaimed, with sudden impatience. "It seems to me that ye're all tarred wi' th' same brush, .you men folk, ivory man jack o' ye, fra' th' highest to th' lowest rts self, self, self, wi' all on ye. There's Sir Lance- lot up at Seaton Callerley, he lets his wife. pine liersel' pretty nigh to death, wantin' his love, and now just when she's gettin' used to bein' without it, he turns round and would lick the very ground under her feet. It's the laws o' contrary that rules the lot o' ye I" . . "That's not the way wi' me, Bell! Aw'rn fair ower wi' love, and ye Wilma hey owt to do wi't ? It's all th' other way wiv us, ye see." •` Love? Ay, what ye call love mebbe?" " Prove it, ma beauty !" 1 "An' how am aw te de that!" she asked, with scornful incredulity. "Marry me, and see what a good husband aw'll be to ye !" <.
take me for a fool? If ye like the smugglice ower weel to give it up afore y've gettin' tne, what chance will there be oye cloin' what aW wish, after ?"
Dick hung his head. He recognised the force of Bell's word, and found them difficult to answer.

"Bell" he said at last, in a humble sort of way, " Aw'm feared aw've not done reet in tyin' ye doon te sic a harum-scarum sort o' chep ? Avem not good enough for ye, and that's a fact! But aw'm no for givin' ye up, hinny, for all that. The idea of ye marryin' anybody else sends me wild, aa can tell ye." " Aw'll never do that, Dick, thou may lay thy life o't !" replied Bell, melted in an instant by his humility, "though often it gets wearisome waitin' on thee, and fancyin' thou doesna' care enough about me to settle down like a decent canny man, be content. But avr euddent bide to think of another lad, for all that 1" Her voice was soft and affectionate, and once more Dick's arm stole around her, and drew her towards him. This time she did not repel th% caress.

The dark . outline of horse and rider appeared flattened and 'clearly defined against a saffron sky; a sky where long straight bars of grey lay across it, near to the horizon. A touch of frost crisped and sweetened the air, and brought every slight sound into prominence. Dick was thinking much of his sweetheart, and a little of his own unworthiness. Warmly within him glowed the freshly renewed flame of his love. It was always a trial to part with Bell, and it was more a concession on her keen sense of the danger he was in, than any active dread of the same danger he himself felt, which held him back from accompanying her, to at least withia sight of Seaton Callerley. As he slowly rode oar-lards ftooha. to his home, he fell completely under the influence 11; of the twilight hour, and grew dreamy and "1 meritaL 'Pleasant day visions wrapped him rotT,' ancUrendered him, at least for the time insensibic to all the dangers and difficulties of time, PreBellt* position. • ow sweet it would be to have a home, a real ho e; of his own ! en the humdrum tiresome business of a fish ts er life !would be tolerable under these circumstances. Ile saw it all as-in a dream. The honest, whole- some, hard-working future that might be his the Choosing. Tha•beautiful face looking out of the dissr ~_' • • ./ ) welcome his return. The clean swept hearth wit" ..;: a bitight fire ',burning there; the firelight glancisg upon a ripp,cheek, and upon golden hair; Pet'hle - —who knows ?—A wee toddler playing upon tnn , floor, holding out plump, chubby, dimpled arms Daddy, and begging to be lifted upon his shoal Hark! What sound was that, breaking in suddenly and SO unpleasantly upon his delightf A subtle consciousness of danger, a preeentitne,t' perhaps, still hovered about -Dick; and made n' suspicious of every unusual noise. il This sound of the trotting of a horse upo frost-bound road, distant but unmistakable, fell 0a Ms ears with a very disagreeable sensation,becao,l ; der. • , the ,presence of a horseman, upon that lonely t°6 -I was an exceedingly rare occurrence. , ~,,,,- ,•,4 Dick began' to turn over in his own railla,',,,, question as to who the rapidlY advancing equest"a— ' could possiblf be. .• Farmer Todd was the tenant of the moorland farm which. he had just passed, and the roal turning down to the house lay like a silver ribanu ---- ..among tha dark grass. This farm house SY'as place• where Jack BrMrctisli had his tiny garret; ' s room, and the people there were as fond of though he had in truth belonged to them. • P, Dick ,Daglisli knew the good farmer and Ids.oll° s well, and had mEny a Vino, after the mannev a? thu times, made free use of the stables. If Farmer Tiidirg,of wind of the pl.Obable landing of a cargo from the-BonnY Bess, he carefully forgot to lock his stable, door, and as carefully refrained from listening,,to any unwonted noises there might ' be during the -night • and. if he found his horses 401 tired and used hp in ;hamming, he would merely i grin to himself, because he knew right well that a ,4 keg Of 'spirits •or a bale of silk would .be hidden, , somewhere about, under a truss of hay, or in Scar' ' " such innocent covert. , ' ' ' la .. Therefore whei)Dick began to fear that he won- be hard pressed by his pursuers,,he thought longi , 1 ingly of the farmhouse ; and wondered if it won' , ~. have been wise to have turned in there, and trusted. • to the inmates to conceal, and to throw dust int° the eyes of those who came after him. His mare had done a hard day's work alresellfr'' ' • and waa completely blown. , It would therefore be both cruel and 'useless t° • urge her into a gallop. What was he to do! , He glanced despairingly around. 1,, a ' ,itt the first place, was it possible that he -s up to the present, escaped the notice of the horo- • man following him? He had been riding along in a very leistirell fashion, and to save the mare as much as 0551 b e: had kept upon the grassy edges of the road. If so, might there not be a chance of hidill''' setting those behind him get ahead, and then strike across country and so steal away from the chase? Ho glanced dubiously at the tree under I°' ) shadow he was riding. These trees formed part of a small plantatir s , i % thickly set together; so thickly indeed that, al spite of the fact that they were shattered and tor° by the winds which blew so continuously in this exposed situatitni, they 'would yet form a veil fail. covert. After a little deliberation Dick decided that his Only chance lay in concealing himself there. Sheltered there, if his horse did iffit hetraY hil by neighing, he might, for the time being t' least, manage to elude his pursuers. The branches of the trees drooped low, hll,,ttiltoe. mare was used to being led under trees, an" all sorts of strange hiding places. HOUSE OF LORDS.—MONDAY. The Lord Chancellor took a seat on the Woolsack at: a guarter-past four. THE FIGII Earl of Kimberley TING IN APRICA.—Lord KNTJTSFORD trild the „ that in the recent attack on Tambi, jn 'ale neighbourhood of Sierra Leone, a British officer and! %member of the police force were killed, while twenty- ! ur persons were wounded. TUE RAINIIILL MURDERS.
DEEMING'S CAREER OF CRIME. FURTHER REVELATIONS.

Frederick Deeming—or Williatias,as at first he was and is still more generally named—was on Saturday brought, before the magistrates at Perth, Western Australia, on the charge of having murdered his reputed wife, Emily Mather, tf Rainhill, 'whose body was recently found buried in cement in a house at Windsor, near Melbourne. He was remanded. The police at Sydney, New South Wales, prompted no doubt by the discoveries at Mel- bourne and Rainhill, are making an examination of thq' house occupied by Deeming or Williams during his stay in that city. The interest of the public in the Rainhill horrors and discoveries shows no signs of abatement. In the meantime, however,the police have made no further investigations in the villa or its immediate precincts ; and though numerous stories are afloat, no fresh light' has been thrown on the ,date, manner, and motive of the murders. From other quarters, however, both at home and abroad, are telegraphed details of Deeming's doings, and suspicions of his deeds.. At West Hartlepool he seems to have carried on, with partial success,a game of swagger and deception. As' to his cafeer in South Africa, it is said that his name was well known at Johannesburg in connection with some extensive jewel- lery swindling and the robbery of £3,000 from a Cape Town jeweller in the Transvaal; 'while it is grimly pointed out that during his stay at Johannesberg, which , lasted a month, two mysterious 'murders occurred. • Many of the articles found in his luggage at Perth, Western Australia, and mentioned in a telegram giving an account of the police court proceedings, have been recognised by the Mather family. The autograph album and the address-book were particularly remembered, the names of Rainhill relatives and friends being written in them just before Deemilag's bride left the village. The heavy box, containing the apparel of the woman and children murdered in Dinham Villa' is to be sent back to St: Helens from Ply Mouth, and will be placed in the care of the Widnes police. One of the latest stories about Deeming is that he stayed at an hotel in Chester in 1889, purchased a double-barrelled hammerless gun from a local gunsmith, and ordered two hundred cartridges which had to be specially manufactured. These cart- ridges were forwarded to "Mr. Lawson, care of Mrs. Matheson, New Walk, Beverley," and their arrival was acknowledged by Mr. Gray on behalf of "H. Lawson, Esq." The acknowledgment was written on foreign notepaper, which bore the heading" Mount House Farm, Queensland, seat of H. Lawson, Esq., breeder of sheep and racing stock." In Adelaide and Capetown Deeming is suspected of robbery, if not of more heinous crime.

div.head: VISITORS AT RLINHILL.
div.p: VISITORS AT RLINHILL.

Thousands of people visited Rainhill on Sunday, and the usually quiet village was turned into a pande- monium for the time being, and there were several fights. The Vicar alluded to the tragedy in his sermon, and said it was suggested after Deeming left Dinham Villa that the house should .be purchased for a vicarage, but fortunately the idea was abandoned. Mrs. Mather, mother of the woman murdered in Australia, states that she did all she could to break off, the engagement, but Miss Mather had every ..confidence in Williams, and would hear nothing against him. A letter had been re- ceived stating that Deeming in October last robbed a London firm of goods to the value of £I3 Iss. Deem- ing told one gentleman resident in Rainhill that he was a nephew of Sir Wilfrid Lawson, and that Sir Wilfrid had paid for his education. He was well known in Liver- pool to several people, and became known to a young lady employed at one of the theatres. He said ho had been a ship's carpenter, but had made a pile of money in Australia, and produced diamonds and nuggets of gold. He made a young lady several presents of a valuable description, but she had an aversion to him,, and when he proposed marriage she declined, though her friends wished her to accept him. At this time the "Jack the Ripper" murders were being perpetrated,and Deeming was very fond of expatiating upon them and the bungling way, as he said, in which the murders were done. It has transpired that the Mather family were possessed of property, and Deeming wag anxious that it should be sold ; but roma members o the family were opposed, and a correspondence took place on the subject.

div.head: CFIRONOLOGICAL TABLE.
div.p: A CFIRONOLOGICAL TABLE.
The following table shows in chronological order the events in the career of the accused under his four aliases

Frederick Bailey Deeming married Miss Mary James. Leaves England for Cape Town lBBO Deeming joined by his wife (now identified as Mary James) in Sydney lBB2 Deeming receives six weeks' imprisonment for theft Ableonds from Sydney on dirge of fradu- lent insolvency lBB6 Returns to England (11th of August ?) and to Birkenhead, leaving that place and his wife after the birth of his fourth ' child, about four months after- wards Arrives in Hull, and obtains jewellery on false pretences, March 15 lB9O Marries Miss Matheson at Beverley. Yorkshire, and deserts her a fortnight ' afterwards Arrested at Monte Video Tried at Hull Assizes on a prosecution of the jewellers, and sentenced to nine months' imprisonment October 1890 Arrives at Rainhill July 1891 Visits Birkenhead, taking Mrs. Deeming and the children with him to Rainhill. Supposed murder August 1891 Marries Miss Mather at Rainhill Sept. 1891 Arrives with his wife in Australia Murders Mrs. Williams, December 25 (supposen) Arrested when on the eve of a fourrh marriage March 1892 OTHER REVELATIONS. On Tuesday Rainhill resumed almost its normal appearance, public excitement having to a great extent subsided. The adjourned inquest next Monday is anti- cipated with great interest. The police are still engaged in perfecting their case. A St. Helens jeweller on Tues- day stated that at the end of July last Deeming instruct- ed him to make a scarf ring, supplying several valuable stones and nuggets of gold for the purpose. Because it was not finished on the appointed day Deeming, who said he was an army offider, got into a great rage. When the tradesman offered to send the ring to any address I Deeming replied that he had no fixed address. On three occasions when he called a lady dressed in blank and wearing a veil accompanied him.: A portion of the furniture sold by Deeming when giving up Dinham Villa was purchased by Mr. Pickering, Mrs. Mather'a son-in-law. • The result of the search amongst these articles on Tuesday was the discovery of a spade which had been purchased at Mrs. Maher's shop. The cement was still adhering to it, and an exam- ination showed that upon the handle were spots, evidently bloodstains. The spade has been banded over to the police, and will be subjected to is microscopical examination. It will be remembered that Deeming made an extor- tionate demand upon the London and North-Western Railway Company for £250 compensation for alleged damage to a pipture while in transit from London to St. Helens. He subsequently placed the matter in the hands of Messrs. Cook and Son, solicitors, St. Helens, but when ho. found the railway company, were not in- clined to comply with his -request for conipensation to the extent demanded he offered to accept £5O in cash if the matter was immediately settled, as he was going abroad. Deeming never received the £5O, nor anything for that matter, but a day or two before he left London for Australia he wrote to his solicitors :-39, Finsbury Square, October 17, 1891. Mr. Cook. Sir,—Received your letter ; also t4e picture. We have decided to stay in England until the affair is settled, so the above ad- dress mill find us.—Yours truly A. 0. WiLraairs." In- stead of staying in England "until the affair was settled," be evidently, finding the railway company were not prepared to admit his claim, seems to have thought better of his intention ; and perhaps the fear of some damaging discoveries at Rainhill may have in- fluenced his mind at that particular time. A Hull correspondent says it appears that the officer of the Hull police force, Detective-Sergeant Grasby, who brought Deeming, alias Lawson, from Monte Video, on the charge of false pretences at Hull, had by no means'a pleasaatlask. It was clear he would have made a des-
DEEMING
LAWSON ...
WILLIAMS
SWANSTON

berate attempt to escape at the ports of ealj had he, been allowed the opportunity, but he was not, and the officer was very glad when he safely landed his prisoner at Southampton and had finally lodged him in the Hull gaol. While on the voyage Lawson smoked heavily, and talked a great deal about himself and the deeds he had performed. Be spoke of fights he had taken part in, and of people be had killed when so engaged. He also told Sergeant Grasby he had amassed a fortune by sheep-raising at Bockhampton, and that he had likewise been lucky as a miner. It was stated the other day that he had in his possession a valuable gold repeater watch in which was an inscription purporting that the watch had been given to " Frederick Deeming " for" meritorious services" at Johannesburg. It has transpired that he obtained the watch by false pretences at Johannesburg, and had the inscription placed in it, stating that it was for presenta- tion to a Mr. Deeming. He was at that time passing under another name. In a letter which was published on Tuesday it was stated that he had obtained possession of certain other jewellery at Capetown. This, it appears, comprised the Masonic jewels he wore when he had his portrait taken at Antwerp.

HAD DEEMING AN ACCOMPLICE? In St. Helens the theory of Williams having a confe- derate or confederates is being accepted. The disap- pearance of the man who forged the cheque on Parr's Bank in the name of James Howarth and Co., who sup- plied ,the cement, and who gave tickets with their printed name on. lends colour to this view. The man had made inquiries at some stables as to the trade done by Mr. Berry, and when he walked into the shop in Tontine-st. and gave Mrs. 'Berry an order for £5 ss. worth of provender he said he knew they did a good business, and supplied both the St. Helens Corporation and Colonel R. Pilkin,gton, of Rainford Ball, with pro- .
