yanifer, Mrs. Derry,_. with characteristic `sbieltr.dness, was not to be caught with the £l7 cheque on Parr's Bank, and refusedld £1.).).55. change.. The same man called at the establishment of Alderman Wilcock,in Baldwin-st., on the same cti.y, and inquired the price of provender, but he 'evidently felt It would be risky to' offer the cheque to the manager, and left, saying he would send an order up lie told the manager he came from Rainhill, and to Mrs. Berry he said he lived oppo- site the Derby Arms, Rainhill, but 'there is no such house..

div.head: ALBERT DEEMING'S DREAIVI.
div.p: ALBERT DEEMING'S DREAIVI.

Another telegram says that Albert Deeming states that the dream he spoke of at the inque4 was based upon actual experience. When the murdered woman arid children left Birkenhead they had a large quantity of clothing made there, including night-dresses. It was the bodies lying in these night-dresses he saw in the vision, and this was the actual fact when ha viewed the corpses at Dinham Villa. Every article of clothing possessed by the murdered woman can be identified. which is important in view of the contents of the boxes at Plymouth. Inquiries made on Saturday show that the three . _ . .
brotiiers Deeming, who reside' at Birkenhead, are all suffering from prostration owing to the terrible revel- ations about their brother, Frederick Deeming a has . . . .
Williams. One brother wag' so seriously ill that a doctor was in constant attendance,and his clergyman remained with him a good portion of the night.
PROOFS OF TEIE PRISONER'S GUILT IN AUSTRALIA. IMPORTANT ADMISSION By DEEEMING.

PERTH (Wasxxax Axismama), TUESDAY.—Swanston, alias Williams, alias Deeming, has been positively iden- tified as Williams, the man who lived at Windsor and whose wife was murdered there, by persons who were well acquainted with him. When the prisoner found that further dissimulation was useless he acknowledged that he was Williams, but declared that he was not guilty of the murder of his wife, and attributed the crime to a man whom he did not name,but who,he said, wag a lover of his wife. Further researches among the prisoner's luggage have, however, disclosed convincing proofs of his guilt. Aindrig other things, a pair of trousers which bear palpable stains of blood and cement have been discovered. At present all knowledge of the ghastly discoveries at Rainhill has been scrupulously kept from him. , MaLaourimi, TUESDAY.—The inquest on the body of the woman known as Emily Williams, wife of Frederick Deeming, discovered at a house at Windsor, was re- sumed to-day. A large number of the general public were present, and the inquiry excited the greatest inte- rest. The jury proceeded to Windsor to visit the scene of the discovery, and on their return, after some formal evidence had been given, the inquest was adjourned till April 5, pending Deeming's arrival from Perth. PERTH (WESTERN AUSTRALIA), TUESDAY.—A detective arrived here to-day from Melbourne, bringing with him a gentleman named Hirschfeldt, who was a fellow-pas- senger with Deeming on board the Kaiser Wilhelm If. on the trip out from England last November, and who now came forward for the purpose of giving 'evidence as to the alleged identity of the man now in custody with his former acquaintance. When brought face to face with the prisoner Mr. Hirschfeldt had no hesitation in identifying him. During the interview the accused was perfectly cool and self-possessed. He has been kept in ignorance of the discoveries made in England since his arrest, and is still under the impression that be is only called upon to answer for the Windsor crime. After his positive identi- fication he admitted that he was Williams,but protested that he was innocent of his wife's murder' and went so far as to suggest another theory. He had, he said, quarelled with his wife on account of her entertaining improper relations with another man, and in his belief it was this clandestine lover who had done the deed. Since his arrest the prisoner's health has undergone considerable alteration. He has lost his appetite and become extremely restless, especially during the night time. The orison doctor has caused him to be supplied with stimulants.

Fresh batches of important new discoveries have been made during the search among the prisoner's luggage. These include a sponge saturated with blood, a long knife covered with bloodstains, a -pair of trousers be- smeared with blood-marks and cement, a small heavy keen-edged plated battleaxe, a photograph of a cottage with a woman standing at the gate, the name "J. B. Deeming" being inscribed on the back of the card, and the certificate of the prisoner's marriage with Miss Mather. The certificate is dated " Rainhill, September 22, 1891, and the names of the contracting parties are given as Albert Williams, bachelor, and Emily Mather, spinster. It is expected that in the course of to-day the accused will be again brought before the magistrate and remitted to the Supreme Court at Melbourne.

div.head: FURTHER EXCAVATIONS._
div.p: FURTHER EXCAVATIONS._

The police made extensive excavations of the floors of Dinham Villa, the grounds, and the stable, but nothing of a suspicious nature, was discovered. The police had two motives in view in their excavations, to discover further remains, if any, and to present to the sight of the jury next Monday, the block of cement in which the bodies were encased. The coal vault, scullery, and coachhouse were each opened by the police, but their search Was in vain, and they a e now satisfied that they have got to the full extent of Deeming' p murders at.Rain- hill. A barmaid at the Commercial Hotfil, on Wednesday, identified a photo of. Mrs. Deeming as the lady who twice visited the inn for refreshments in company with the murderer, he passing her off as his sister on each occasion. A letter has been received at the Commercial Hotel bearing the Huddersfield postmark, and addressed to "F. B Deeming." Mr. Short, landlord of the Com- mercial Hotel, Rainhill, on Wednesday received three letters from Deeming, written .before his arrest in Aus- tralia. The contents of these letters will be made known at the inquest.

div.head: RETURN OF DEEIVIING'S BOX.
div.p: RETURN OF DEEIVIING'S BOX.

Deeming's box, which was despatched to Plymouth from Rainhill in the name ot.Wilson and was only un- earthed last week at the London and South-Western Company's goods statiln, arrived at Widnes on Wednes- day. The box is one of dealt and is Bft. 7th. long and 21t. 21n. wide. The depth is Vt. Bth. It was very securely fastened. When the box was opened in the presence of Superintendent Keigialey, Inspector Pattin- son, and several officers, it was found to contain princi- pally clothing. No doubt remains in the mind of the police here that the box belonged to Deeming, and that the clothing is that of the Rainbill victims., The emptying of the box occupied a considerable time, each article being written down and minutely insrcted as it was taken out of the box. The friends and relatives of Miss Mather are very indignant at Deeming's foul aspersion oh her character as to the cause of her murder in Austra- lia, he alleging she was unfaithful to him. They say they received a letter signed by the murderer days after he had murdered his wife at Windsor full of kindly ex- pressions and intimating their approaching departure for Hong Kong, addiag that they would write at each port of call. DINHAM VILLA TO BE DEMOLISHED.

• Mrs, Haves the landlady of Dinham Villa, in the course of an interview on Thursday, stated that it is her intention to demolish the notorious villa, the scene of the Rainhill murders. The keys are at present in the hands of the police, and nothing will be done until all criminal purposes are served. The moment, however, she regains possession of her property it Will be razed to the around, and another villa built on or close to the site.

The Thursday half-holiday was the cause of a Urge influx of-visitors to the- kdene of the-Minn/ tragedy; The villa was stormed, and the policeman in charge could not resist the crowd bent on satisfying their curiosity. They rushed into the kitchen of Dinhatn Villa, there to satisfy their desire of seeing the graves.

div.head: CEMENTED FLOOR IN AUSTRALIA.
div.p: A CEMENTED FLOOR IN AUSTRALIA.

PERTH WESTERN AUSTRALIA, THURSDAY.-It has been discovered that the floor of the cottage which " Swans- ton " occupied at Southern Cross.where he was arrested, has been taken up, and the excavations made under- neath , filled up'with cement, in the same manner as in the case of the houses at ttainhill and Windsor. Digging operations will be begun at once, as it is thought ex- tremely probable that a considerable quantity of gold which the prisoner is suspected of having pilfered while employed as engineer at Fraser's Geld Mine will be found concealed there.
WARRINGTON WESLEYAN QUARTERLY
MEETING.

' The Wgisleyan quarterly meeting of the Warring- ton circuit was held at Bold-street Wesleyan School, on Monday. After the usual tea, the chair was taken by the Rev. J. flannel!, who was supported by his colleagues, the Revs. A. Freeman and T. Ross •, the circuit stew,ards, Messrs. W. Silcock, and E. Richard- eon; and a large number of church officers from all parts of the circuit. The financial statement showed a balance in the hands of the stewards after all claims had been met. The Chairman submitted the numerical state- ment, of which the following are the more prominent , features 1---Church members, 888 ; candidates for mem- bership,ss ; removed to other cirpuits, 10; deaths, three; lapsed, 13; new members received, 22. The Rev. T. Ross presented the annual report of the day and Sunday schools ; also the report of the Bands of Hope and Adult Temperance Societies, all of which evidenced steady growth. The Rev. John Kirtlan of Sevenoaks, was unanimously invited to succeed the Rev. J. Gunnell in the superintendency of the circuit at the next Confer- ence. Both the Rev. A. Freeman and the Rev. T. Roes received a cordial vote of thanks for their faithful ser- vices in the past year, and were heartily invited to stay a taint year: In each case the invitation was accepted: The resolutions embodying the thanks ' and invitation were spoken to with great warmth* and appreciation by the Chairman, Messrs. Richardson, Cook, Place, Davey, Taylor, Weaver, Evans, and others. Various matters affecting the welfare of the circuit were discussed, and a very pleasant meeting was brought to a close soon after nine.

In the afternoon of the same day, the annual general trustees' meeting was held,at which all the trust estates of the circuit were brought under careful review, and the income and expenditure of the year was reported. The trustees were gratified to learn that of the 20 chapels and schools in the circuit, several report a balance in hand on the year's working, while only two are encumbered with more than a small debt on current account. The following places have greatly enlarged or improved their trust property lately : Lymm, £350; Padgate, £650 ; Penketh, £1,200. A new Sunday school, with class- room, is in course of erection at Sankey Bridges, to cost £1,400.
WARRINGTON WORKING - MEN'S INFIRMARY COMMITTEE.

A special meeting of this committee was held on Monday even i ing, n the ![own Hall. Mr. John Roberts occupied the chair, and there was a fair attendance. The Crtinimsar remarked th at that was the first meet- ing since the re-formation of the Working-men's Com- mittee. Speaking with regard to the work of the com- mittee, he considered that it was very satisfactory. Be- fore the formation of the committee the contributions amounted to between £5O and Tee a year. For the year 1891 the money collected amounted to OM es. 100., and in addition to that they were to receive £l7 103. 3d. from the Cheshire Lines Company. If possible, he hoped they would this year increase the amount collected from £491 es. 10d. to £450. (Applause.)—Mr. John Taylor, the deputy chairman of the commit- tee, said he would be willing to resign his position in favour of Mr. Burton, who was a repre- sentative of large ironworks, viz., Messrs. Monks, Hall, and Company, where accidents were liable to occur frequently. It was pointed out that Mr. Burton was already the treasurer, and the proposition that Mr. Taylor be re-elected was proposed, seconded, and car- ried. Mr. Burton was unanimously re-elected treasurer for the coming twelve months. Mr. I. Roberts, the secretary, stated that he would be glad if the committee would elect someone else in his place, as he had already too much work on his hands. Mr. J. Taylor was elected. The Chairman then read a letter from Mr. J. L. Tuns- tall, joint secretary of the Infirmary and Dispensary, which ran as follows :—" Dear sir,—l am desired to intimate to you that at the annual general meeting of this institution, held to-day, it was decided that a second member' of your committee, in addition to its chairman, should become a member of the Board of Management. The selection of the member in question is left with your committee. I am also to acquaint you with the following resolution, which was unanimously passed: —" That special thanks be given to the Workingmen's Committee, and those they represent, for the handsome sums which they have subscribed to this institution during the past year, and that they be encouraged .7.0 continue their praiseworthy labours." It was proposed and seconded that Mr. Burton be appointed. Mr. Thompson was also proposed and seconded. A show of hands was taken, when it was found ttiat there were ten for Mr. Thompson, and five for Mr. Burton Mr. Thompson being accordingly elected. A hearty vote of thanks was accorded to the late secretary for the good work he had done. Mr. Roberts having replied, the meeting terminated.

div.head: INQUEST ON A CHILD BURNED TO
div.p: INQUEST ON A CHILD BURNED TO
DEATH.

On Tuesday afternoon, Mr. S. Brighouse. coroner, held an inquest in the new Dispensary, adjoining the Warrington Infirmary, concerning the death of Mary McCabe, a child aged 2 years and 4 months, who died at the Infirmary in consequence of burns received on Sunday last. Eliza Jane McCabe, of 2, Back Moss-st., deceased's mother, said about half-past three on Sunday afternoon, the child went out to play on some waste ground off Winwick-st., with some other children ; and some time after a little girl came running in to witness and shouted " Mrs., there is a little baby on fire," and she ran out, and when she got to the waste ground she heard that a young man had carried the child to the Infirmary. Mrs. Martha Warburton said she lived right opposite the waste land. On Sunday afternoon, a child came to her and said "Oh, Mrs. Warburton do come, there is a child burning." She ran across the field, and shouted to her son, who came and threw his jacket round the child,who had been burning ten minutes. All its clothes were burnt to tatters. Some boys had had matches in the field, and had been burning the grass, and she fancied the deceased and some other children had been trying to do the same thing. They were all very young children. . _

Walter Warburton, son ot the preceding witness, said he heard screams coming from the waste ground about a quarter to four o'clock. He ran out and found the child there on its back burning. He pulled his jacket off and wrapped it round her ; brought it into the house, and then took it to the Infirmary. He saw bits of straw and paper burning in the field. The child was so severely burnt as to be past cryieg. Ella Smith, nurse at the Infirmary, depored to the child being admitted, there on Sunday, with burns all over the body, except the head, and to her dying about half-past two the following morning. The jury returned a verdict that the child died from burns, through its clothes accidentally catching fire. The Coroner remarked that that was the first inquest held in the new Dispensary. It had been intimated to him through Dr. Bowden that he could have the use of the room for inquests, in cases of death at the Infirmary, subject to the work of the Institution,and he said he was very much obliged for the offer. It would be more con- venient, and the nurse would always be at hand to give evidence.

div.head: HOSPITAL SUNDAY AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: HOSPITAL SUNDAY AT WARRINGTON.

On Sunday sermons were preached and collec- tions made in aid of the fuads of the Warrington Infirmary in most of the churches and chapels of the district. The Mayor and Corporation attended, in state, so to speak, the morning service at the Parish Church on Sunday, at which a sermon was preached by the Rector. Meeting at the Town Hall at ten o'clock, a procession was formed,headed by 32 mem- bers of the police force, under the direction of the Chief Constable. They were followed by a dozen firemen, in- cluding the superintendent, Mr. Turner. Then came the Mayor having on his right the Deputy- Mayor, Alderman Francomb, and on his left Alder- man Burgess, and the following members of the Corporation : Aldermen Wright and Chandley ; Councillors R. T. Fairclow,,h, Dr. Cannell, A. Browne,T. Hutchinson, John Bonnell, James Muir, William Tins- ley, James Smethurst, James Hill, James Fairelough, and James Hepherd ; Mr. T. Longdin (borough surveyor), Mr. George F. F. White (deputy magistrates' clerk), Mr. John Fairhurst (borough collector), Mr. W. S. Had- dock (gas engineer), Mr. Frederick Taylor (secretary of the gas department) ; Mr. James Bolton (elective audi- tor) ; Mr. Samuel Sutton (deputy clerk to the Board of Guardians) ; Messrs. E. Auktand, W. Gill, and Alfred (Gnardians) ; and Messrs. William Fairhurst, John Chidlaw, and Robinson. On arriving at the Parish Church gates, the police and firemen drew up to allow the members of the Corporation to pass, and they then walked into church, headed by the clerk and beadle and Mr. N. B. Percival (rector's warden), and Mr. Alfred Woods (people's warden). There was a large congregation, which included many soldiers from the Barracks.

The Rector took for his text Romans viii. 19-22, " For the earnest expectation of the creature waiteth for the manifestation of the sons of God," &c. The preacher asked the congregation to look around and see all the suffering which existed in the world, and said that if they did so the questions must force themselves upon every thoughtful mind—" How did all this suffering arise ? Why does God permit it? What can we do to lessen it ?" Those were the three points he submitted for the consideration of his congregation. He mentioned over 4,000 cases were treated in the Infirmary last year, being an increase of about 240 upon the previous 12 months. He asked the congregation to give accord- ing to their means. He knew that these were days in winch they were asked to give in every direction. There were many calls upon thein, but they must give systematically and liberally. We understand that the collection realised the sum of £2l 2s. 7d.

div.head: COAL CRISIS.
div.p: THE COAL CRISIS.

WORK RESUMED. • There was a general resoniption of work on Monday in the coalminPs in the Manchester district, and it is repoqed that as many men as usually go down the pits ,on Mondays put in an appearanee. In some cases the return of miners was delayed for a day or two for various reasons. There appears to be general satisfaction amongst the 20,000 Nottinghamshire miners at the termination of their" holiday." The behaviour of the men during the week's idleness has generally been exemplary. Meetings of the men employed in the districts of Stanton Hill and New Hucknall were held on Saturday, at which it was decided te resume work. It was also resolved to ask the Council of the Notts Miners' Federation to allow the men employed in the pits of the Stanton Iron and Coal Com- pany to have Saturday instead of Monday as their holi- day in carrying out the London Conference in favour of working only five days a week.

div.head: ST. HELENS.
div.p: ST. HELENS.

The miners of St. Helens have acted upon the resolu- tion of the Conference in London, and have resumed work, a fact which has given general satisfaction, it being the general opinion that trade will soon begin to improve, and that the number of unemployed in the town will be considerably lessened. The men have returned to work on the old conditioas, but Mr. Glover. the agent, will shortly give notice that on after a cer- tain date, five days a week will only be worked. The Conference has fixed the 11th of April as tha first Mon- day upon which the men will "play."

div.head: HAYDOCK.
div.p: HAYDOCK.

The whole of the Haydock colliers employed by Messrs. R. Evans and Co. have now returned to work. About half of them put in an appearance on Monday, but by Wednesday all the miners had descended the pits, hav- ing signed the usual agreement to work six days per week.

div.head: CONFLICT IN DURHAM.
div.p: THE CONFLICT IN DURHAM.

Meetings of Durham miners were held all over he county on Saturday, resolutions to continue the strike being adopted at each gathering. The men have been greatly encouraged by the motion of sympathy and promise of financial support from the National Federa- tion, and it is anticipated that this will result in the strike being prolonged to a period not before expected. There were fresh outbreaks of disorderly conduct on Monday at New Seaham Colliery, where stones were thrown,windows smashed, and other damage done. The police were powerless to quell the almost riotous mob. The colliers in Oldbury district have decided to act in accordance with the resolutions passed at the conference. IMPOKTING COAL AT THE HARTLEPOOLS.

A Durham correspondent states that the " deputies " who have been working at Lord Londonderry's pits since the stoppage began came out on strike on Tuesday, in sympathy with the miners. A West Hartlepool corres- pondent says :—From exporting coals at the rate of about 25,000 tons per week, the Hartlepools are now compelled, by force of circumstances, to import that commodity. There was a renewal on Tuesday after- noon of the disturbances at South Heaton, and the aid of the police had to be obtained.

div.head: " JOHN -TTIMIEUS !"
div.p: " JOHN -TTIMIEUS !"

Aw've bin hevire a dream, An' it gen mi a freet, Fer aw woke wi' a scream, Wi' mi clooas aw weet; Aw seed two chums feyglitin' like blazes, An' awll never loze thowts o' that seet ! One o'th' chaps thay caw'd John Wur ez reawnd ez a tub; An' he kept up his size Wi' good ale fro a" Pub"; But fer aw that he's very good comp'ny; An' aw'm not goin' to gie him a snub ! 'Tother mm they caw'd Tuna— (Not "0' Pegs !"—that be blow'd !) An' he allus look'd grum Wen thay sed he wur brode; An' he, too, wur a deawnreight good fellow, Ez ever reel't under a load. Th' row begun thro a choir Bein' drest up i' shirts, An' aw dreamt the word liar, Cud be heerd i' spurts ; An' sum terms—well, they caun't be caw'd blessins', That bed L in, an' summut like" fire!" John sed wimmin wur th' best To sing anthums an"irams, Wile Turn caw'd um a pest, An' swore lads hed less wims; Then," chowterreds," " waistrels," an' " bulleis," Geet mixt wi' sum purrin"o limbs! Then thay jumpt up to feight, An' Turn dubblet his fist, Wile be geet on his legs, "An' he hit, but he miss'd !" Which aw'm thankful to say saved an inquest, An' his throttle a drop or a twist ! 1 Aw thowt John made a rush To punch Tummus's nose; But we gen him a push That spoilt th' aim o' his blows; Wen he turn't an' coss'd us in his fury, But we cared nowt, as yo may suppose! If yo'd heerd um sheawt. Yo'd ha' blest aw yer stars, ,That they coom clear eawt, An' not covered wi scars; But a marciful Providence kept um Fro showin' they'd bin in the wars ! Well, aw'm reet glad to say Twur a dream, an' that's aw; Ther wur nothire to pay, An' no fotchin' o' law— It's a luxerry rayt her expensive, To " fork " fer a barrister's " jaw !" So, mi morril is this— Wen yo goo fer a drink, It'll ne'er be amiss If yo'le tak time to think, It's far th' best to settle church matters Wi' oather a nod er a wink !
TEM 0' PEGS. Nyowton God bless o'. March 22, 1892.
THE SHROPSHIRE TRAGEDY.

An inquest was held on Monday evening at Welling- ton, Salop, on the body of the man Corbett, who drowned himself after battering his wife's skull with a poker. The jury found deceased committed suicide while temporarily insane. The injured woman is still alive, but her recovery is considered hopeless.

div.head: STRONG MAN CASE.
div.p: THE STRONG MAN CASE.

Sir Peter Edlin, in charging the Grand Jury at Clerkenwell Sessions, on Monday, gave his opinion that there was sufficient on the depositions to justify a true bill against the strong man Sampson. Subsequently Mr. Paul Taylor applied, on behalf of tho prosecution, that the recognizances of the witnesses might be dis- charged, Mrs. Bernstein being now of opinion that Samp- son had no felonious intention of stealing the diamonds. Subsequently Sampson was admitted to bail.

div.head: WIGAN OUTRAGE.
div.p: THE WIGAN OUTRAGE.

At the Wigan Borough Police Court, on Monday morning, Joseph Moran and John M'Ourr, both well- known police characters, were brought up on remand charged with a brutal assault and outrage upon a woman named Bridget Murray. Prosecutrix stated that she was in the neighbourhood of Mill Meadow on the night of the 14th inst., when she met the prisoners. After asking for money and being refused, prisoners dragged hes into an entry, where they subjected her to shocking outr.i.ge, culminating in the woman being stripped of her clothing and left in a state of nudity, I kicked and battered until she was almost senseless. 1 Since that date she has been an inmate of tho Wigan In- I firmary. Chief Constable Bell stated the case, which was corroborated by the prosecutrix in detail. Both prisoners were committed to the assizes.

THE MILLOM MURDER. EXECUTION AT CARLISLE. Joseph Wilson, who was sentenced to death at Carlisle Assizes for the murder of a married woman named ro man, with whom he lodged at Millom, Cumberland, was executed in Carli,le Gaol, on Tuesday morning. The unconcerned demeanour assumed by the prisoner at his , trial never forsook him. He retired to rest about ten I o'clock on Monday night, and ten minutes after was fast was Sacrament at executioner, r asleep. He rose about six o'clock and partook of break. fast, aa nt hd sa op -f instantaneous. The prisoner being of fast, and afternwirndgtos of the pthaerecnhtalyplabineing slender build and only twenty-four years of age, was al- lowed a drop of eight feet. Wilson was a quarryman. Ile lodged at Mrs. Cross. man's house at Millom,and on the morning of the murder made some complaint about his breakfast. Words en- sued, and Wilson took a gun belonging to Mrs. Cross- man's husband and deliberately shot her. Before his death the prisoner asked the chaplain to make it known that he was thoroughly penitent for his erime,and would not have commited it had he been in his right senses at the time.

It seemed for the mo- ment as if there was danger of a wreck on the Early Closing rock,seeing that the Shop-assistants' Association were pledged to devote their energies, in the first instance, to securing the half-holiday. But, as we pointed out last week, assuming that Objecting tradesmen were in earnest about early Closing and the half-holiday coming into opera- tion simultaneously, there should be no difficulty about a joint effort to accomplish both objects. Meesrs. HENRY MILLING and Co., Limited, took the lead in presenting what may be called the Tradesmen's Manifesto; and they were very much blamed in some quarters by those who thought counter-action would result in a break-down of the half-holiday movement. It does not seem to have been noticed that what they were asking for Was really more than the shop-assistants them- selves requested, for, whilst the latter were con- tent to begin with the half-holiday, Messrs. MILLING and their co-signatories laid it down that the new departure should be elle of half-holiday and early closing. In order that there may be no misapprehension in the matter, Messrs. MILLING and Co. have intimated that they will commence to close on Thursday afternoons, on April 28th, on the understanding that early closing is included in the articles of the Shop-assistants Association. This is very credit- able to them as a firm; and, as showing their bona 'ficle-B,it will be the means of removing any irritation Which may have arisen. We can quite uriderstand the importance which is attached to early closing by tradesmen who are in the habit of closing early. iS hardly the thing for a shopkeeper to give a 11, all-holiday and take it back,so to speak, by keep- ing open an hour later than other shopkeepers 'our nights in the week, and two hours later on Saturday. The Assistants are, of course, Perfectly alive to this ; and they will do ,Well to direct their energies to early `-'3eing, which really means equalising hours, 'er if they fail in this latter respect there will al- Ways be risk of a total failure. It must be borne le• Mind, too, that the proposed change will involve e(wisiderable re-arrangement of work, especially in the larger houses, and it is a matter of course to expect that shop-assistants, in whose interests the Change is made, will render active and willing ser- vlce in meeting the difficulties to be encountered. There is only a certain amount of business to be tiGne in Warrington; and if it can be demon- atrated, in a practical way, that the same business et`a be transacted as well with a half-holiday and early closing as without them, we are quite sure that employers will not begrudge a concession 'Which will be a relief to them as well as their 49s18tants.

div.head: "TOUCH AND GO."
div.p: "TOUCH AND GO."

The Countess of Cork is responsible for the Tol- lowing excellent story: On Mrs. George Hudson, the wife of the Railway King, being taken over a peer's house, she was shown the bust of Marcus Aurelius. She gazed at it with bated breath, and then asked—" If it was the late Markiss.-

Mrs. Osborne's friends would best serve her by saying nothing more about her. It is sheer bosh, in face of the evidence of her cool scheming, to urge that she was not accountable for her actions when she stole the pearls. A better case could be made out for 99 thieves out of every 100 than for her. Reducing the sentence is out of the question.

Mr. Pritchard Morgan, M.P., is quite grieved because the Crown—exercising rights over his Welsh gold mine—insists upon a royalty upon product rather than profit. The dispute which has arisen will draw attention to the royalties ques- tion. If the nation had its own, it would be in possession of the entire product ; and royalty rents would enrich the State rather than individuals.

Judging from the reply made by Sir James Fer- gusson to the deputation from the London Cham- ber of Commerce, there is a prospect of the Post Office Department taking up telephonic supply. It ought certainly to be done;t it is absurd that an important means of communication standing mid- way between a letter and a telegram should be left in the hands of private companies. A State Tele- phone would pay with charges greatly reduced.

The other week we had occasion to show that even Lord Salisbury had referred to the late Lord Beaconsfield (Mr. Disraeli), as a poliOcal adven- turer. This is what Carlyle thought of him,accord- ing to the reminiscences of Sir Gavan Duffy : "A cunning Jew got a parcel of people to believe in him,though no man of the smallest penetration could have any doubt that he was an impostor, with no sort of purpose in all he was doing but to serve his own interests."

The Local Government Board have deferred the proposed extension of St. Helens in the direction of Windle, " until proper provision has been made for the purification of the sewage of the borough before its discharge into Sankey Brook." This will put the Corporation on their mettle ; and if it leads to the construction of successful purifica- tion works, it will be a good thing all round. San- key Brook is certainly foul enough ; it is simply a large open sewer.

The strike amongst the miners of Durham goes on,although the miners in other parts of the coun- try have resumed work. It was the object of the play week to reduce stocks, keep up prices, and thus render a reduction in the Durham district unnecessary. So far that object cannot be said to be accomplished, masters and men alike remain- ing firm. There ought to be a way out of this deadlock. What of arbitration, or reference to a Board of Conciliation?

The Eight Hours Bill for miners was rejected in the House of Commons, on Wednesday, by a majority of 112. Although Liberals, as a rule, supported it there was considerable cross-voting, Mr. Chamberlain being amongst those who sup- ported it, while two labour representatives—Mr. Burt and Mr. Fenwick—opposed the measure. It is clear that miners are not themselves agreed upon the question ; and until there is something like unity amongst them it cannot be expected that there will be unity in Parliament. But it is some- thing gained that the ball has been set rolling.

"Reception's the word" since the Liberals of Warrington have made it so popular; so the Tories are going to have a " Reception." Not that they would flatter their opponents by imitat- ing them; not a bit of it. They have had a " Re- ception " in mind since the creation of the world ; but they have only just recently been able to fix the date. Curiously enough, the object of the " Reception " is to enable Sir Gilbert Greenall to " bid farewell to his old constituents." Some people would call that a leave-taking ; but " what's the odds, &c." "Reception's the word."

It is very gratifying to observe that all oppo- sition to the East Coast Railway was withdrawn when the Bill came before the Select Committee of the House of Lords on Tuesday. This means that it will pass as an unopposed measure; and, further, that various Railway Companies have made such terms with the new Company as will enable them to make ire of the line. With a ter- minus on the Shin Canal at Warrington it ought to be the means of stimulating trade ; and mean- time the making of it will bring money into the district.

What price policemen P It used to be co*, sid- ered second only to wilful murder to assault a constable" in the execution of his duty ;" but a change seems to be coming over the spirit of the scene. At the Warrington Police Court, on Monday, James Templeton was convicted for hav- ing struck P.C. Hollingsworth on the mouth, on Sunday night, and knocked him down. The Bench thought the justice of the case was met by a fine of 10s. and costs. Perhaps they took into account the fact that the defendant acquired a black eye in his struggle with the constable. Preaching before the Mayor and Corporation on Hospital Sunday, the Rector of Warrington, dealt with sin and suffering, and the mystery of pain. It is a subject which has occupied the minds of many thoughtful people, and it still remains a mystery. An old Lancashire rhyme bearing upon the matter is as follows:
Some people say as pain is sent To be a kind o' punishment, When we've done badly. It may be so—aw kornd deny— But when aw hear th' poor childer cry Aw'm puzzled sadly.

Lord Salisbury suggests a circus rather than a Parish Council; but that is not the view taken by the Rev. W. Tuckwell. He thinks the Council will have plenty to do. Writing in the " Contem- porary " he says :—" The Council will bring gas to the country; will pave and light the dark muddy streets; arrange as do French villages, a ball and a concert ; will tempt actors, conjurers, minstrels, lecturers; will constitute bazaar and flower show ; lay out cricket-ground and swimming bath ; store village libraries.' Very good ; but when are we to have thesa Councils , Will the present Govern- ment die and make no sign?

The question is sometimes asked—how is the State-pension scheme acting in Germany? Some authorities say it is doing very well; others very badly. Dr. Wilhelm Bode, who is a strong opponent, says :—" It is a sad time for Germany. Prices are high ; wages are low; woric is slack. Among the reasons for this state of affairs we find —not in the fir,st place, but not in the last place either—the burden of State Socialism." But the pension burden is small compared with the mili- tary burden. The fact is the scheme has not been sufficiently. long in operation to furnish data for definite opinion.

There are people who occasionally read history upsidedown, and Alderman Sutton is one of them. He told a Warrington audience on Monday even- ing, that "it was Lord Beaconsfield and a Tory Government that gave to all householders a vote." He didn't explain that Lord Beaconsfield's bill was not a household suffrage bill, and that it was Gladstone and the Liberal party who out- voted the Tories again and again in order to secure household suffrage. Lord Salisbury retired from office rather than have anything to do with any extension of the franchise; but when the measure was in its last stage he said it WKS not Lord Beaconsfield's bill ;it was Mr. Gladstone's. What of authorities? Does Alderman Sutton pit him- self against Lord Salisbury and the whole world?
An Amsterdam telegram states that five persons were killed and twenty injured, seven of them seriously, by a fire which broke out on Tuesday night, on the Keisers Gracht Canal.
The representatives of the Miners' Federation met in London, on Thursday, and decided to recommend the constituencies to turn out at the next election the mem- hen who epposed the Eight Hours Bill.

The Runc.-;rn magistrates on Monday granted the transfer of the license of this Inn from John 'loft, de- ceased, to Albert Edward Mather Milton.

BRUNSWICK MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY, RUNCORN. At the weekly meeting, on Wednesday night, an in- teresting paper was read by Mr. D. Somerville, of Weston, on " David Livingstone," There was a good attendance. UMBRELLAS BECOVERED.—J. and W. DUTTON, Sankey-et., Warrington.—.Advt. WIDNES PETTY SESSIONS. .

div.head: CAMDEN BAND OF HOYE, RUNCORN.
div.p: CAMDEN BAND OF HOYE, RUNCORN.

A public meeting in connection' with the above was held on Tuesday evening, in the Camden Schoolroom. Mr. Thomas Wilson, who was in the chair, gave an ad- dress in support of the temperance cause. Recitations and songs were rendered. The accompanist was Miss Temperley. There was a good attendance.

div.head: SIIIP CANAL MISSION, RUNCORN.
div.p: SIIIP CANAL MISSION, RUNCORN.

_ On Tuesday evening a miscellaneous entertainment was given in the Ship Canal Mission Room, Runcorn, when there was a fair attendance. The Mill Brow Brass Band gave several selections in gond style. Several vocalists rendered a number of pieces in a thoroughly enjoyable manner. The chair was occupied by Mr. A. Jones, of Halton-road, Runcorn. The proceeds trre to be devoted to the fund being raised in connection with the band, and the Mission. UMBRELLAS RECOVERED.—J. and W. DUTTON, Sankey-et., Warrington.—Advt. TICE BURGLARY FROM WIDNES CENTRAL STATION,

_ Before Mr. J. Lister, at Widnes Police Court, on Mon- day, Wrn. Pritchard, alias Wm. Lynch, baggage man to the Whipping Post Company was brought up on remand charged with breaking and entering the booking office of the Manchester, Sheffield. and Lincolnshire Railway, at Widnes, and stealing 24. in money, two suits of clothes, and a number of keys. The circumstances of the affair have been reported. The prisoner was com- mitted to the Assizes for trial.

div.head: BIBLE SOCIETY MEETING AT WIDNES.
div.p: BIBLE SOCIETY MEETING AT WIDNES.

On Thursday evening the annual meeting of the British and Foreign Bible Society was held in the Waterloo-road Schools, under the presidency of the Vicar, the Rev. G. H. Garrett. The Rev. G. A. be Bert read the financial statement, showing that £4 12s. was contributed to tlie society by Widnes. The Chairman urged the claims of the society, and the Rev. J. E. Sy- monds delivered an interesting lecture on the work of the society, and stated that drink was the greatest enemy that the missionaries had to face.

RUNCORN MUSICAL SOCIETY'S FORTHCOMING CONCERT. The Runcorn Musical Society will bring to a close on Monday evening, one of its most successful seasons, from a musical point of view, and it is to be hoped in a financial sense as well, by the performance of Haydn's 'Creation," in the Public Hall. The artistes are Madame Conway, Mr. Maldwyn Humphreys, and Mr. Bantock Pierpoint •, all vocalists of recognised talent, and the chorus and band will be of the usual strength and under the respective leadership of Mr. Elvynne Humphreys and Mr. Collinson. Particulars as to prices of admision are advertised.

div.head: UNITED METHODIST TREE CHURCH.. WIDNES:
div.p: UNITED METHODIST TREE CHURCH.. WIDNES:

A sale of work in connection with this Church was held on Thursday in aid of the debt on the Sanday School. Mr. James Hargreaves performed the opening ceremony, and the afternoon and evening proceedings were very successful. There were four stalls well stocked with miscellaneous articles, and presided over by Mrs. Houghton. Misses A. Betuey, Harrison, Holland, Evans, and J. Betnay ; Messrs. S. Wilcock and Whitty had charge of the young men's stall, and the refreshment stall was presided over by Mesdames Birkenhead, Locker, Wilcock, Martin, Forest, and Miss Causey.
A NEW MISSION ROOM .VI. WIDNES.

In connection with St. Mary's Parish Church, Widnes, a mission roora was opened at West Bank on Monday afternoon by the Rev. Dr. Royston, D.D., assistant Bishop of Liverpool. The building, which is of corrugated iron, lined with wood, is capable of accomodating about 250 persons,and was erected at a total cost of £159, of which ZI2O had been already obtained. Prayer was offered by the Rev. G. El. Garrett, the vicar, and the Rev. C. W. Wooll, vicar of Ditton, read a portion of the scriptures, after which Dr. Houston delivered a sermon,in which he dwelt upon the advantage of having such a mission room, where the service would be more simple and social than was usual in the churches, and he asked for the aid of all true believers in the church. In the evening a sacred concert was held under the presidency of the Vicar, and a capital programme was gone through by Misses Fogg and Rathhone, Rev. J. R. Jones, and Mr. J. R. Lea. The Rev. W. Stanton Jones was the accompanist. Appropri- ate speeches were delivered by the Chairman, the Rev. G. H. Lander (Farnwurth), Mr. R. A. Naylor (Warring- ton), Rev. It. Meiklejohn, Rev. W. S. Jones, and the Chairman.

ST. JOEIN AMBULANCE ASSOCIATION, RUNCORN BRANCH. The annual meetina of the members of this Associa- tion was held on Wednesday evening, in St. John's School, Runcorn. The chair was occupied by Dr. McDougall,and there was a good attendance. Mr.Epps, the secretary, submitted his report, showing the male and female membership now stood at 150, and that 80 persons had taken certificates during the past twelve months. The financial statement set forth that there was a balance in hand of £lO 13s. 10d. The selection of officers was as follows :—Mr. J. Brundrit, J.P., presi- dent; the other magistrates of the division vice-presi- dents ; secretary, Mr. Epps ; treasurer, the Rev. P. Williams; and committee, Messrs. W. Bankes, S. Hender- son, J. W. Boyle, S. Coventry, J. Clare, Davenport, Newton, and R. It. Clark, P.S. Woolley, P.C. Crowder. and P.C. Thompson. It was resolved unanimously that a fee of one shilling per share be charged, to consti- tute membership for the future, fox which every certifi- cited member would be entitled to all the privileges and advantages, free of charge. It wag also decided that during the winter months a drill be held every four weeks, to keep the members efficient. Votes of thanks were accorded to the officials for their past services. Tau NEPREsENTATION OP THE NORTHWICH Drvisiorr.

On Saturday afternoon, a meeting of the Execu- tive Committee of the Northwich Division Liberal Association was held at the Gladstone Club, North- wich. Mr. 11. Bratt. C.C., the Chairman of the Com- mittee, presided. There was a large attendance from all parts of the division, Mr. Brunner, M.P., being also present. The object of the meeting was to make arrangements for the annual meeting of the General Council. and to discuss plans for the coming electoral campaign. A good deal of discussion upon various matters took place, and a resolution recom- mending the Council to request Mr. Brunner to again contest the division at the approaching general election was carried unanimously, amid much enthusiasm. Mr. Brunner delivered a short speech, in which he expressed himself willing to become their candidate at the next elect'on, if it was the unanimous wish of the party. At the close of the meeting the delegates partook of tea, pro- vided by the Misses Gibson, of Castle-st. UMBRELLAS RECOVERED.—J. and W. Durrog, Sankey-at, Warrington.— Advt.
THE EXAMINER, SATT) RDA Y, MARCH 26, 1892.
RAILWAY FATALITY NEAR WARRINGTON.

On Thursday a man named Daniels, employed by the Cheshire Lines Committee, was working on the line at Glazebrook station, and stepped out of the way of an approaching train when the Manchester and Liverpool express came up in the contrary direction, knocking him down and killing him._ _
SAFETY BICYCLES:—J. S. Garland, 51. Bridgebt., War- rington. See advertisement on page 4. THE UNITED ALKALI COMPANY'S ANNUAL MEET- ING.

The first annual meeting of this company was held,on Thursday afternoon,in the Law Association Rooms, Liverpool, Sir Charles Tennant presiding. There was a large attendance of shareholders. A dividend of 7s. per share on the preNrence stock and ss. per share on the ordinary stock, which, added to the interim dividend paid last August, makes seven per cent, per annum, and on the latter five per cent, per annum was declared. The report of the directors gave an encouraging account of the affairs of the company.
, ACE-BRAND SPADES.—J. S. GARLAND, Ironmonger, Bridge-at., Warrington. CONFIRMATION AT NEWTON.

On Thursday afternoon the Rev. Dr. Royston, as- sistant Bishop of Liverpool,held a confirmation ser- vice at St. Peter's Church,Newton, for Newton.L.,:w- ton,and Wargrave. There were altogether 109 can- didates for confirmation, being 20 from Lowton, 27 Wargrave, and 59 St. Peter's. The following clergy- men were present—Rev. Canon Whitley, 11. Monk, E. J. Hack, F. W. Johnston, and F. Smith. Before the confirmation service and after Dr. Royston de- livered interesting and instructive addresses to the candidates. The arrangements were carried out by the churchwardens, Messrs. Stuart and Hindley. _ _ _

Burt, Broadhurst, Pickard, Abrahatn, Sinclair, Wil- son, and Seton-Karr to provide for certificates to persons in charge of steam engines and boilers on land. C0MP.......1QN OF BORING AT FIDDLERS FERRY. What is considered an important engineering feat was successfully completed on Thursday morn- ing in boring an aqueduct under the Mersey from the Cheshire to the Lancashire side near Warring- ton for conveying a supply of water to Liverpool. It is four years since the work was first undertaken. The total cost of the work is £25,000. The length of the tunnel is 623 feet. By means of a driving shield the work of boring has been accomplished in 14 weeks, or at an average of 34 feet a week. The greatest distance driven in a single week has been 57 feet. UMBRELLAS RECOVERED.—J. and W. DUTTON, Sankey-st. Warrington.—Advt.
ST. HELENS POLICE AND THE Sr. JOIIN AMEU-
LANCE ASSOCIATION.

On Thursday the annual distribution of certifi- cates and medalions to members of the ambulance class connected with the St. Helens Police Force took place. Colonel R. Pilkington presided, and staten that during the ten years the centre had been formed upwards of 700 certificates had been granted. It was a matter for gratifica- tion and congratulation that the police had ta- ken full advantage of the opportunities offered. The Mayoress then distributed the certificates and medallions, and at the request of Chief Constable Wood presented Dr. Robertson with a marble time- piece, subscribed for by the men, in recognition of his services as lecturer.—Dr. Robertson expressed his thanks for the timepiece, and said it had given him a great deal of pleasure to be with them, and he should only be too glad in the future to do simi- lar work. UMBRELLAS RECOVERED.—J. and W. DUTTON, Sankey-at.. Warrington.—Advt.
WIDNES LOCAL BOARD ELECTION.

For the five vacant seats on Widnes Local Board twelve candidates have been nominated as follows: —Robert Cook, Penketh Works, manager; John Houghton, Albert-road, Widnes, insurance agent; Joshua Mid wood, Birch Ylouse,Ditton, estate agent; and Henry Sutton Tim mis, Beech wood-road, Aig- burth, soap manufacturer. The above four retiring members were nominated by 15 ratepayers. Samuel Owen, 76' Albert-road, Widnes, described as an estate agent, was nominated by 24. Alfred Brouchemlte. 1, and 3, Victoria-st., Widnes, described as a lodging-house keeper, had four nomin- ators. John Williamson, 74, Victoria-road, described as a tailor and draper, and Wm. O'Hagan, Crown Vaults, Ann-st., brought forward by the Widnes Irish National League, received 10 nominations. Thomas Gerrard, Alexandra Hotel ; Thomas Smith, grocer,Mersey-rcad ; Henry Singleton, butcher, Victoria- road, and James Carroll, pawnbroker, Widnes-road, were brought forward by the Ratepayers' Association, and received nine nominations. H. Singleton and J. Carroll received 11 nominations, T. Smith, 10, and T. Gerrard nine. . .
At one time it was thought that a contest could be avoided but this is now impossible, snd from the oppos- ing forces that are arrayed an exciting election is expected.

div.head: ELECTION OF GUARDIANS OF RUNCORN
div.p: ELECTION OF GUARDIANS OF RUNCORN

UNION. The annual election of guardians of the poor for Runcorn Union takes place next week. To-day is the last day for receiving nomination and, so far as can be gathered there will be contests in Runcorn and Frodsham district. Up to yesterday there had been nominated six gentlemen for the five seats at Runcorn, namely the Rev. Dr. Gastaldi, Messrs. P. Speakman, C.C., S. Taylor, J. W. Ligbtburn, T. Lea, and Alfred Norman. The first-named five are the retir- ing members. At Frodsham a contest is certain. For the twoseats there ere nominated Messrs. H. E. Hey- wood, James Edwards, John Moseley Williaing, and Henry Q. Linaker. At Weston Messrs. Aaron and Kirk- ham will be unopposed. In view of the election, the following list of attendances of the Guardians for the past year will be of interest to the voters :-Thomas Hewitt 4, Henry Lowe 2, Rev. J. W. N. Tanner 20, Jos. Knowles 13, John Whitlow 12. Win. Wilkinson 5, Robt. div.head: RUNCORN COUNTY COURT. -- TUBSDA.Y.—Before His Honour Judge Wynne- Ffoulkes. THE CAUSE LIST comprised 2 adjourned plaints. 4 default summonses. and 48 ordinary summonses.
div.p: RUNCORN COUNTY COURT. -- TUBSDA.Y.—Before His Honour Judge Wynne- Ffoulkes. THE CAUSE LIST comprised 2 adjourned plaints. 4 default summonses. and 48 ordinary summonses.
A FAN" ILY SQUABBLN.

John Cardus, labourer, Wiaston Hills, Halton-road, sued Mary Ann Pmbin, of the same place, for £4, made up as follows :—L3 ss. value of goods illegally detained, and 15s. damages for the detention. Mr. E. Wynne Humphreys appeared for the plaintiff and Mr. J. Burton for the defence. After hearing the evidence on both sides, his Honour said it seemed to him to be a family squabble,and it was a pity such a case had been brought into court,and he asked them to agree as to the amount. The parties were unable to do this, and his Honour then ordered the goods to be returned, or 17s. paid in lieu thereof, with Is. damages. . _

div.head: FARM LABOURER'S DISPUTS.
div.p: A FARM LABOURER'S DISPUTS.

Richard Coombe, farm servant, of Sutton Weaver, sued Anna Bate, of the same place, for 12s. 9d., wages alleged to be due. Mr. Lake defended, and it having been proved that the defendant had left his work after a month's notice, although he was hired as a yearly ser- vant, the judge gave a verdict for the defendant. A KINGSLEY FARMER'S WILL.

An application for partition and sale of freehold cot- tages at Kingsley, was made by Mr. J. Burton. on behalf of Robert Lloyd, and Mary Ann, his wife, and children, and others, against Daniel Downes, of Alverthorpe, near Wakefield, and Samuel Harvey, the elder, farmer, Kings- ley,executors of the will of the late John Spruce,farmar, Kingsley. The application had been adjourned from last court, and his Honour said the will was a curious document, evidently drawn up by one inexperienced in those matters. It contained no express devise to any- body, and the property given to Mrs. Lloyd, his daugh- ter, and her children was bequeathed to her "alter five years after his death." The testator also directed that his widow should have the use of one of the houses and sufficient furniture to furnish the same, and further directed that his executers should pay her 4s. per week so long as she remained his widow. As to the applica- tion, his Honour had come to the conclusion that the property belonged to Mrs. Lloyd and her two children, and it must be sold under the supervision of the court, the daughter taking one-third, and her children one- third each.
WESLEYAN HOME MISSIONS AT RUNCORN.

The annual services in aid of the Wesleyan Home Missions were held on Sunday in St. Paul's Chapel. The Rev. S. F. Collier, of Manchester Central Hall Mission, occupied the pulpit both morning and evening, and delivered two elcquent and stirring sermons to large congregations. His texts were respectively " She bath done what she could " and " Photograph of a fool." In the afternoon Mr. Col- lier gave an address entitled "Sketches from life." The collections for the day amounted to .£l9 os. 10d. —On Monday evening the annual public tea meet- ing was held in the chapel, under the presidency of Mr. R. Rawlinson, who was supported on the platform by the Revs. S. Chadwick, of the Leeds Mission ; S. F. Collier, T. Wilkes, W. Arrowsmith, and J. Hanby ; Gipsy Smith, Evangelist preacher and singer, and Messrs. P. Speakman, C.C., S. Taylor, F. J. Norman, A. Norman, and S. Pope. After an appropriate opening speech from the chairman, the Rev. W. Arrowsmith submitted the 36th annual report of the Wesleyan Home Mission and Contingent Fund for the support and spread ! of the Gospel in Great Britain and Ireland. The income for 1891, including £4OO from the Reserve Fund had bee' £34,782 14s. 2d. and the expen- diture £35,032 Bs. 3d., showing a deficiency of £249 14s. Id., and, adding the balanca of £359 3s. due to the treasurers last year, making a total deficit on cur- rent account of £509 .2s. Id. There were 84 home mis- sionaries an i the circuits assisted were more than 350. The total amount raised in Liverpool district, which in- cluded Runcorn, was £2,238 183. id., and of that sum Runcorn circuit contributed £92 63. sd. last year. Ad- dresses were also given by the Revs. S. Chadwick and S. F. Collier, the deputation, upon the importance and necessity for home missionary enterprise urging all to take part in this social and evangelistic work. Gipsy , Smith also sang a selection of sacred music and delivered an earnest speech. The usual vote.; of thanks were ac- corded. The collection realised £23 3s. 10d., making al total of £42 4s. Bi. for the two days.
CONSERVATIVE DEMONSTRATION AT RUNCORN.

div.head: SPEECHES BY LORD CRANBORNE AND MR.
div.p: SPEECHES BY LORD CRANBORNE AND MR.
W RITELEY.

Under the auspices of the Northwich Division Conservative Association, a public meeting was held in the Runcorn Public Hall on Tuesday night, and a large audience assembled, the body of the hall being crowded. The Royal Standard, flanked by Union Jacks, was conspicuous at the rear of the nlatform. Mr. John Brundrit. J.P.' presided, and he was supported by Lord Cratiborne, M.P. for Darwen ; Mr. G. Whiteley (Unionist candidate), Sir Richard Brooke, Bart., Rev. Canon Wood, Rev. Dr. Preston, Bev. :V. Fielden (Sutton), Col. Ashton, Messrs. T. Ward (Northwich), T. Timmins, .T. J. Speakman, J. Meadowcroft, S. Pope, C. J. Hughes (Northwich), E. Imison, A. Hornby Lewis (Marbury Hall), W. Mellor, J. Weston, J. W. Lightburn, G. Hewitt, G. Summersfield, G. J. Knight,J. Ockleston, Dr. MacKenzie, &c. Letters of apologies were read from Mr. Jas. Reynolds, J.P., and Mr. Harvey Talbot.

The Chairman, in opening the proceedings, said there was no doubt a dissolution would take place very shortly and it was on that account that the Unionist party in that division had thought it desirable to hold a meeting in Runcorn, so that the electors could hear addresses on the political aspect of affairs as the Unionist party looked upon them. (Applause.) In eulogistic terms he then introduced . . .

Lord Cranborne who said that if the people of Che- shire were anything like the people of Lancashire, he I was sure they would fully appreciate the worth and value of Mr. Whiteley. (Applause.) Many a time and often had Mr. Whiteley pleaded for the great Conserva- ; tire and Unionist cause in the division of Lancashire he (Lord Cranborne) had the honour to represent, and be ; was very glad to be able to tell them,that if they elected Mr. Whiteley as their member—as he hoped they would they would have a man who could hit hard, who would ' never run away, but who would show that quality of grit which they in Lancashire were so proud of, and of which Mr. Whiteley was so conspicuous an example. (Applause.) Ile did not disguise from himself that they had a hard fight before them. He wished them all suc- cess, and no candidate, and no party, ever had a finer cause to fight for than the cause of the present Govern- ment. (applause.) It was one of the most active and energetic Governments of modern times and he asked was it nothing to have reformed the complete system of Local Government in England ; to have given free education to the working classes of the country. (Applause and a voice " Assisted.") Well he would be frank with them. He was not particularly fond of free education, but his friend lathe crowd was quite wrong; it was free education and not assisted education. (Applause.) A parent had only to demand it, and the authorities were bound to grant free education under the new act. (Applause.) Again was it nothing to have converted the national debt, and to have diminished by a million and a half a year the amount of money that had to be paid on interest. (Applause.) The navy had been strengthened to a point when it might properly compete with the great obligations which were cast upon it ; our coasts were defended in a way they had never been defended before; Ireland had been restored to tran- quility (applause) and last and not least the foreign affairs; of the country had been so conducted that Englishmen were not alarmed for the morrow and were not ashamed to look their enemies in the face. (Applause.) Dealing with the Home Rule question, he tiaid the Unionists were unable to tears what it meant. They had a right to know what Mr. Gladstone's Home Rule Bill was, and as the Liberal party were always ad- vocating trust in the people, let them trust the people with the details of the Bill. (Applause.) Mr. George Whiteley, the candidate, who was heartily applauded on rising, said Runcorn had been a source of anxiety and solicitude to the leaders of the Liberal Unionist party in this division. He believed they held the key of the position in that town of Runcorn. It was his firm belief that Mr. Brunner sat tor that division ("he will sit again" applause)—never pro- phesy until they knew. (Applause.) But he believed that Mr. Brunner sat for that division largely owing to.the Gladstonian folk in Runcorn, and if the Unionists in Runccrn would work hard and if they could get any- thing like an equal vote upon their side to the Gladston- ian vote in the town, the division was won. (Applause). Be wondered what their opponents would. ray to that capital meeting they had there that night, he wondered how the Gladstonian Home Rulers, Parnellites would feel next morning and in what sort of condition would they be. (Laughter). Alluding to Home Rule the speaker said they had heard nothing about this matter from the eminent statesman who had styled himself the Old Parliamentary Hand. He would not show his cards; with that eminent statesman who had at various times been described by his friends as the Grand Old :Spider, and tbe guileless Old Gentleman—with that eminent, gentle" mum" was still the word. To borrow a simile from Pickwick, in the graphic words of" Samuel Veller," ; he was dumb as a drum with a hole in it. (Laughter). ; I And for this very good reason that he could not formu- late a scheme of Home Rule that would not offend ens extreme or the other of his party. (Applause). The electors in that division bad a 'right to kn from Mr. Brunner what his ideas of Home Rule we- ; they bad a right to nag at him until they learnt ; to metaphorically take him by the throat and shake him ' until they could get some information from him. (Ap- plause.) He (Mr. Whiteley) was prepared to admit that absentee landlordism had been somewhat of a curse to Ireland, but now that they had Land Acts, Land Pur- chase Bills, and Ashbourne Acts : now that the tenant farmers of Ireland, the peasants of Ireland could be- come their own landlords on easy terms,he thought they would agree with him that the evils of absentee land- lordism would in all probability be abated. He was very well acquainted with Ireland ; he had been there a great deal, and he understood the state of the country. He did not believe that one-tenth of the people of Ire- land really desired Home Rule, and that one-tenth was composed of what they might call the broad- cloth element in Ireland—men who thought that in an Irish Parliament fat offices, lucrative posts, and snug sinecures would be found for them. Ireland was made up of two races, the Protestants and the Catholics, the loyal and the disloyal—(" no, no")— and if ever an attempt was made to put Protestant Ulster under the domination of a Catholic Parliament sitting at Dublin, one of the bloodiest civil wars that ever devastated this fair country would break out in the sister isle. (Applause.) If an Irish Parliament were granted, every penny of English capital that could be withdrawn would be withdrawn, and Irish industries would languish and die, and decay, and we in England would feel the competition of cheap Irish labour, and the wages of the working-men would be reduced in conse- quence. There was a great deal talked about justice to Ireland. Was there no justice for England? If ever am Irish Parliament was granted to Ireland there would arise the cry" England for the English," and freedom from that roughshod domination from which net only in Parliament but in the country we suffered at the hands of the Irish politicians, Irish rebels, Irish agitators, and Irish seditioniste. (Applause.) He wished to make an appeal to the English Catholic voters in that division. The question of this denominational education of the young was in the Catholic mind supreme and para- mount. (Hear, hear.) One of the first acts of a Glad- stonian ministry would be to place the denominational schools ot this country under the secular power. Were the Catholics prepared to put up with that ? He said no, and he asked every gentleman present to place that before every Catholic in the district, and he thought they would be able to claim and receive from them pro- mises of assistance and support at the next election. (Applause.) Mr. Hornby Lewis moved and Mr. T. Ward seconded a vote of confidence in the Government which was carried without dissent.—Mr. E. Imison moved a vote of thanks to Lord Cranborne and the other speakers; and on being seconded by Mr. John Weston was carried un-
animously.—A vote of thanks was accorded to the Chairman on the proposition of Mr. Whiteley seconded by Mr. W. Mellor, and the proceedings terminated.

div.head: UNIVERSITY EXTENSION SCHEME
div.p: THE UNIVERSITY EXTENSION SCHEME
AT 107NCORN.

The series of lectures on the History of Florence, in connection with the Oxford University Moll-- went was brought to conclusion on Monday ing, when the Rev. W. Hudson Shaw, M.A., deal\ ' with the subject of "The fall of the Republic and Michael Angelo." The large audience which had assembled in Bethesda School-room were treated to a highly learned and interesting disquisition on the life and career of the great painter and sculptor, and upon the main phases of Florentine History, and the lecturer's descriptions were aided by a number of lime-light views shown by Mr. Horace W. Handley.—At the conclusion Mr. G. Summerield proposed a hearty vote of thanks to Mr. Shaw for the intellectual treat he had afforded them by his course of lectures, and also to Mr. Handley for the excellent way in which he had shown the pictures on the screen.—Mr. Cunningham seconded the motion, which was carried by acclaination.—ln reply Mr. Shaw said the best way in which they could thank him was to assure him that in Runcorn centre they were not going to let the work drop. The Rev. Canon Wood then ad- dressed the meeting. He suggested that it would be wise for them to form an association of those who were de- sirous that an effort should be made to carry on the lec- tures for at least another session.—Mr. E. Wynne Humphreys, the hon. secretary, expressed an earnest hope that the lectures would be continued. It was decided to take the names of those who were desirous that the lectures should bo continued as they left the building.

div.head: ANNUAL VESTRY MEETING AT RUNCuRN.
div.p: ANNUAL VESTRY MEETING AT RUNCuRN.

The annual township meeting for Runcorn was held in Bethesda schoolroom on Thurday night tinder the presidency of Mr. E. hnison. Amongst those present were Dr. McDougall, Messrs. S. Tay- lor, W. Handley, H. Coleburn, J. K. Digges, John Littler. W. Jones, D. Bishrown, W. Littler, W. Nickson, T. Jones, W. Mellor. %Vm. Sutton (assist- ant overseer), and G. W. Yates (clerk.)

BURIAL BOARD ACCOUNTS. On the motion of Mr. W. Littler,seconded by Mr. Tay- , lor, Messrs. J. K. Dig,ges and John Littler were ap- pointed to audit the accounts of the School Board ; and on the motion of Mr. W. Handley, seconded by Mr. Bis- brown, it was resolved that the accounts must be ready for audit on 7th April, and that the adjourned meeting of ratepayers be held on the 21st April.

THE LIST OF OVERSEERS. Mr. H. Coleburn nominated the following gentlemen for the office of overseer :—Messrs. Edwin Imison, Samuel Taylor, Wm. Mellor, Richard Morris, William Flankinson, H. J. Grice, James Pritchard, and W. H. Rogerson. As there %v.-re no other names nominated this list will be submitted to the magistrates.

div.head: THIS. TOWNSHIP FINANCES.
div.p: THIS. TOWNSHIP FINANCES.

The Chairman said in conformity with the usual cus- tom, he would give a statement of the finawces of the township. The overseers commenced the year with a balance of £960 12s. 84. They laid a rate of 2s. in the L, which produced £5,536 19s. 7d., and the Ship Canal Company paid on their deficiency account £B4 ss. From the sale of voters' lists there was received £1 Os. 6d., and interest was estimated at £3 is. 34. ; making a total of £6,586 4s. 6d. On the other side they had paid justices' clerks' fees, £l2 10s. ; rent of offices, vestry room, assistant overseer's salary, and other sundry ex- To' nses, £306 9s. 64., and registration of voters, £59 14s. Bd. The Burial Board had received £l2O, the School Board £950, and the Board of Guardians £3,895; and the estimated bolance at the close of the year would be £1,242 4s. 4d. The rateable value of the town- ship at this time last year was £56,072 ; this year, £57,153, an increase of £l,OBO. The office expenses have been £5 less than last year, the registration of voters cost £1 103. more; the Burial Board had received £6O less than last year, the School Board £lOO more, and the Board of Guardians £646 more.

div.head: THANKS AN COMMINDATION.
div.p: THANKS AN COMMINDATION.

Mr. Handley moved a vote of thanks to the retiring overseers, Messrs. Irnison and Taylor, for the excellent way in which they had manaeed the township accounts. —Mr. Hankinson seclnded and Mr. B isbrown supported the motion, which was carried by acclamation.—Mr. Taylor acknowledged the compliment.—The Chairman also acknowledged the vote, and mentioned that Mr. Handley held the office of overseer for seven years, and he put the business on such a footing that it had been comparatively easy work to succeed in it. (Hear,hear.) He added that they had an exceptionally capable assis- tant overseer.
On the motion of Mr. Mellor, a vote of thanks was accorded to the chairman and the meeting concluded.
RUNCORN BOARD OF COIIMISSIONERS.

div.head: TECHNICAL INSTRUCTION.
div.p: TECHNICAL INSTRUCTION.

A special meeting of this Board was held on Wednesday night, at the Town Hall. Mr. H. J. Once presided, and there were present Messrs. F. Wiswall, J. Pritchard,J. 31eadoweroft,13. Ilisbrown, W. R. Wass, W. Hankinson, P. Speakman, C.C., J. W. Lightburn, F. A. Lake (Law Clerk), E. Marshall (secretary), and M. Barker (surveyor.) Mr. Wiswall moved the adoption of the following minute :—(a)—The Runcorn School Board having in- timated that the delicency incurred in connection with the Science and Art classes amounts to about £l2O and that in addition to this abmt .C 25 is required for the purchase of cupboards &c. for the storage of apparatus, the Technical Instruction Committee recommend that a further grant of £75 be made to the School Board in addition to the £75 voted as per Resolution No. 1,734 ; and that a cheque for £l2O be drawn on the County ' Council grant in favour of the said Board (E3O having been paid on account). He stated that it was impossible to make a detailed statement until the examinatious had been held and the amount of the Government grant ascertained, and the passing of that minute was a , formal matter.—Mr. Pritchard secoaded.—Questions by Mr.Meadowcroft elicited that £l9B had been received from the penny rate and £222 from the County Council and of these sums £193 had been spent in the purchase of apparatus and £147 had been paid the School Board for the maintenance of the science and art classes. There was a balance in hand of EH Ms. 7d. The resolu- tion was carried unanimously.
IRRECOVERABLE ARREARS.
On the motion of Mr. Hankinscn, seconded by Mr. Speakman, irrecoverable arrears amounting to £52145., the second instalment of the general district rate, were written off.

div.head: CHAIRMAN AND THI RAILWAY CO.
div.p: THE CHAIRMAN AND THI RAILWAY CO.

The Chairman said having seen a statement that the London and North-Western Railway Co. had been mak- ing a revision of their rates, he had called upon one of the leading officials at Lime-st. Station, in order to as- certain which would be the best mode to adopt to get fares between Runcorn and Widnes reduced. He was sorry to say that he got very little encouragement. He was told that Mr. Norman, Mr. Shaw, and Mr. Taylor had been there, and of course lie was there—(laughter)— and he got very little oncouragement.—Mr. Rankineon asked if anything was said in respect to Sunday trains. —The Chairman replied that it was merely a general conversation.

A GRANT FROM THE COUNTY COUNCIL. As the Secretary had received no intimation of the matter, Mr. Speakman informed the Board that the County Council had decided to make a grant of £2OO a year for the maintenance of the road from Halton-road Boundary to the Railway Station over iVaterloo Bridge. —The Chairman said no doubt every member of the community would be pleased at the success achieved, which was owing to the determined action of their two representatives and especially of Mr. Speakman, who bad taken a prominent part in making the arrangement. Mr. Pritchard said the grant was equal to a penny in tilt, £ saved from the rates.—The subject then dropped.
DEEP DOCKS: Mr. Lightburn : Heard anything from the Ship Canal Co. with respect to Deep Docks P—The Secretary: No. The meeting then terminated.
WIDNES POLICE COURT.
