THINGS HEARD AND SEEN AT RUNCORN, &c.
BY AN OCCASIONAL CORRESPONDENT.

It has occasioned much regret that Mr. W. Ockleston has been seized with serious illness, and the gathering of Liberals which had been arranged to compliment him on his gallant attempt to wrest Runcorn North from the "independent " party, has had to be postponed. He suffers from Iritis,and his medical attendant has forbidden him to leave the house, or to read and write under the penalty of total blindness. That he may be speedily restored to complete health is the hearty wish of his numer- ous Runcorn friends.

The meeting of the Liberal Executive, at North- wich on Saturday, was the largest and most repro. sentative gathering, it is said, that had been held since the Association was formed, and the member was filled with enthusiasm at the prospect of a good fight at the approaching Genera-I Election. The resolution to again adopt Mr. Brunner as the can- didate was carried with spontaneous unanimity,and there is no doubt that the Council at the annual meeting, on .Saturday next, will follow a similar course.

We, in Runcorn, had an opportunity of seeing and hearing the Conservative, or as the Tories love to call him, the " Unionist " candidate, on Tuesday night, and a large number of people turned up to do so. Unfortunately, Mr. Whiteley was suffering from severe hoarseness, and it was impossible to judge of his capabilities as a platform speaker, but he is evidently fluent of speech and is possessed of an extensive vocabulary,though, as was observed in more than one quarter, he will have to improve his arguments before he has a chance of carrying Northwich Division. The voters are not to be caught by such salt as he metaphorically endea- voured to put upon their tails, and the piling of adjectives upon Mr. Gladstone will hardly win him one cross at the ballot box.

He was very anxious to know what the Glad- stonians, the Home Rulers, and the Parnellites would say in the morning about the capital mef.A- ing the Tories were 'having. I may tell him, as a mere observer, that there were sufficient believers in the policy of Home Rule present to have swamped the vote of confidence which was passed in the Government had they wished to hold up their hands, but they had no desire to spoil Mr. Whiteley's plea- sure in viewing so unusually great an assembly at a Tory demonstration in Runcorn. It was pitiful to see such a public response to the Chairman's request" Those in favour " from such a mass of people.

As an old electioneering hand, Mr. Whiteley has ' found out the weakest spot in the party whose support he is receiving ; and he will find to his discomfiture when the election day arrives that Runcorn does hold the key of the position. The Liberals of Runcorn are not to be drawn away from their allegiance to their principles of liberty and progress, nor made to abate one jot of their vener- ation for "the grand old spider " by such stale, flat, and unprofitable pabulum as was dealt out to them on Tuesday evening.

Mr. John Ashton, the clerk to the Runcorn union is an exception amongst his fellows, and I fancy in this instance the exception does not prove the rule. A proposal was on foot to grant him extra remuner- ation for some legal work he had performed for the Rural Sanitary Authority, but Mr. Ashton declared his wish not to accept the money, because it was understood when he was appointed that no charge would be made for ordinary legal business, and he was satisfied if he had won the confidence and good will of the Guardians. On this declaration the pro- posal was not proceeded with. There are few men who would have declined an increase of salary, and all Lonour to Mr. Ashton for his straightforward conduct.

A contest for the five seats on the Whines Local Board is now assured,and the result will be awaited. The formation of the United Alkali Company has greatly altered the balance of the voting power, and the householders and shopkeepers are now the com— plete masters of the situation, and it will be instructive to all how they use their advantage. This contest will be to a great extent a guide as to the composition of the Town Council in November next—that is if the circumlocution office in London will send the Charter by that time.

It is a regrettable fact that the University Exten- sion movement has not met with great success in Runcorn. Last year when there were two courses of lectures there was a considerable clack, and this year with only one course a similar result is to be deplored. The lectures have signally failed to attract the working people, for whom they were originally organised, and the middle class are, apparently, not very enthusiastic, as only about two dozen people have given in their names as willing to join the association advocated by the Vicar. Would it not be best to divert the energy from this University movement, to our proposed Technical Institute, which is in need of help and which will fulfil to a great extent the object of the Extension Lectures?

The increase of success which has attended the Science and Art Classes in Runcorn this winter augurs well for the need and usefulness of the Technical Institute. There are 13 subjects taught to an•average of nearly 200 subjects, and, as Mr. Lightburn observed, at a special meeting evening, the Government examination must not be made too rigid a standard of the good accomplished. If the County Council will only make the town a generous grant from £22,000 they have lying idle in their coffers for Technical Education, the Board of Com- missioners will proceed in their scheme with confi- dence and vigour. The Science and Art Department of South Kensington have just made a building grant of £l,OOO to the Lancashire town of Nelson for a similar institution. May we in Runcorn hope for such a handsome contribution?

div.head: BY A.N EARLESTOWN CORRESPONDENT.
div.p: BY A.N EARLESTOWN CORRESPONDENT.

The all absorbing topic in Earlestown this week, and one which has caused the utmost excitement, is the death of the lad Hal, who it was alleged had died from injuries caused by being struck on the head with a cane by a pupil teacher. At the in- quest, however, it was proved that the death did not arise from any injury to the head, but from inflammation of the bram,althongh the doctor could not say how this had set up. The Coroner spoke strongly against the use of canes by pupil teachPrs. He said, however, that one should be kept, but to bu used only by the head master or mistress.

The coroner is a sensible man. He is the father of a large family, and no doubt feels keenly on the point. Every other father and mother of large families will agree with him, that it is not wise for pupil teachers to be given the power of chastising children with pointers, mind you (not canes) how and whenever they like, and often for the most trivial offence. To strike a child wearing knicker- bockers, on the leg below the knee with a pointer is out of all reason, and perhaps the other pupil teachers will take the hint, and amend their ways.
WIDNES AND THE LANCASHIRE COUNTY COUNCIL.

_ ln consequence of the elevation of Mr.T. Soape to the Aldermanic bench, a vacancy occurs in Widnes South on the Lancashire County Council. The exe- cutive of the Liberal Association decided to nomi- nate Mr. R. Wade-Deacon, J.P., as Mr. Snape's suc- cessor. _ -
Yesterday was the last day for the receipt of nominations for the vacancy. The candidates nomi- nated were Mr. H. Wade-Deacon (Liberal) and Mr. G. E. Sayee (Conservative).

div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.

CHARGE OF STEALING TIMBER.—THE CHESHIRE LINES COMMITTEE AND THEIR MEN'S HOURS OF WORE. At the Warrington Borough Police Court, on Monday, Henry B)wker was charged with stealing on Sun- day morning, the 13th inst., a piece of timber, value 9d., the property of the Cheshire Lines Committee. Mr. Forshaw appeared for the prosecution and Mr. Brow ne for the defence.—P.C. Edson, employed by the Cheshire Lines Committee, said about six o'clock on the morning in question, he saw the defendaa in the Che- shire Lines Committee's yard, and after he had gone away looked over the fence and observed the piece of timber in the defendant's yard adjoining. The defen- dant then came up, and said he had taken it for a clothes prop, and begged him not to report him, as it would ruin him. Witness compelled him to put back the timber. Bowker was acting as a temporary night watchman for the Cheshire Lines Committee. The con- stable created much laughter by refusing to answer some of Mr. Forshaw's questions, and he was reminded that that gentleman was his own solicitor—Cross-exa- mined by Mr. Browne, he admitted having quarrelled with the prisoner about 4 a. m. on the 13th inst., and on a previous occasion.—An engineer employed by the ompany, said the prisoner had told him he had used the timber for putting the lamps out, which it was his duty to do before the men came.—Mr. Browne,in addressing the court for the defence, said his client at the time had been on duty 24 hours at a stretch for the Company, and would hardly have his senses left after such a number of hours' work, to think of putting the prop in his own yard. He did not know what the Cheshire Lines Committee thought, but he knew what the public would think about one of their men being worked to this extent. He had used the prop simply to reach to put out the lamps. It was known what Rail- way Companies were, that they had no conscience and they did not take out summonses if they could apprehend, but his client had been summoned, thus proving that the prosecutor did not think the case was a strong one.— The case was dismissed on payment of costs.

div.head: MINO It CASES. WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT. MONDAY.—Before the Mayor (Alderman J. Greenall) and
div.p: MINO It CASES. WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT. MONDAY.—Before the Mayor (Alderman J. Greenall) and

Aldermen Francomb and Harrison. DRUNK AND REFUSING TO Williams was charged with being drunk and refusing to quit the Three Feathers Hotel, Bridge-st., on Saturday night, and assaulting Peter Wilson, (the landlord's son). The defendant appeared with a wound on his eye. From the evidence it appeared that the defendant went into the public house drunk and used foul language because he could not be supplied with drink, and knocked a man's glass over. He had to be put out twice, and in the struggle the defendant committed the assault. He was fined 40s. and costs. DRUNK AND DISORDSRLY.—John Crow was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Bridge-street, on Saturday night, and assaulting P.C. Rylatt. He threw himself down and kicked and bit the constable several times, tie was committed to prison for a month's hard labour.—James Templeton, was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Wilderspool-road on Sunday morning. and assaulting P.C. Hollingsworth. The con- stable on requesting him to leave a house in the street named for his disorderly conduct, was struck by him in the chest. He took him into custody, and had to struggle with him for a quarter of an hour. He wanted 'to stay all night where there were only three young women, one of whom he was courting, the father being in the Infirmary. He was fined 10s. and costs.—Jane Cartledge and Ellen Ttoberts were charged with being drunk and disorderly in Edelsten's Yard, on the 12th Inst. The women had had three rows between 10 and 11 o'clock. They were fined ss. each.—Bridget Kenny, and Wm. Ward drunk and disorderly on Friar's Green, on the same date, were fined,the former 2s. 6d., and the latter ss.—Edward Burke, in the Market Place on Satur- day night, was fined ss. and costs.—Wm. Hall, labourer, 2, Bakehouse Yard, for being drunk and disorderly in that yard and there assaulting his wife Ellen Hall, was sent to jail for 14 days. DRUNK mr CHARGE OF A HORSE.—Frederick John Cleaver, carter, 28, Elizabeth-street, for being drunk in charge of a horse and spring cart in Bridge-street, on the 15th inst., was fined ss. CHIMNEY ON FlRE.—Hamblett Dobson, a moulder' 17, Walker-st.. was fined is. for having his chimney on fire. SNOWBALLING FACTORY GIRLS.—Wm. Brooks, for snowballing on the 11th inst., girls employed at Cock- hedge Mills, was fined is. .TUESDAY.—Before Messrs. R. Garnett (chairman), and E. J. Guest. A STRANGR CHARACTER. Thomas Stephenson was charged with being found wandering about in Marsh House-lane, the previous afternoon, without any visible means of subsistence.—A constable deposed that the man had the appearance of being insane, and had no visible means.—The Chairman: No visible means of what ?—The Constable: Subsistence.—The Chairman: Well, the man is not to blame for that. What kind of way was he behaving 2—The Constable: All kinds of antics anti silly questions. He had been turned out of the barracks.—The Chairman: Was he drunk P—The Constable: No, he was quite sober.—Sergeant Gaythorne, of the barracks, said the prisoner had been in the army four or five weeks, and discharged as not likely to make an efficient soldier.—The prisoner said in the ordinary course as a prisoner at the bar he had something to say, and after asking the Chairman if he was a magistrate, and Mr. White if he was the magistrates' clerk, and be- ing satisfied on these points, proceeded to say "I am myself, Thomas Stephenson," and then made a lengthy and pretty consecutive statement as to certain articles and money of his being kept back at the barracks, de- daring excitedly, that with God's permission he would ' fight it out if he had to go before the Queen of England, and he was staving in Warrington to combat his enemies, and he would do it with God's aid and his own strength. —The prisoner was evidently a man of some education, and betrayed a strange mixture of mental derangement and clear-headness. It appeared he had originally been a clerk, and since a navvy. It was understood that he should be disposed of by being handed over to the Re- lieving Officer, or to his mother, whom the prisoner de- sired should be brought from Liverpool. WEDNESDAY.—Before Councillor James Fairclough (chairman), and Alderman Wright. DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—James Griffin, in Market Place, the previous night, ss. and costs. AN OBNOXIOUS WOMAN.—Eliza Smith, for objection- able conduct on Tuesday night, was discharged on pro- mising go back to the Workhouse. THURSDAY.—Before Alderman Chandley (chairman), Alderman Wright, and Councillor James Fairclough. NON-EDUCATION F CHILDREN.—The following parents ' were summoned by Mr. G. Riley, school attendance officer, for not sending their children to school :—Thes. Craddock, Longford-st. This was the case of a boy, and the mother who appeared, said she had birthed him for not going to school; and his father desired that he might have a ood birching in the police stations She begged that the magistrates would order this.—The Ch,irman thought that was the best thing for the lad. The birch- ing he: would get there was very different from that she would give him. Two strong men would get hold of him and deal with him. The lad promised to go to school more regularly, and the case was dismissed.—Peter Gar- land, furgetnan, Watkin-St., was next charged. Mr. Riley mentioned that the boy lived only a few steps from the school, but it was a fact that the nearer the schoal

the worse the attendance. The defendant was fined ss. —The case of Ann Griffiths, Eldon-st., was dismissed, on promise of amendment.—Patrick Hanlon, scrap iron dealer, Halifax-st. The mother. appeared, and blub- bered and cried almost continually. The Bench asked why the husband was not present, and Mr. Riley remarked that the defendants alwass sent their wives because they could dive way to emotion. A fine of 53. was imposed, and the woman exclaimed. "Thank you ; God bless you?—Mary Johnson, laundress, Kean- st., ss.—Peter Marsh, plumber and glazier, Rawlinson- st. In the course of this case the question of payment of fees came up, The Chairman asked if the Ist, 2nd, and 3rd Standards were not free in Warrington. Mr. Riley said they were not, except at the Roman Catholic Schools. The defendant was fined 2s. 6d.—Lydia Wil- cock, Arnold-st., a lady of independent means, 2s. 61— John McDonald, Bank-st., ss. FRlDAY.—Before Aldermen Harrison and Wright, Mr.

John White, and Dr. Gornall. ASSAULTING A COUNTY COURT BAIL I FF.—Frederick Shaw, New-road, Latchford. was charged with assault- ing Harry Faulkner, County Court bailiff, on the night of the Bth inst. Mr. Browne appeared for the prosecu- tion. The complainant said he went to the defendant's house with Mr. Frain, another bailiff entering at the back door. The defendant pulled off his coat to wash himself, that he might come, as he said, to see Mr. Browne, solicitor, then suddenly struck witness under the ear and knocked him against the table, then picked up a stick, and witness and Frain had to hold him to keep him from violence.—He was under the influence of drink.—Thos. Frain, the other bailiff, said the defendant attempted to strike him, but his wife restrained him. Witness corroborated Faulkner's evidence.—Alderman Harrison did not sit on the bench in this case.—riae defendant was fined 10s. and costs. NON-MAINTENANCE OF HIS MOTHER. Hoult, pattern maker, 25, Sand-st., Salford, at the instance of Mr. B. Shearer, on behalf of the Guardians, was com- mitted to prison for a month, for non-compliance with an order for maintenance of his mother. CRUELTY TO AwlltALS.—George Binnersley, Challinor- st., was charged by Inspector Dovrty, 11.5.F.C.A., with cruelly treating a dog by kicking it on ths 18th inst., belonging to Mr. Partington' of Friar's Green. He had kicked the dog so severely thal its eye had been knocked out. He was fined £1 and costs.—Wm. John Latham, a carter, Burtonwood, was charged by Inspector Dowty, with cruelly treating a horse by working it while in an unfit state, on Monday, and John Latham, carrier, with causing it to be so worked. The defendants were fined 10s. and costs each. CHARGES OF ASSAULT. —Jane Berry, School Brow, and Ellen Clough, 5, Hopwood-st.,were charged with assault- ing Mary Alice Bradshaw, 8, School Brow,Berry's sister- in-law. Mr. Browne appeared for the prosecution.— Clough was dismissed and Berry bound over in the sum! of £.5, to keep the peace for 6 months, and mulcted in I the costs, 12s. Bd.—Jane Davies, of Lymin, was charged with assaulting Annie Nicholson, of Booth's klill,Lyinm, and fined ss. including costs. Thomas Sheldon, a little, youthful - looking man, residing at 37,1 Golborne-street, was charged with assaulting Susannah Skeldon, his wife, a big portly looking woman. The fact of her charging him with assault created mnch laughter in court.—The defendant stated that she had run at him with a knife on the occasion.—Mr. White said he thought she might keep him in order if ' she liked. (Laughter.) She wanted a separation, but the Bench could not grant her that, and she was bound over to keep the peace, said ordered to pay costs, AN ABSENTEE APPRENTICE.—EIIen Ogden, apprentice, 18, Dutton-st., was charged by Edmund Mills, fustian cutter, Orford-street, with absenting herself from his service, putting him to the loss of 303. ; and Benjamin Ogden, her father, was placed in the box with her as responsible for payment of damages as her surety.--Mr. Mills having deposed to the circumstances of the case, the defendants called as witness Mary Jane Evans who said she had seen Mr. Mills give the fern de defendant four or five months since a smack in the face and knock her almost staggering aud come out with beastly language.—The defendant denied this, as also an assertion by her father, that he had said he would send her off and let her go on the streets.—The Bench accord- ingly made an order for £1 damages and costs and for the girl to go back.

WARRINGTON OCCASIONAL COURT. WEDNESDAY.—Before Mr. W. Mortimer. ALLEGRO TRIIFT OF HORSE BEM—Walter Warbur- ton, was charged with stealing, on the 20th inst. 31b. of horse flesh, value 6d., the property of Mr. James Toole. —Arthur Watson said he was caretaker, in the employ of Mr. Toole. The premises were surrounded by a fence about five feet high. He left his master's warks about a quarter past four o'clock on the Sunday in question,and went into a field near. From what be was told shortly aftewards he went towards Mr. Toole's works, and saw prisoner climbing over the fence. When de saw witness he tried to hide the flesh,which was in a handkerchief, behind the fence. He went tl the fence and found the meat. On going to the slaughter-house his found it had been cut off a hind quarter. He told his master of the occurrence.and witness was directed to give information to the police.—Michael Griffin, Tanner's-lane,forgeman, gave evidence as to seeing prisoner go over the fence and return in about five minutes.—Prisoner, who denied the theft, and said he went after a rat, was remanded to the County Session.

div.p: RUGBY.

WARRINGTON A v. FAILSWORTII OLD BOYS.—The weather was splendidly fine, and a crowd of moderate dimensions had assembled when the visitors started,and, with a strong breeze, quickly assumed an aggressive at- titude, eventually securing a try, the place failing. Dropping out, Antrobus, by a smart bit of play,enabled his side to gain a foothold in their opponents' quarters, but retaliation on the part of Taylor carried the struggle to the home line, and a minor was thought desirable to afford a slight relief. The Failsworth forwards quickly got together, and, screwing the scrimmages splendidly, got a footing in the Warrington territory. The im- minent danger to the home line made matters look ominous, but Ashurst exhibited fine defensive abilities, and Westall, Hampson, and Knowles obtained tempor- ary relief. While the game was fluctuating in the neighbourhood of the home 25, Lally passed smartly to Antrobus, who got splendidly away to the opposing 25. After this Daniels made a grand run to the line,but when the visiting ;forwards got together the defenders were soon attackers. Ashurst again proved the saviour of his side, but notwithstanding all his efforts another try was secured by the visitors, and halt-time arrived with Failsworth 0-2-3 to nil. Warrington restarted,and from a tricky throw-in, Webster secured and scored in the first minute. A reversal of matters to the previous half took place. A bout of passing between Antrobus, Lally,and Daniels,and some rushes by Molyneux, Barnes, Forster, and Warburton, forced the leather to the line, and Daniels throwing to Webster, the latter again scored Ashurst converting. By the aid of the drop out, Fails- worth took the warfare to the home quarters. Sampson, Barnes, Webster, and Russell ;leered any danger, but, the Old Boys returning to the attack, Sampson by a screw kick sent the game to midfield. Then Knowles, Hampsoe, Molyneux, and Forster showed their dribbling capacities, and Webster,picking up the ball at top speed, secured a fine try. After this Lally secured possession, making a fine effort to score, being forced into touch a yard from the line. Barnes with a run and kick was next prominent, but Failsworth, taking advantage of a bad miss, got right away to the other end. An exciting piece cf play ensued, Ashurst being called upon to save a dribble, screwed splendily down the field, and Lane mulling the ball, Westall raced up at full speed, seized the leather and passing beautifully to Hampson, this player ran in behind the posts for Ashurst to convert. The game continued to be prosecuted with vigour, the Warringtonians having a decided advantage, and at length Antrobus stole away " grandly, and passing to Webster, that player ended the scoring by securing his fourth try, Ashurst increasing the value of the point, and Warrington won by 3-2-1 to 0-2-3.
THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MARCH 26, 1892.

div.head: WARRINGTON v. BARROW.
div.p: WARRINGTON v. BARROW.

The visit to Barrow has always been en- joyed by Warrington, but perhaps the journey north was never more relished than on Satur- day, when Cavendish Park was patronised by four thou- sand spectators. The first match had resulted in a de- feat of the Warringtonians, and with this fact in view, the home executive sent a capital fifteen to do duty. Webster and Buckley cried off from the original list, letting in Potts and Bailey, so nothinc, was lost by the change. The day was beautifully fine, and a slight breeze blew from goal to goal. Warrington had the ad- vantage of this, though Barrow had won the toss, and Turner's kick off saw Berry and Jolley spoiling T. Bow- ker from returning. Passing by, Marshall and Harvey saved the attack, and Moore and Weatherall dribbled to Warrington quarters, Boscow saving. From the scrim- mage Bate stole away, and ran to the home quarter flag, but Evans failed to make headway, falling into the clutches of Harley. Heesom improved the advantage, and play was under the posts, and some cross passinz between Bate and Berry saw Handles collared on the line. Bowker relieved, Evans nipping up the oval from Weatherell's feat, and sending it past half way. Eventually Harley saved from a kick by James Bate. On the drop out Bowker got away, through Potts tackled him finely, but, despite this, the hornasters forced the game on the Warrington line. Turner and Teare headed the forwards to near the centte flag, but again Barrow attacked, this time Marshall and Haney being prominent. Jolly dribbled beautifully through the opposing backs, and Handles joining in the movement, with the aid of Bate, Potts, and fleesoin, Warrington were once more placed in the premier posi- tion, and Barley again saved. Bate maintained the attack, wm m mist Berry was almost a scorer from a tricky piece of work. Some fine forward play by' Davies, Thorniley, and Bailey frustrated Dickenson's effort to clear, but Jolley again showed up with a dribble. Boa- cow had now a chanced distinguishing himself, and a

dribble by Treweek was more than equalized by a judi- cious kick, which found touch near the quarter-flag. Tessin. by the Warrington backs saw Boaden intercept- ing, but Evans had his man, and another effort by Potts and Heesom registered the third minor. Barrow now had a chance, but some passing by their backs lacked finish, and Warrington cleared by the aid of Ashton, Turner, and Bate. Another rush of the home forwards was responded to by Ashton, Donohue, and Teare, and Bate and Berry treating the spectators to some neat pass- ing Jolley and Bandies finished up by taking play near to the line. It was now Warrington's chance, and, the oval being heeled out in double quick time, Berry, Bate, and Heesom passed well, and the latter ran in a fine try near the posts. The same player failed at the easy place. A penalty kick next fell to Warrington, but the kick was short, and Boscow responded. Ashton, Potts, Turner, and Jolley soon had the oval in the home lines again, but a fine run by Marshall was assisted by his forwards, and a try seemed imminent when Davies saved, a yard from the line. Evans eased the attack, and a penalty kick being taken by the last-named, the visitors rushed down the open, Berry and Turner being the shining lights. Turner essayed a drop at goal, but Harley ran the oval out, and Bate was held near the line a moment later. Berry next experienced hard lines, but fortune smiled on Warrington a minute from the call of the interval, for a rush by Berry saw Jolley completing a well-deserved try,and Heesom again failed at the easy place. Score at half-time : Warrington 0-2 —3 ; Barrow nil. Treweek restarted, and Barrow, with the aid of the stiffish breeze, soon attacked! A spell of give-and-take play was now indulged in, and for a while scrimmages monopolized the attention. A fine dribble by Turner, Bate, and Teare took play direct to the Barrow lines, and although Haney relieved, Bate, Berry, and Bandies, soon had the Furness men on the defensive again. Berry got away after Dickenson had punted to the quar- ter flag, but Handles held the oval too long, and a capi- tal chance of scoring was lost. Heesom tackled and saved splendidly, whilst Potts never failed to account for his man. A passing movement, initiated by Haney, was spoiled by Evans, and a smart kick by Boscovr negatived one by Dickenson. Warrington wete now having the worst of the deal, and it required all Bate's endeavours to prevent Marshall making headway. The attack was kept up for five minutes, and eventually Dickenson ran in from some loose play, but although Barrow's position was ridiculously easy, they too failed to convert. This was Barrow's last chance, for barely ten
minutts remained to beplayed.. Boscow was cheered -for a

fine piece of play, which gained twenty yards. The Warrington forwards asserted themselves in the latter stages of the game, Thorniley being prominent in one rush especially, whilst a fine run by Bate along touch was deserving of a score. Near time Jolley dribbled from half-way, and Harley only got up in the nick of time to kick dead. Final result: Warrington, 0-2--4; Barrow, 0-1-1. Teams :—Warrington: J. Boscow, back ; J. W. Evans, F. Heesom, and C. Potts, three-quarter backs; James Bate and James Berry, half backs; H. Ashton, Fair Turner, J. Jolley, W. Bandies, T. Donohue, H. Teare, J. T. Thorniley, T. Davies, and E. Bailey, forwards. Barrow: A. Harl3y, back; F. Bowker, Dickenson, and Boaden, three-quarter backs; Marshall and Haney, half backs; Witherall, Moore, Greaves, J. Bowker, Leach, Blezard, lialsall, E. Dickenson, and Treweek, forwards.

div.head: ASSOCIATION.
div.p: ASSOCIATION.

WARRINGTON GRAMMAR SCHOOL V. PENILETH FRIENDS' SCHOOL.—This match was played at Penketh on Satur- day, and resulted in a victory for the visitors by five goals to nil. The goals were shot by Dandy (2), Fen- nellv (2), and Isherwood (1). WARRINGTON' ASSOCIATION RIASHRTS Y. PENIERTH RH- maim—This match was played at Penketh, on Satur- day, in beautiful weather, before a large number of spectators. Penketh kicked off ,and at once pressed, and, their forwards, making a rush up the field, scored. War- rington retaliated, and after several ineffectual shots Mather scored. From the kick-off the visitors still main- tained the pressure. As the result of nice combination on the part of Thompson, Mather, Cornforch, and New- ton, the ball was neatly worked to the Penketh goal, but further progress was stayed by one of the Penketh backs handling, this bringing halt-time. Score—Pen- keth, one goal. Warrington, one goal. On resuming play Wanington again began to press, the backs, Dut- ton, Brooks, and Newton, playing a grand gams, the ball seldom if ever getting beyond the half-way line. From a combined rush of the visitors' forwards, Lavall scored, and shortly after Thompson shot through. The remainder of the game was a continual bombardment of the Penketh goal, and Warrington eventually ran out winners by three goals to one. Mather, Thompson, Brooks, Newton, Dutton, and Jones played splendidly. WARRINGTON ASSOCIATION Y. AIOBURTH VALE RESERVH. —Played at Warrington in splendid weather. Warring- ton had a strong sun to face, and Aigburth, kicking o'ff about 330 p.m., were early put on the defensive, Nor- man scoring three minutes from start. 'I he home team continued to press, Younger and Butler defending in a splendid- rnanner ; but Ball managed to increase the score for the home team after a bit of good passing. The visitors were the next to attack, resulting in Jones being beaten. After this reverse, Warrington playing with more vigour, the Aighurth goal was completely bombarded, Younger, Butler, and Grace playing a splen- did game. However, Norman, taking advantage of an opening, scored, with a splendid shot. The home team continued the attack, but half-time arrived, with the score—Warrington, 3 goals ; Aigburth, 1. Restarting, play was kept in midfield for a time, till Powell and Tickle, getting possession, soon made tracks for the visitors' goal ; bnt their final effort was weak. Apple- ton and Evans next had a try at Jones, Appleton managing to score the second point for the Vale. Even play followed until close on time, when Pierpoint man- sapghederteonneowtchtrtahveefloleudrtrlaippiodilnyt ffroorriltheenehoemhde etefatmhe. field ed to the other, each side trying to increase their score. The half backs tried with long kicks to lower the visitors' colours, Mather and Phillips making good attempts, but the opposing halves met them with some splendid head play, Goodwin and Cooke playing well. However, time was called with a score unaltered, Warrington winning a good game by 4 goals to 2.

div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.

FOOTBALL —RUGBY. The ties for the Yorkshire Rugby Cup were very liberally patronised on Saturday, that at Park Avenue being withessed by 15,000 spectators. Pontefract were not supposed to have much chance against Bradford ; nor had they, the latter winning by the large margin of 21 points to none. This was pretty decisive, but it was completely put into the shade by Leeds, who ran up no fewer thanlo points to ‘Vakefield St. Austin's two only. Potter was again very successful as a place-kicker, as he kicked 12 goals out of 16 chances. Huddersfield also , ran up a tall score against Normanton St. John's, as did Wakefield Trinity against a minor club. Dewsbury,how- ever, just scrambled into the next round by a single point only, their opponents being Hull Kingston Rovers. Halifax were similarly fortunate against Oxley. Brig- house Rangers, who are believed to have a good chance for the Cup, were among the winners, all the best clubs proving victorious. Two of these will meet in the next ties—viz., Huddersfield and Halifax. The match between Lancashire and Devonshire on Wednesday at Whalley Range resulted in an easy win for Lancashire by 2 goals and 3 tries (16 points) to 2 tries T. BCt ate, te' of Warrin,gton, again took his Lancashire, and in the first half p(4lapcoeianttsh.)aifla. got twice over the line, but on one occasion the ball was ruled back. The Devonians, though badly beaten, showed some nice play and their secand try was the out- come of an exceedingly smart passing movement.

ASSOCIATION. Despite the fact that Lancashire had no representa- tive in the final for the Football Association Cup, there was a tremendous gathering at the Oval on Saturday. Some of the estimates placed the attendance as high as 35,000, which, if anything like correct, is a record so far as this ground is concerned. For a full hour before the game started the enclosure was packed. There were many special trains from the Midlands, all of which were heavily freighted. It WAS only natural that Aston Villa were the favourites, as they had a much better record for the season than West Bromwich Albion. But, as was the case in 1887, the favourites were beaten. Then the Albion were generally' expected to win the cup for the first time, but the Villa beat them by two goals to none. Now almost everybody predicted the easy overthrow of the Albion, but again the prophets were wrong. The West Bromwich players rose to the occasion in a marvellous fashion, and, although they had to battle with the breeze in the first half, they opened the scoring in five minutes, and eventually won by three goals to none.

Viewed in the light of their very poor League record, which is. after all, the best test, the success of the West BroMwich men is surprising. They immediately settled down in a commanding style, and were as cool and col- lected as possible. They had not nearly so much of the play as their Birmingham rivals, but their tactics in front of goal were much more workmanlitce. Bassett's dashing runs down the right invariably led up to serious attacks on the Villa goal, and he was admittedly the smartest forward on the ground. The Albion half-backs also came off with flying colours, Reynolds putting in a vast amount of work. The backs were equally useful and perfectly safe, whilst Reader won golden opinions for his grand goalkeeping. He has shown great consistency all season, and is undoubtedly one of the best goalkeepers in the country.

The Villa had counted upon the Cup as a certainty for them, and they were deeply chagrined at their downfall. Their failure is surprising, in the face of their fine form against Sunderland, and their 12 goals to two defeat of Accrington in the League. The forwards passed in nice style, but their combination gave way before the deter- mined attention of the opposing half-backs. The latter trio were much cleverer than those that did duty for the Villa. Indeed, the Albion were a better team in every respect, and their great victory was well received by the vast crowd.

div.head: INQUIRY OFFICSR.S.
div.p: INQUIRY OFFICSR.S.

A letter was read from the Local Government Board, agreeing with the Board dispensing with the services of Mr. George Ward and Mr. Geo. Howard, as school in- quiry officers.—Mr. Brandreth moved that the inquiry officers for B ud worth and Frodsham district be suspended. He pointed out that they had now nothing to do.—Mr.. Speakman said they were now only paid one shilling a' week each, and as they must have someone to do the work a shilling a week was not much for an official.— The motion was carried.

div.head: SUNDAY _CLOSING,
div.p: SUNDAY _CLOSING,

The Chairman said he had received a circular letter requesting the Board to sign a petition in favour of the Sunday closing Bill for England introduced into the House of Commons by Mr. Broadhurst, M.P.—Mr. J. Edwards moved that the petition lie on the table.—Mr. Baguley moved that the petition be. signed.—Mr. T. Lea seconded.—Dr. Gastaldi supported on the ground that it would be a benefit to the working classes, and he believed that a Sunday closing act would lead to the spending of the Sabbath in a more befitting manner.— Mr. Lightburn seconded Mr. Edwards's motion and said he did not think Sunday closing would be an advantage to thecause of temperance. He thought closing public houses entirely on Sundays would lead people to drink in private houses, outside the surveillance of the police. If they would go in for having the houses open for din- ner and supper beer he would advocate such a measure. —For signing the petition 20 voted and the Chairman said he need not put to the contrary. There were 33 members present.

div.head: CHURCH ARMY.
div.p: THE CHURCH ARMY.
A communication from the Church Army with regard to able-bodied paupers was laid on the table without com- ment.
ASSESSMENT COMMITTEE.

Mr. Aaron presented the report of the Assessment Com- mittee, who unanimously recommended that, the Clerk be paid the usual salary of £B5 per annum and 20 guineas for legal expenses and expenses out of pocket. Usually the expenses had been from £4O to £6O a year.—The Chairman said the average legal costs for the past six years had been £4s.—Mr. Aaron moved that the report be adopted.—Mr. Speakman seconded.—Carried unani- mously.
SCHOOL ATTENDANCI4.

The Soho.' Attendance Committee recommended that the Clerk's salary for the past year be £3s.—The Rev. J. W. N. Tanner moved and Mr. Edwards seconded the adoption of the recommendation, which was carried unan4mously.
APPOINTMENT OF MEDICAL_ OFFICER FOR V RODSELM'.

The Itoard than proceeded to the appointment of a a medical officer for Frodsham District. The applicants were Dr. Robinson, Dr. Burton, and Dr. Wilkinson, and on the proposition of Mr. Speakman it was decided to make the selection by ballot.—Dr. Burton received 23 votes, DT. Robinson 9. Dr. Wilkinson 1, and the first- named was declared elected.

div.head: DEFAULTING OVERSEERS.
div.p: DEFAULTING OVERSEERS.

Mr. Btandreth, as chairman of the Finance Commit- tee reported that the balance in the treasurer's hands amounted to £4,252 19s. id., and said there were three townships that had not paid their calls, viz.—Freston- o'th-liill, £69 : Helsby, £77; and Sutton, £lo2.—Mr. Brandreth said he knew of one case where the overseer had had the money for a month, and he moved that the various overseers be summoned unless the calls were paid within 7 days--Mr. Aaron seconded. div.head: RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.
div.p: RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.

The fortnightly meeting was held on Tuesday, at Dutton Workhouse. Mr. J. Mclntyre presided, and there were present the Rev. J. W. N. Tanner, Messrs. ti. E. Heywood, E. Aaron, J. jitoWkeesir,,W.L.BEallgtile)' Ellison, J. Bate, J. Pickering, J. Hall, H. Lowe, P. Hall, J. Edwards, J. Brandreth, J. Smith, C. Mountield, John Whitlow, Jas. Whitlow, W. Whitlow, J. Lewis, J. Knowles, Jae. Parr, J. Ashton (clerk), and G. Ashton (deputy clerk). THE CLERIC AND LAW CHARGES. Mr. Heywood said that with reference to the proposi. tion to make the Clerk an allowance of £10) for law charges, the Committee appointed to deal with the sub- ject had received a letter from the Clerk, who stated that he did not bring the list of law charges forward with the view or the wish that the Board should vote him an extra iemuneration. He was asked to prepare it. He did feel, however, that the salary ought not to be less than Mr. Linaker's, but he never contemplated anything extra being voted in lieu of law charges, and he hoped the Committee that had been appointed would not think so' and moreover that they would not vote for it, for when he was appointed Clerk to the Board he was sure it was understood that general law charges would be in- cluded in the salaries, and he should not like the Guar- dians any wtay of e breakinge I tlt at he of ra ithose supportedh Clerk e him w e rceo con- tinued: n- tinned : I have every confidence that should there at any

time be an extra amount of legal work the Authority will take it into consideration, but at present there is not. I feel that during the time I have held office the Guard- ians have been well satisfied, and that a kindly feeling exists between them and me, and I would not, for any amount that might be voted me, have that feeling dis- turbed. To my mind the relations between a Board of Guardians and their Clerk should be, not that what he does is for the sake of getting extra pay, but that they should have confidence in him that his advice is entirely ' unbiassed by any pecuniary motive ; and the work will be much pleasanter for the Clerk, and the interests of the Board will be better served, and my wish is to gain that confidence, and to do all I can in the interests of the Bodtd, and, as a consequence, of the ratepayers. I shall call the Committee together, not with the view of getting an extra vote f•d- law charges, which I should not feel it right to accept, but because it will be re- corded on the minutes that I was directed to do so." Mr. Heywood said the Committee after considering that letter were of opinion that the subject of extra remuneration had better be dropped in the present instance and had passed a resolution accordingly.—Mr. Brandreth seconded the recommendation, which was carried.

div.head: NEW BOOKS, &c.
div.p: NEW BOOKS, &c.
"The Scott Library," is the title of a new series of prose volumes which has been commenced by Mr. Walter Scott, whose "Canterbury Poets," "Great Writers" and Camelot volumes have been so won-
derfully successful. The intention is to publish, in volumes at is. gd. each, well-known works of Flog-
llsh and continental literature, and translations classical works, The first of the series to band is
kyindication c=f the rights of woman," by Mary

Wolstonecraft, with an introduction by Elizabeth Robins Pennell. 7lie re-issue of this work is espe- cially appropriate at a time when the rights of women are receiving yearby year practical acknow- ledgmen at the hands of the legislature. It is jaet 100 years-since that she celebrated vindication _was
published,. and it is One to Mary. Woletoneeraft to say that it was the beginning of a revolution in the treatment of women the effects of which we are
feeling to-day. The work is an essentially argu- mentative one. It is written in a vivid and

picturesque style, and, unlike most treatises of its class, it may be said to be alive from beginning to end. The introductory note gives a brief and criti- cal account of' the career and works of a woman who was famous in herself, and as the mother of the girl who became the wife of the poet, Shelley. " German Ballads" is the title of the latest issue of the Canterbury Bbets series of volumes,- as translated and edited by Elizabeth Crahranyle, whose introc3uctory note will be read with especial interest by all students of literature, and especially ballad literature'. The con- tents include the ballads of Goethe, Schiller,. Burger, Uhland, Heine, Ruckert,Platen, Freiligrath, Herder, and

, other writers. It is a matter of course to say that the purchaser of this shilling volume obtains some of the to choicest selections of German literature. Following the ballads are a series of notes which greatly add their interest.

"Queen Elizabeth," by Mr. Edward Spencer Bees4v, has just been published by Messrs. Macmillan and Co., in their " Twelve English Statesmen" series. These short biographies seek to present in historic order the lives and work of those leading actors in our affairs who by a direct influence have left an abiding mark on the policy, the institutions, and position of Great Britain. Judged from this point of view, Queen Elizabeth, is re- garded as a statesman of a high order, although-it can- not be said that she had a high character as a woman. She has been represented by some writers as narrow, mean, and selfish, but that is not the opinion of the writer of this biography. He says:—" In her intel- lectual grasp of European politics as a whole, and of the interests of her own kingdom, Elizabeth was probably superior to any of her counsellors." Referring to Mary, Queen of Scots, he says :—" In ability and in- formation she was not at all inferior to Elizabeth. In promptitude and energy,, she was her superior. These masculine qualities might have given her a, vic- tory in a bitter duel, but that in the all-important domain of feeling her sex indomitably asserted itself, and weighted her too heavily to match the superb, self- control of Elizabeth. She can love and she can hate. Elizabeth had only likes and dislikes, and' therefore played the cooler game." The work is throughout dis- passionately written, with a view, of course, of judging. Elizabeth as a ruler rather than a woman. It betrays - a thorough mastery of the subject, and is written in a. style which is alike solid and interesting. " Natural Science," is the title of a new monthly review of scientific progress. It is published by Messrs. Macmillan and Co., price is. The object of it is to in- terpret simply, and without excessive technicalities,.the main results of contemporary work in natural science to those who try to follow the general progress of modern thought. Amongst the papers, some of which are il- lustrated, we have "The evolution of fins ;7' " Marine snakes" " Deep sea deposits ;" " English. lake dwel- lings ;" "Explorations of coral reefs by borings ;" " The mammals of Indiaotc." It will be seen that the magazine makes a capital start, and there is every reason to be- lieve that it will be found acceptable to a large body of, readers. _ _ _

Part 6 is to hand of Green's " Short history of the English people." It has for frontispiece a reproduction in colours of " Matthew Paris at the feet of the Virgin and Child." The present part, like its predecessors, is profusely and admirably illustrated, and there is a repro- duction of the Great Charter.
The" English Illustrated Magazine" for March leads off with a fine portrait of the late Duke of Clarence. _ . _ . .

It is followed by a-paper "The Queen's Riviera residence," with illustrations by Major Ricketts. Other illustrated : articles include "Athletic Sports at Oxford and Cambridge Universities," " Among the Western song-men," " The Royal Mews," !!tc. " Lost," a capital complete story of the Australian bush, by Mary Gaunt, is beautifully illus- trated by Mr. E. F. Brewtenall, R.W.S., formerly of Warrington. The leading paper in the" Westminster Review" is on "Liberal prospects at the general election," and is from the pen of Mr. J. Douglas Holms. It is a careful and thoughtful summing up of the contingencies on all sides, and results in an estimated Liberal majority of 90. The Rev. L. J. Wallace has something to say in favour of vivisection. In view of the reckless statements which are made as to the cruelty of vivisection, the article is one which ought to be carefully considered. He cites numerous instances of the progress in science which has resulted from experiments in vivisection, and shows that it would be a loss to humanity to abolish them. There is a wide difference, it need hardly be said, between vivisection as it is freely practised on the continent and as it is practised in this country, under the restrictions which the law enforces. The moral of the paper would seem to be that so far as the United Kingdom is concerned, there is no need for the public to trouble themselves about the practice of vivisection. Among the other papers in this month's issue are" The New Forest and the War Office," by Joseph King ; " The logic of a despot's advocate," by D. G. Ritchie; "4 The West Indies as a winter resort," by H. F. Abell ; 'The platform," by the Right Bon. G. Osborne Mor- gan, Q.C., M.P. ; " A new State University," by S. H. Boult ; " The great Civil war in England," by M. W. Whelpton •, " Rectification of frontier," by J. Da- costa ; and " Contemporary literature " ; with the usual review of science, philosophy, theology, sociology, politics, voyages and travels, history and biography, belles lettres and poetry. In the "Century Magazine" there is as a frontispiece a fine portrait of Paderewhiski, the celebrated pianist. In the body of the magazine itself there is a biographical sketch by. Fanny Morris Smith, followed by a poem by R. W. Gilder on "H,w Padere whiski plays!' A paper on St. Paul's Cathedral is splendidly illustrated from pic- tures by Joseph Pennell and W. J. Baer. "The United States Fish Commission," which is illustrated, is an ex- traordinary revelation of the marvels of sea life: Gior- gione, one of the old Italian masters, is dealt with this month by Mr. W. J. Stillman. Other illustrated papers are on "Middle Georgia rural life " ; " Our Tolstoi club" ; and "The village romance." The supply of story and verse is, as usual, excellent, and there are some choice things under the head of "'ln lighter vein." The "Strand Magazine" keeps up its distinguishing feature by giving portraits of celebrities at different times of their lives. " The adventures of Sherlock Holmes "have reached the 9th paper, and lose nane of ! their interest. Sir John Lubbock contributes a second illustrated paper on "Beauty in Nature," and there is. a good supply, as usual, of short stories, along with an illustrated "*lnterview with Professor Blackie." "The Ladies' Treasury" for March maintains its high position as a household magazine of literature, educa- tion, and fashion. There is an exceptionally good por- trait of Princess Victoria Mary of Peck, with a brief historical sketch. There is a good supply of fashion plates, several interesting short stories and papers and a portrait of Spurgeon, with a sketch, of his career. " Hygiene ' is a capital sixpenny sanitary and social monthly magazine. It would be well for the health of the community if it were more generally read, and especially such papers as that by Professor Goodfellow on" Recent hygienic improvements in breed-making." " The New Era," price 2d., is a review of social work and movements in the churches. Its contents are of a most varied character, and it is brightened by several excellent portraits.

div.head: TRADES COUNCIL CONCERT.
div.p: TRADES COUNCIL CONCERT.

The second annual concert under the auspices of the Warrington Trades and Labour Council was held in the Public Hall, Warrington, on Saturday evening. There was a good attendance. The pro- gramme comprised the following :—Selections by the band, a duet by Madame Dick and Miss Fan- ahaw, songs by Madame Dick, Miss Panshaw, Mr. Grounds, Mr. N. Cook, and Mr. Dockrey, a duo by Herr Praeger, which was remarkable for being a simultaneous performance on the piano and the violin; and recitations by Mr. Furniss. The duet was encored ; and Madame Dick, Miss Fansintw, Mr. Grounds, and Mr. Furness. Mr. George Riley acted as accompanist. During the interval, Councillor Flood, who occupied a seat on the platform ad- dressed a few remarks to the audience. He said the aim and object of a Trades Council was very apt to be misunderstood by the people. Some were under the impression that it was organised for the express pur- pose of fomenting discord and bad feeling between employers and employed. That was quite a misappre- hension. If it were not for the intervention of the Trades Council a great deal more trouble woold exist between capital and labour in Warrington than there did. It had been the aim and object of the Trades Council to keep in check anything like an antagonistic spirit, and promote peace and conciliation between them. Many difficulties had occurred in Warrington that might have been prolonged and might have resulted in disaster or failure to both parties but for the exertions of the Trades Council, and the wisdom and spirit of good will and good fellowship that prevailed upon it, and which to the credit of Warrington at present largely existed between the employers and employed of the town. The concert had been organised for the express purpose of raising funds to promote lectures for the education of the people upon questions of the relations between capital and labour.—The proceediugs concluded with the singing of the National &ahem,
NARROW ESCAPES FROM DROWNING.

At VVicklow Assizes, on Wednesday, James Hanley, aged 17, brother of Daniel Hanley, who was on Satur- day found guilty of the murder of Mary Anne Lyons, was convicted of taking part in the same offence and sentenced to be hanged. The jury recommended him to mercy on the ground of his youth. Sentence of death was passed at Cork Assizes on Wed- nesday on a man named Joseph Joyce for the murder of Patrick O'Leary, a fish merchant. Prisoner, who was a Parnellite, had made hostile remarks concerning the deceased, who was an anti-P,trnellite, and on February 61-h, he struck him a fatal blow on the head with a cleaver.

div.head: BRAVE CONDUCT OF A MOTHER.
div.p: BRAVE CONDUCT OF A MOTHER.

A mother and her child, living at Howley Quay, at Warrington, had a narrow escape from drowning on Saturday evening. It appears that shortly after six o'clock Lottie Rivers, six years of age, daughter of George Rivers,a joiner in the service of the Itlan- chester ship Canal Company, while playing with other children on the river side, opposite her home, fell into the water. The shouts of the children on the bank attracted the attention of Mrs. Rivers to the accident She ran up to them,and seeing Lottie in the water,jrimped in after her, withoul a mo- rnent's hesitation. She succeeded in catching hold of her clothes, but it is probable that both raother and child would have been drowned but for the

timely assistance of Joseph Foster, the foreman em- ployed at an adjoining tannery, who threw a life buoy into the water. This enabled the woman to float while a boat was lowered, when she and her daughter were ressued,the mother being very much exhausted.
PRESENTATION TO MR. A. RATHBONE.

On Saturday evening, Mr. A. P'..e,,thbone, until lately sub-manager at the Whitecroes Company's workerat Warringtoil,but now manager at Messrs. Smiths, of Dallam-lane„bras presented with a hand- some cabinet which had been subscribed for by workmen at the Whitecroes Works. The presenta- tion Viraa• made at a largely-attended social gather- ing held in the Co-operative Hall, Sankey-et., pre- sided ever by Mr. S. Roberts. Prior to, the pre- sentation meeting an excellent tea was partaken of by a large number of persons. The CHAIRMAN, in opening the proceedings at the meeting, said he had been acquainted with Mr. Rathbone for tepwards of 030 years and lie•did not think thereiwas a man who could say anything against him, If any of the workmen had: had a complaint to make he had listened to them,. and if their request was reasonable he had alwayslallen In with it. He had done his, duty to the men and also to the masters. (Hear, hear and applause.) When it came to the knowledge of the men that Mr. Rathbone was about to sever his connection with them they determined to make a presentation to him, and that presentation, had taken the form, of a cabinet, which would no doubt often remind him of days gone by.. (Lena applause.) The presentation was afterwards made by Mr. J. CaowTnismwho said it was with the greatest plea- sure that he performed the duty he had to perform: that evening. He might say that he along with many others, was surprised when he heard that Mr. Hathbone was about to leave' them, but every one seemed to be of opin- ion that they should not let him go without showing some appreciation of the feeling with which he had always en- deavoured to carry out his work amongst them. (Hear-, hear.) He could tell' Mr. Rathbone that there had never been anything contributed with, more liberality or greater spontaneity than had the contributions for that testimonial, which was to show him their appreciation and respect. (Applause.) Mr. Rathbone had always shown both moral and mental qualities which it would be worth their while to try to practise, and he thought ' they would all agree with their chairman when he said that if ever the men had a grievance Mr. Rathbone was always prepared to listen to what they had to say. (Hear, hear.) Another good quality that he had was that of patience. 'They would agree that he had been endowed with a good deal of that, and it was certainly worth the while of all of them to try to emulate him in that respect. (Applause.) Though Mr. Rs t hbone had left them he carried with him their best opinion. Mr. Crowther then, in a few well-chosen words, made the presentation to Mr. Rathbone. . Mr. RATHBONE, who, was received with much applause, . _ . . . .

, thanked them for the beautiful testimonial which they had given him. He had laboured amongst them for a period of nearly a quarter of a century. Upwards of 24 years service had he given to the Whitecross Company,. and about half that time he had spent in the position which he lately occupied amongst them. He had always endeavoured to do his duty, for the best interests of the firm which engaged him; consistent with that which was right and just towards the men he had under his charg.e. (Hear, hear, end applause) From the first he had set the task before him, that he would always give.an attentive ear to any grievance that the men had to bring before him. He had always listened to what the men had to say and had endeavoured to put himself in their po;ition, and he thought that had had the result of inspiring confidence in him and had helped him vary much:in the duty he had had to perform. (Hear, hear.) He again warmly thanked the donors for the handsome gift, and added that he would always greatly value it not because of its monetary worth but because of the motives which moved them to present it to them. (Loud applause.) In the course of the evening a short address was alto given by Mr. T. Birchall, and an excellent programme of music was well rendered.

div.head: LATE CHARLES BRAD LAUGH.
div.p: THE LATE CHARLES BRAD LAUGH.

On Monday evening a meeting was held in the Winwick-st. Co-operative Hall, under the auvpices of the National Secular Society, at which Mr. G. W. Foote, president of that Society, and editor of the " Freethinker," gave an" Oration on Charles Brad- laugh.' The chair was taken by Mr. Jno. Peers, and there was a fair attendance.

The CEL4.2IIIV.N. in his opening remarks, said that al- though a much better chairman might have been secured, he at all events possessed two qualities for the• position. He was, first of all, undeterred from taking the chair by the spirit which kept people from doing right through fear that somebody else should think they were doing wrong ;, and, in the second place, he was ectirely unat- tached and unbiassed by any religious opinion. In fact for any man to pledge himself in the present state of re- ligious, opinion was an act of folly. With regard to the subject of the lecture there that night, he recognised in. Charles Bradlaugh one of the latest of the long list of champions of intellectual freedom which this country has produced. They had personal liberty in England, but they also wanted liberty of the intellect, and Charles Bradlaugh worked very efficiently in that direction, and if there were no other cause for their consideration of him that alone should give them a great regard for his memory. (Applause.) Mr. FOOTE, who was received with applause, said they were that evening to spend an hour in considering the career of a great Englishman, for, since Charles Brad- laugh's death, all parties had agreed to recognise him in that light. Thirty years ago he was one of the best abused and misrepresented men in all England. He was poor in circumstances and without influential friends. He had risen, so far as he had risen, from the lowest rung of the social ladder. Owing probably to the ad- vanced opinions upon all subjects which he entertained and propounded, and, in short, in consequence of his being very considerably in advance of his time, he was hated by the prejudiced and privileged classes and libel- led by the populous race of bigots, and that seemed to be a species which England produced in greater abun- dance than any other country he knew of. (Hear, hear.) No conamon man could have so altered the public estimate of his character, no man could have climbed honestly, as Charles Bradlaugh did,, without being the possessor of great intellectual and moral qua- lities. It was well that that ',fact was now admitted, but how much better it would have been, if those who had wasted vain tears of regret over his grave, had only been sensible enough to recognise his greatness. before they tried to ruin him. Had they refrained. from that his life would have been prolonged and his great intellec- tual ability and force of character would have been in- valuable in the legislature of England. (Applause.) Mr. Bradlaugh was the most determined and inflexible man he had ever met in the course of his life, and public work had thrown him in contact with hundreds of public characters. When he had once set his mind up- on anything he kept it in view and never forgot it. He meant to reach a certain place, and in a given time he was bound to arrive there. (Applause.). Having ex- pressed the opinion that Charles Bradlaugh was the greatest popular orator of his time, Mr. Fbote went on to refer to the struggle for admission to the House of Commons. He (Mr. Foote) had said at the funeral of Mr. Bradlaugh that two things had killed him. The first was the Titanic struggle with the bigots of the House dCommons, and the second was the nen-pay- ment of members. The first sapped his strength, and the latter finished him. If a country wanted a man to serve it the country should pay the man a wage for it. (Applause.) It has sometimesbeen said that Bradlaugh was amassing wealth at the expense of his dupes, bat that wealth proved to be nothing when he died. He died worth absolutely nothing, yet he lived plainly. (Hear, hear and applause.) After the lecture a question was asked by one of the audience as to what Bradlaugh had done to diminish human suffering, and in answer to this Mr. Foote men- tioned the beneficent measures Bradlaugh had struggle for, and also alluded to acts of benevolence of which he made no display. coVneoltuedseod hftthearankesetitg.othe lecturer and the Chairman and Trisau POPULARSupper i su seasons iciaactAorzßuitsregotco. trohoeonmf,rtZef4a. strengthening, dvt. 1 pure. div.head: WEEKLY HALF HOLIDAY QUESTiON.
div.p: THE WEEKLY HALF HOLIDAY QUESTiON.

Sir,—l observe in the local papers that a large number of the shopkeepers have decided on supporting a Thurs- day afternoon closing, and that a large number have decided against it. Now, it must be palpably apparent to every oue that it would be exceedingly inconvenient for people coming from the country, to say nothing about townspeople, to find on a Thursday afternoon, if they come to do shopping, one half of the shops open and the others closed. It would be neither one thing nor the other. I would therefore suggest that, inasmuch as Saturday afternoon is, and has been for many years past, observed as a half holiday in all works, artisan trades, and professional offices, that the like should be observed in all shops and trades, of every kind. Let Friday, and Frida y evening, be the day and time for show and shopping, instead of Saturday; let all wages be paid on Thursday and Friday instead of Saturday; and let all shops close at one on Saturdays. This would be by far the simplest and most generally convenient and satisfactory plan. It would also be in accordance with the custom now prevailing in all the principal shops and places of business in London, Manchester, Liverpool, and other large towns, and the Saturday half holiday would afford the shopkeepers and their assist- ants the opportunity of taking a holiday from one on Saturday till Monday morning, and enable them to avail themselves of the Saturday afternoon football, cricket, &c., &c. To take a half holiday on Thursday, and that only by one half of the shops,when all the works,offices, and other artizan places of business are open and in full swing, and to remain in the shops on Saturday after- noons and evenings up to 10 or 11 o'clock, when all works, offices, and artisan places of business are closed, seems to be a most inconvenient arrangement. Let it be an all round Saturday afternoon holiday, and it will work well and satisfactorily for all shopkeepers, assist- ants, and the public.—Yours truly "As ADVOCATE FOR A HALF HOLIDAY." Warrington, March 24, 1892.

div.head: RICHMOND & CO.'S STATEMENT BY MR. SANDERS.
div.p: RICHMOND & CO.'S STATEMENT BY MR. SANDERS.
END OF THE STRIKE AT MESSRS.

At the request of Mr. H. Sanders, General Secre- tary to the IN ational Stove Grate Workers' Union, a representative of the " Examiner " on Wednesday had an interview with him on the subject of the strike of unionists in connection with the above- named works, when he made to him the following statement :-This strike was brought to an abrupt conclusion last Monday. The cause was mainly that the men lost confidence in each other in consequ- ence of a number of them secretly endeavouring to get re-instated by Messrs. Richmond as non-union men. Of the 70 men who struck, a few have obtained em- ployment in the same or other trades in Warrington' and elsewhere, while most of the others have applied to be again employed at Messrs. Richmond's but, so far as Mr. Sanders can learn, only about 20 have been re- engaged, there being vacancies for no more, though pro- bably some are anticipating accepting employment under the firm when the extension of their works at , present being carried out is completed. About 40 men remain unemployed and will still be provided for by the union and, perhaps, public subscriptions. The people , of Warrington' chiefly the working-men, have during the four weeks of the strike subscribed £e9 19s. 21. in aid of the unemployed men. It has been asserted that the subscriptions were remitted by the Strike Com- mittee to the central union, and that less than the amount subscribed was returned for the men. This Mr. Sanders says is false, the whole of the subscribed funds having been dealt out to them on receipt by the Strike Committee alone. The union during the strike has allowed to the men strike pay to the amount of £129 Ts. 9d., and incurred additional expenses amounting to is. Bd., making, that is, after deducting the subscriptions ; a total expenditure of £l2O 9s. 3d. The strike pay has been allowed, although none of the men were really entitled to it, having only been mem- bers of the union a few months. Mr. Sanders desires to give an emphatic denial to a statement made by Mr. Browne,solicitor, on the occasion of the three men charged with picketing being brought up at the police court, that he (Mr. Sanders) wired to the men to leave their work. On the contrary, he says, he wired to the men to continue work pending negotiations and to the firm suggesting arbitration,but received no reply from the latter. The fact that Messrs.Richmorni in their advertise- ment for employes, stated " No union required," was a confutation of the assertion made by Mr. Browne that the ' firm objected only to the National Stove Grate Workers' Union and not to other unions to which their min be- longed. There is, he says, no other union in existence in the trade worthy of mention, the largest of the others not numbering more than 250 members, and being for fitters only, and hence the National Union can hardly deserve to he styled, by Mr. Browne a bastard or illegiti- mate Union. So far from having sought to compel the members of the other unions to join it, nothing has been done beyond endeavouring to persuade them, and as a matter of fact, it has allowed equal strike pay to the three men among the strikers who belonged to other unions, and would have done the same to any number of such men.

div.head: CONCERT.
div.p: CONCERT.

On Thursday evening—a- -concert in aid of the unem- ployed men was given in the Co-operative Hall, Sankey- street, There was a pretty good audience. The artistes were Miss Coriield, of Manchester, soprano, who took the place of Madame Cecilia Hawksey. of the same city; Miss Bessie Fanshaw, contralto ; Mr. Wm. Dockrey, 1 tenor ; Mr. Robert Anderton, basso; and trombone soloist ; Mr. George Taylor, Tyrolean vocalist ; Mr. Richard Scarisbrick, comedian, and Mr. 0. J. Praeger. accompanist. During the interval, Mr. John Price, predident of the Trades' Council thanked the audience on behalf of the men, for their support that night, and those who had supported them in the past; and appealed for the continuation of it till they got employment. The proceedings concluded with the national anthem.

A verdict of "Suicide whilst of unsound mind" was returned at an inquest held on Wednesday, on the body of Mr. Arthur Goring Thomas, aged 41 years, musical composer, whc met his death at the West Hampstead station of the Metropolitan Railway, on Sunday evening tut

Widowed women Fatherless children

An' o' for th' sake 'o' one fezzant ! Well, that's one way o' lookin' at id, an' it's wod aw co' a double-barrell'd squint, to say th' leeast. A lot o' pappers 'll say owt as is unfair abeawt cases o' this soort, for th' sake o' mekkin' pollitickle capital eawt o' th' job, an' they co' th' Hooam Secke- tary too ill to brun ; Tory an' Radical alike, mind yo' for there's isn'd a pin to choose between 'em. As for private individuals an' their excited expressions ov opinion sent to th' noospappers—well there's olez a lot o' men an' wimmen ready to mek ony excuse for geddin' a big dose o' maudlin' sentiment off their chest, they dud.id o'er Mrs. Maybrick. an' Mrs. Os- borne. They tawk abeawt th' widows an' orphans o' th' two pooachers as were hung last week, an' th' family o' th' pooacher as were stranspoorted, but never a word o th' two widows an' eight childer o' th two gamekeepers as were brutally morthered th' execution o' their duty in' th' same way as two policemen met be killed.

Yo' know there were wonst a young chap (sooa th buzz goas) as morthered his fayther an' mother, an' at his trial he bed th' cheek to plead for mercy on ackeawnt ov his bein' a Orphan ! Well, thad may be a bit cry a ratchet, but iv id isn'd aw'll bet as some o' th' noospappers o th' time lied sympathetic headers ov his plea, an' letters fro' " Indignant Englishmen" on th' Judge bein' so callous as to ignore sich a affectin' appeal. Yigh, aw'll bet on thad. Aw'm as ready as onybody to own as its a gret pity as ony reckless or unthinkin' chap should be hung for th' sake of poachin' a hare or a fezzant, or for borglin' a bit o' stuff nod woth th' vally o' ayther ; but laws are laws an' mon be enforced, or else—!

div.head: This tawk abeawt payment o' members o' Perlyment suits mi. _

_ Yo' see aw've ambitions thad rooad mysel,— nod for payin' th' members, but beim' paid as a member: aw think there's more brass i' thad nor weyvin', an welly as mich as there is in a inshurance book. Aw could speawt,iv aw were paid wee! for (loin' id; an' aw could agitate; 07 aw could howd mi din— iv th' pay were th' same. Aw know wod werkin' chaps wont, an' they owt to ha' hed o' th' lot jener- ations sin'—an' they wod ha' bed 'em iv they'd lied th' reight chaps to represent 'em. Fost ov o' they want this poetical item: Eight heawrs werk,

Eig-ht heawrs Eight heawrs sleep, An eight bob a day. Then they want th' jerry-shops keepin' oppen neet an' day, and Free Booze as weel as Free Eddi- cation ; they dorn'd keer whether it's a Radical or Tory Government as confers this boon. Aw could frame a popular measure affectin' Free Libraries, sooa as bleak could coss herd up i' th' readin' reawrn, an spit on th' floor, an' smook thick twist, and leet their pipes wi' a leeaf eawt o' th' book they were lookin' at. An' th' laws relatin' to public perks wants awterin' to alleaw everybody as walks through 'em to poo a rooasy for their button-hoyle, an' to tek a handiul hooam for th' childer ; an' abeawt Kesmas time to help thersels to a duck off th' lake. There's a tooathri moore things as aw hey up mi sleeve as'll force eawt trumps, but aw'm savin 'em to play mi lection address ; onybody as wants forther perticklers should send seven penny stamps. Wonders never do ceease. Tly chap as wrooat them plays an' things for William Shakespeare tawkt abeawt id bein' waste- ful an' ridiculous excess to paint th' lily; but thad's wod fooak's beawn to do. An' nod only wi'lilies, but wi' other fleawers as wee!. Fancy, hevin' a blue , an' yellow striped lily, ur a green pink, or a rooasy as piebald as a circus hoes I Happen these scienti- ' flck chaps 'll gooa forther bi addin "an odour to thb violet "—yigh, an' to th' Pork-cap lilies aboon o' ; iv they do that they con pleease thersels abeawt gildin' refined (marl) gowd. Aw do hooap they'll discover th' way to do this pertumin' atoor plantin' i' aniline dyes comes i' th' fashion, an' then th' vegetable kingdom 'll be perfection; at present a Pork-cap lily bi ony other name wod smell as—ronk au' stop ony clock at fifty,t7ds, heawever mony hoyles id were jewelled in we pig iron.

Let's congratulate one another on th' end in' o' th' bit o' th' halladay th' Miners hes bed. We're fain to see 'em back, an' we hooap they'll stop. An' between this an' th' next halladay we're unanimous wishin' they'll arrange for things bein' settled beawt ony bother, sich as we've just bed ; thad Bill as aw'm i' favour on—eight heawrs werk, ets3ttera —is wod th' colliers want, an' they owl to here id! div.head: EXHIBITION OF GAS APPLIANCES AT
div.p: EXHIBITION OF GAS APPLIANCES AT

WIDNES. On Tuesday an exhibition of the gas appliances for domestic purposes made by Messrs. Richmond an Company, Limited, gas engineers, Warrington, was opened in the Lacey-street, schoolroom, Widnes The exhibition was promoted by the Widnes Gas Department, and in connection with it demonstra- tive lectures on cookery were given by Miss E. E. Golding, of London. Amongst the chief features of the exhibition was an admirably contrived Cooking range, which might be used or many purposes. The top of the stove is formed of bars upon which pans are placed for boiling purposes. The bars are removable in three parts so that they can be lifted off when the burners beneath require cleaning. The hot plate of the range is fitted up with various boiling burners, two being for sitnmering purposes. A chief feature of the hot plate is a grilling burner for grilling chops and steaks and frying bacon, and which will, it is claimed, toast a piece of bread on both sides in one minute. On the top of the oven is a white en- I amelled plate which makes the cleaning very much easier. The oven of this stove is con- structed on the outside of cast iron, the inner part being lined with enamelled steel plates, and between the two there is a packing of slag-wool which is a non- conductor of heat. The interior of the oven is fitted up with shelves, and a special feature is that everything can be removed from the inside, which, of course, very greatly facilitates cleaning. There are two sizes of the stove, the larger being suitable for a family of from eight to ten persons, and, it is said,that breakfast, dinner, and tea can be prepared for that number of people at a cost of not more than 10. worth of gas. Both this stove and a smaller size for six or eight parsons are hired out by the Gas Department if required, the former at a charge , of 3s. and the latter of 2s. 61. per quarter. In addition' to these ranges, there was also a large selection of draw- I ing room and sitting room gas fires, including some fine specimens of bronze stoves; tubular stoves, suitable for offices, shops, &c., where it is inconvenient to have a flue ; and smaller heating stoves for bedrooms. Amongst other features of the exhibition were a patent gas iron which is kept hot all the time ironing is going on by the fact that a small gas jet is kept burning within ; and also a considerable variety of chandeliers, hall lamps, &c., which were shown by the Local Board. At the time the opening of the exhibition took place there was only a small attendance. The members of the Local Board present were Mr. H. S. Timmis and Mr. J. I Taylor, and, in the absence of Mr. Brown, the chairman of the Gas Committee. Mr. Tirnmis, declared the exhibi- tion open. That exhibition, he said, was promoted be- cause the Local Board believed that when they had such stoves as those supplied by Messrs. Richmond and Co., and could get gas at the price it was sold at in Widnes, the use of gas stoves was a great economy. The Local Board also wanted to sell all the gas they possibly could, for the more they sold the cheaper they produced it, and that again benefitted the people of Widnes.
