div.head: TORY WAIL.
div.p: A TORY WAIL.
" REMOVED FOR CONVENIENCE OF SALE."

ANV'M gettin' quite sick o' eaur Party, Thay caunt tell me wheer "Robert's" gone; An' aw caunt be expected t' be hearty, Wen aw cannot discaver my mon. One tells me aw don't need to wurry, An' sez aw shall know i' my kail; Wile another, sez, lookin' quite merry, He's "removed fer convenience o' sale!"
That seaunds like a Okshuneer's sayin', An' Suttonly looks rayther quare ; But it met be an owd Baalum prayin',
Fer wot aw eawr Leeaders care. Wen aw tell um ez 'tother side's 'Onston
Eawr Candidate eawt bi his tail, They reply, in a tone that's quite helpless, He's "removed fer convenience o' sale !"

Mester Edditur, maybe yo'll tell me, • If "Robert" hez hookt it fer good; If he's travel't across thi wide oshun, An' desertet uz aw cowd blood. But if this is a fact, aw'll excuse urn— Aw caun't be surpriz'd at ther wail ; If it's true, an' it's sed to amuse um— lie's "removed fer convenience o' sale !"

Eaur newspapper's getten bie portrait, But that'll not help us o'er th' job; An' if aw'm anny judge o' a picter, Aw doen't think it's chep at a One Raddikle thickyed advis'd me, To trickle sum sant on his tail, An' then aw cud sware, if aw miss'd him, Be' "removed for convenience o' sale!"

But "where and oh, where" hez he gone to, Aw ax in a shiverin, swat; Is ther noan (saw/ Party con find him, Or make eawt wot he means to be at? O'er his absence, aw'rts grievin' no lunger, Nolunger aw'll sit on a rail; Aw'm noan goin' to work for a joker Woze "removed ter convenience or see I" TR EDDLEHOY LE. Warriton, 26,3, 92.
EXPECTED FATAL TERMINATION TO A FIGHT AT WIDNES.

On Thursday at Runcorn Police Court, before Mr. Alfred Thomas, Thomas Rawlinson, labourer,oi Salkeld-square, was brought up under a warrant charged with unlawfully wounding, with intent to do grievous bodily harm, Frederick Pilling, ot 11, Sutton-street, Runcorn, on the 12th inst. Tames Irving, watchman, at the Old Quay Works, spoke to seeing Pilling shortly before eleven o'clock on the night of the 12th inst. He was the worse for drink.. About 11.30 witness heard a row, and on going into Mersey- St., saw a crowd watching several men fighting. He saw Pilling and the prisoner, who were among those quarrel- ling. Pilling tell and his head came in contact with the ground. Those on the ground were like two dogs worrying one another. He did not see kicks exchanged.. He did not see Rawlinson strike Pilling.—P.S. Woolley spoke to having been to Filling's House that morning. He was a shade better. He was still unconscious. Dr. McDougall had been attending him since the 12th, and was still doing so. The man had all along been con- fined to his bed. He was suffering from paralysis of the left side- Superintendent Atherton asked for a remand for a week, to see how the man went on. The prisoner said he did not know anything about the matter. He , wished to engage a sollcitor.—Superintendent Atherton —Dr. McDougall dos not think the man will get better. The remand was granted, and bail was refused.

div.head: CONSERVATIVE MEETING AT WA RRINGTON.
div.p: CONSERVATIVE MEETING AT WA RRINGTON.

Under the auspices of the Conservative Associa- tion a meeting of Conservatives and Unionists was , held on Monday evening, in the Assembly-room, at ' the Conservative Club, the chair being occupied by Mr. John White, who was supported on the platform by Mr. J. IL Bottomley (of the National Union, London), Alderman Francomb, Alderman Sutton, Mr. L. Voisey, C.C., Councillor William Tinsley, Mr. John Fairclough, and Mr. John Hampson (registra- tion agent). There was a large attendance in the body of the room. The CHAIRMAN, in opening the proceedings, apologized for the absence of Mr. Robert Davies, who had been an- nounced to preside. He also explained that the receo- tion which should have been held on the 20th April had been postponed to the 28th of that month, to suit the converbence of Sir Gilbert Greenell, who would on that occasion bid farewell to his old constitutents. (Applause.) Alderman SUTTON moved "That this meeting of Con- servatives and Unionists of Warrington.hereby declares its unabated confidence in the policy of the Government and pledges itself to use every legitimate means to re- turn Mr. Robert Pierpoint as a member for the borougti, to support the Unionist party at the next Parliamentary election." He held that for happiness, peace, and pros- perity such a Government as the present had never existed in this country. The working classes, he added, were indebted to the Conservatives for every good mea- sure which had been passed for many years. (Applause.) Councillor SMITIIIIRST seconded the motion, and urged upon his hearers the importance of " work,work, work." Their candidate had not a good wife to work for him, and they had, therefore, to ask the ladies of the party to do so. And ladies could work. (Applause.) But, if Mr. Pierpoint had not a good wife, he had the next best thing, and that wasa good sister, who had done more for tile people of Warrington than Mrs. Houston would be able to do if she lived to be a 100 years old. Misst Pierpoint did not go about singing in this, that, and the other place,but she visited and helped the poor. (Cheers.) Mr. BOITOMLEY, who was received with applause, said that, with all respect to the Conservative candidateie sister, he thought Mr. Pierpoint had something even better to recommend him, and that was a good cause and a good government. (Applause.) He hoped they had good workers amongst them, and they were deter- mined to have him as their representative at the next election. He had often looked at the newspapers, to see what was going on in that part of the world, and when he saw that Dr. Houston had been selected as the Liberal ' candidate, he was irresistibly reminded of the cartoon in " Punch "some time ago. A farmer had lest a frisky yodng bull, and after looking for it along time,. be at last found it in the middle of a railway, tupping at an express train that was coining along. He looked at the animal for a minute, and at last said," Young man, I admire your pluck, but dash your discretion." (Laughter.) He was bound to admire Dr. Houston's pluck, but his candidature did not say much for his discretion, if he thought he was going to be returned as member for that borough. But he quite agreed with the last speaker, that if they wished to succeed they must "Work, work, work, work." (Applause.) He also contended that the present Government was the best they had had iu modern times,and that there was not a class in the community for which something had not been done by it. Having enumerated many of the mea- sures passed by the Government, he added that, there had been a reduction of 2d. in the £on the income tax, for the benefit of smokers, they had reduced the on tobacco. To please the wives they had re- duced the duty on tea' and currants. (Ap- plause.) Whilst they were 'mud of what had been done elsewhere, they were still more proud of the record of the good administration of Mr. Balfour in Ireland. Let them ask Dr. Houston what he meant by Home Rule, and he could not tell them. Why ? Because Mr. Gladstone had not told him yet. (Laughter.) He could repeat the words" Home Rule," as all Liberals could. He some- times thought that people over-estimated the ability of Mr. Edison They said he was a very clever man, but be thought Mr. Gladstone was the cleverer of the two. Mr. Edison had made machines into human beings almost, but Mr. Gladstone had done the opposite he had made human beings into machines. (Renewed laughter and applause.) The resolution was then submitted and carried unani- mously. Alderman FRANCOMB addressed the meeting, and moved a vote of thanks to Mr. Bottomley for his able, interesting, and instructive address. Mr. L. VOISEY, C.C., seconded the motion, and con- tended that what Mr. Balfoar had done in the West of Ireland was sufficient to endear him to the whole Irish nation, if he had done nothing else. (Applause.) The resolution was carried. Mr. Borroattav briefly returned thanks, and proposed a vote of thanks to Mr. White for presiding. Mr. Aantua BENNETT seconded, and the motion hav- ing Peen agreed to the meeting terminated.

The Press Association says that intelligence has been received from Cape Clast Castle, announcing the death of Saekity' King of Crobe, from influenza, supervening on malarial fever. Letters of administration have been granted of the estates of the late Mr. Charles Stewart Parnell to his widow, Mrs. Katherine Parnell. The value of the estate is declared at £11,770. div.head: ASSOCIATION.
div.p: ASSOCIATION.
NEWTON DIVISION LIBERAL
A MEETING AT PENKETI-I.

A meeting in connection with the Newton Division Liberal Association was held in the Wes- leyan Day School, Penketh, on Monday evening. There was a large attendance. Mr. C. E. Parker pre- sided, and was supported by Mr. Wm. Neild, the Liberal candidate for the Division ; Mr. Taylor, Eccleston Hall; Mr. Gummersall, Mr. White, and others.

The Chairman said: I would like in the first place to congratulate the people of Petiketh on enjoying for the first time the right of gathering together as English- men in the village school, freely to discuss subjects of national importance. I have for many years contended tha:. any building serving the purpose of a village school, and receiving Government grants ought to be available for the legitimate purpose of a political meeting. (Hear, hear.) I have urged this plea again aud again to those who have authority over this building, but until the present occasion to no purpose. This time we have been successful, and I stand before you for the first time =- muzzled. For although we have had many social meet- ings here, our mouths have been muzzled as far as poli- tics went. The reason for this charge is that Mr. Herbert Gardner, the Liberal member for Saffron Walden, has at last been successful in receiving an acknowledgement of the justice of the claim from the House. He has again and again brought this matter before Parliament, and it has always been resisted by the Conservatives. I don't know whether it is the effect of the coming election casting its shadow before, but the other night Mr. Gardner forced an acknowledgement from the head of the Government that the matter should be dealt with. And now, passing froro this subject of local government over the school at Penketh to the larger one of local government in the sister country of Ireland, it will be within the recollection of most here that at the last gene- ral election of 1886, when the question of Home Rule occupied then as now the first place, we were pro- mised a bill by the Conservatives. Mr. Leigh, however, promised us nothing, and haa done nothing. I have never seen his name associated with any reform, and as far as he has a policy at all it is one of blank negative. It was mostly the Liberal Unionists, those estimable gentlemen who appear to think that when they left the Liberal party they took all the virtue with them, who were forward in promising a bill that would satisfy all the reasonable aspirations of the Irish people. It was to be a bill wide and comprehensive and to give to Irish- men the freedom and power to govern themselves lo- cally as Englishmen do. After a delay of aix years, a bill has been brought forward in fulfilment of these pro- mises. I have heard Liberals speak with contempt of this measure, and I was anxious to see if the bill was really as bad as it was painted. I therefore procured a copy of the bill and found it hedged about with so many ' so-called safeguards, which were realty limitations of the power of the people, that I do not wonder that the measure has been indignantly refused by both sections of the Irish party. Offering it to the Irish people as a local government measure is little less than an. insult. (Ap- plapse.) In the first instance, the Parliamentary fran- chise is departed from, and illiterate voters are disen- franchised. After a considerable period, when educa- tion has been free and compulsory, then anyone who cannot write must be little less than an idiot, but at present there are many who are not able to write, not as the result of ignorance or want of effort, but solely for the want of opportunity, and to disenfranchise such were unjust. Then further the Council was made in all capital expenditure subservient to a Standing Joint Committee composed of fourteen members, seven of whom were elected by the council, and seven appointed by the high sheriff of the county who in his turn was appointed by the Lord Lieutenant. The sheriff was to act as chairman of this Committee and have avcasting vote. The control of the money for any new expenditure such as the mak- ing of a road, the digging of a well, or any such change was to be made subject to the approval of this Commit- tee in which the elective element was in the minority. Then again the Committee were liable to be summoned before two judges, and if found guilty of certain vague acts were liable to be extinguished, and the Lord Lieu- tenant, not the electors, appointed a council to serve during the remainder of the term of office. The bill right through illustrated the profound distrust with which the Conservatives regarded the Irish people. (Applause)

, Mr. Taylor proposed the following resolution That this meeting records its continued and unabated confid- ence in Mr. Gladstone and his colleagues, and expresses its strong conviction that upon the leading political questions the majority in the House of Commons is no longer in conformity with the wants of the people." The Speaker then proceeded to descant at length upon the present land laws. Referring to Mr. Chaplin's Small Holdings Bill, Mr. Chaplin had, he said in introducing it stated that there was plenty of land to be got, and it must be got by agreement with the landlord. That was all very well in some places, but not to he done everywhere. If the land was to be got by agreement with the landlord that left them pretty much where they were at present. The Liberals proposed a different stateof things. they proposed, and although it was an experiment he thought it was a very hopeful one, that parish councils or some such bodies should have the power of acquiring land compulsorily ; and letting it out in small portions either as allotments or small holdings. He would like to ask if anyone present seriouslsrthought they would get a measure of land reform front the Tories, but he did think they would get it from the Liberals. As to the labour question, he thought it was hardly necessary to say that the Liberals would do more than the Conservatives for the working-men. Who gaim the present franchise ? The Liberals gave that one of the greatest measures in the interest of the working-man ever passed. The Tories had previously extended the franchise as Mr. Disraeli had said at the time to dish the Whigs ; and the measure was really a Liberal one car- riedby the Tories. One of the most important labour questions was really the payment of members, which would enable working-men to send their own represen- tatives to Parliament. He did not think they Were likely to get any payment of members from the Tory party. The Tories were going to the country en the record of the past. That record was a very meagre one. Their policy had been entirely one of negation. But a great wave was spreading over the country, and before very long Mr. Gladstone would be brought back to power with an enormous majority ; and lie certainly trusted that the Liberals of Penketh would do their utmost to prevent Newton division being left out:in the cold. (Applause.) Mr. Neill seconded the resolution. He said they were very rapidly approaching another general election, and it would be the duty of the constituency to decide between him and the Tory candidate. He did not know whether they had satisfied themselves as to what the views of the Tory party were; he had not been able to find them out. As far as he could gather; they had got no views for the future at all, and he came to that con- clusion for this reason, that he found Mr. Goschen only a few nights ago calling on the country to support the Tories, not on account of what they were•going, to do in the future, but of what they had done in the past. Now what had they done since they came into power? They promised that there should be no, pledging of English credit to purchase land in Ireland, and that there should be no coercion. These pledges had been, broken. Every one of their promises had been broken. He had no doubt the Primrose dames if there were any there would come to them and try to make them. believe what won- derful things had been done by the present Government. He did not say that they had not passed some good measures, but their passing these Liberal measures re- minded him of the man who stole the clothes of the man who was bathing. The Liberal clothes had been put on by the Tories much as the negro of Central Africa put on a suit which was given him. He stuck his feet through the arms of the coat and pulled it round his waist, wore the trousers round his neck as a scarf, and hung the tall hat at his side and used it to put his pipe and ether things in. (Loud, laughter.) The Allot- ments Act of the Government the speaker charac- terised as a complete failure,, and he asked the working-men if they could. find a single Act passed by the Government from which they derived the slightest benefit. He did not know that the English Local Government Act was of much benefit to tliem. The Irish Local Government Bill was then severely crLicised, and the speaker advocated Home Rule as the only remedy for Ireland's present condition. As to the threatened throwing out of the Home Rule Bill by the House of Lords, the answer to be made to that cry was like that which Stephenson made when asked what would happen if a cow got in front of his engine" All the worse for the cow.' If the House of Lords proved an obstruction all the worse for it. (Applause and laughter.), The speaker proceeded to maintain that the death duties ought to be equal, for real and personal property, and advocated more control of the drink traffic, referring to the fact that last year 141 millions had been spent in alcoholic liquors in Great Britain and Ireland. He, however, was not in favour of total prohibition, or class legislation which would allow the rich facilities for drinking denied to the poor. The resolution was put and carried unanimously. Mr. Gummersall proposed :—" That having listened to I the address of Mr. William Neill, this meeting of the Liberals of Penketh, Sankey, and Cuerdley, considers him a fit and proper person to represent the Newton Division of the county of Lancashire in Parliament, and pledges itself to use every legitimate effort to secure his triumph- ant return." Mr. A. White seconded. Some questions were put to Mr. Neill, in reply to which he said he was in favour of an Eight Hours for Miners Bill ; but as to mining royalties he could not give a definiie answer at present. If they were abolished the purchasers not the miners would benefit. He would be in favour of a sliding scale of royalties, which weuld benefit both the coal owner and the miner. In answer to another question he said he would be in favour, of a bill aifowing marriages in Nonconformist Churcltes with- out the intervention of the Registrar. The seocnd proposition was unanimously adopted, Mr. Neill thanked the meeting, and it vvitS cuaduded with a vote of thanks to the Chairman.
RAILWAY DISA.STER IN AMERICA.
LOSS OF 13 LIVES.

NEW YORK;. THURSDAY.—A railway disaster, which is described as the worst which has ever occurred in Cen- tral America, is reported by the " Herald "in a telegram from San Salvador of yesterday's date. A train on the Acajulta Railway ran off the line at Sansonate, thirteen persons being killed and thirty-one injured.

div.head: SIR ED WA RD) WA TKO. 'S BETROTHAL
div.p: SIR ED WA RD) WA TKO. 'S BETROTHAL
EXTENT OF THE LADY'S FORTUNE..

The "Daily Chronicle" says :---Our announcement of the proposed marriage between Sir Edward Watkin and Mrs. Herbert Ingram has given rise to the wildest rumours as to the extent of the lady's fortune. The truth is, we believe, the lady is worth, about £300,000, and that she has the absolute disposal of her property. Since the famous and startling announcement of the betrothal of Lady Burdett-Coutts, to Mr. Ashmead- Bartlett, there has been no such cry of astonishment as has been raised over the rumour that Sir Edward Wat- kin is to marry Mrs. Ingram, widow of the late pro- prietor of the" Illustrated LondonNewarherself bearing eighty blushing summers without blame. Sir Edward is seventy-three. Mere is great opposition from the mem- bers of the family, for most of the wealth of the Ingrams is now in the amorous octogenarian. widow's keeping. Sir Edward Watkin is, however, a "masterful chid " when he pleases, and will fight hard ere he loses his affianced bride.

div.head: PARNELL-WOOD WILL CASE.
div.p: THE PARNELL-WOOD WILL CASE.

The action in which Mrs. Parnell, formerly O'Shea, claims to be the sole legatee under the will of the late Mrs. Wood, of Illtham, whose estate is said to amount to about £200,000, was down for hearing, on Thursday, in the Probate Division, before Mr. Justice Jenne and a special jury. The defendants, General Sir Evelyn Wood and Mr. Charles Wood, opposed, among other pleas al- leging that the will was obtained by undue influence,and that the testatrix was not of sound mind, which allega- tions were denied, and among the interveners was Captain O'Shea, former husband of Mrs. Parnell. Sir Charles Russell led for the plaintiff, and the Attorney-General for the defendants. Among those in the court, which was crowded, were Sir Evelyn Wood and Capt. O'Shea, but Mrs. Parnell, remained in one of the waiting rooms. At the opening of the court there appeared to be a disposition to settle the case, and counsel retired to talk the matter over. After a short consultation, Sir Charles Russell announced that terms had been agreed upon,and that it was proposed to prove the will in solemn form. The will having been formally preyed, it was decided that the question as to the in- terests of the children should be discussed in chambers before the judge.

div.head: SHIP CAITAL.
div.p: THE SHIP CAITAL.
NEW CONTRACTOR FOR NO; I SECT/ON.

The directors of the Manchester Ship Canal Compony have let the contract for No. 1' section of the unfinished portion of the Ship Canal to Mr. J. Jackson, contractor, Westminster. Seventeen contractors applied for quan- tities, and fourteen tenders were received. The directors were naturally anxious to ,get the first contract into the hands of a substantial and experienced contractor, and they believe that in Mr. Jackson they have secured one who will give them, thorough satisfaction. He has re- cently been engaged at the new Tower Dndge and at the Barry Docks. ANOTHER, FATAL. ACCIDENT

_ Art inglest was held at the Ship Canal Hospital, Latchford, on Thursday afternoonconcerning the death of David Morris, night watchman, who was killed by falling down the Ship Canal cutting at Stockton Heath. —Louisa Morris, his daughter, gave evidence as to pass- ing the spot where the body was found, and hearing groans at a quarter to nine. She knew it was het father, and pTocured assistanoa, A. cab was sent for, the de- ceased conveyed to the hospital. The doctor found that Morris had a broken leg, and one side of his face smashed.—The jury returned a verdict of "Death from exposure and shock."

div.head: ACTION AGAIMT A WARRINGTON
div.p: ACTION AGAIMT A WARRINGTON
PUBLICAN.
A COSTLY SHOT.

At Manchester, on Thursday, Lord Chief Justice Coleridge and a special jury heard the case of Ful- ford v. Dainteth, an action to recover damages for personal injuries. Mr. Bigbam, for the plaintiff, stated that his client was a young man living with his father in Chester-read, Old Trafford, and the defendant was the landlord of the Dog and Dart public-house at Warrington. On the 19th May last the plaintiff was with a rook-shooting party on the High Legh Hall estate, near Lymm. The plaintiff was not shooting„but received a bullet in his thigh. The plaintiff was confined to bed for eight weeks, and to the house for a further eight weeks. The defence was that the bullet came from the rifle of another member of the shooting party, and not from Mr. Dainteth's ride at all. after hearing two other witnesses for the defendant, the judge expressed the opinion that the defence was hopeless, and the jury said they did not wish to hear any further evidence. Mr. Russell then addressed the jury in mitigation of damages. The jury assessed the damages at £125, and judgment for that amount, with costs,, was given.

Swanay, of the Gold Coast and London, and the foulth had killed his wife. One of them sang Moody and Sankey' hymns while being pinioned. Sir George Elliot, who was on board, hearing that she was from his native county (Durhaml„ ordered her every comfort, whilst the Dean et Westminster, who was also a passenger, baptised the child, Sir Georga Elliot becoming a sponsor. COUNTY OF CHESTER. VOTICE IS HEREBY GIVEN, that the next .01 GENERAL QUARTER SESSIONS of the Peace for the COUNTY OF CHESTER will be held at the COURT HOUSE, NETHER KNUTSFORD, in the said County on MONDAY, the 4th day of April next, at half-past eleven o'clock in the Forenoon. The hearing of all Appeals arising within the Hundreds of Bucklow. Macclesfield, and Northwich, forming the I Knutsford District, and the trials of all prisoners com- mitted from such Hundreds, will take place at such Sessions. The Grand and Petty Jury for the Knutsford District must be in attendance at the Court House, Knutsford, at the epening of the Court on MONDAY, the 4th day of April next, at half-past eleven o'clock in the Forenoon. THE Court will be Adjourned to the Castle of Chester on THURSDAY, the 7th day of April next, at Eleven o'clock in the Forenoon. The hearing of all Appeals arising within the Hundreds of 13roxton, Eddisbury, Nantwich, and Wirral, forming the Chester District, and the trials of all prisoners committed from the last-men- tioned Hundreds will take place at such Adjourned Ses- sions. The Grand and Petty Jury for the Chester Dis- trict must be in attendance at the Castle of Chester at the opening of the Court on THURSDAY, the 7th day of April next, at Eleven o'clock in the Forenoon. REGINALD porrs, Clerk of the Peace. Chester, 14th March, 1892.

COUNTY OF CHESTER. CONTAGIOUS DISEASES (ANIMALS) ACTS, 1878 AND 1888. FOOT-AND-MOUTH DISEASE. VOTICE IS HEREBY GIVEN, that at a meeting of 1.11 the Executive Committee of the Local Authority of the County of Chester, held at Chester Castle on Sat- urday, the 19th day of March, 1892. 1. IT WAS ORDERED, that from and after the 19th day of March, 1892, the Regulations made by the Execu- tive Committee of this Local Authority on the 7th day of March, 1892, shall be and the same are hereby revoked. 2. AND IT WAS FURTHER ORDERED, pursuant to the power contained in Article 11. of the Foot and Mouth Disease Order of 1892, that from and after the 19th day of March, 1892, the movement by Land or by Water of Animals (i.e., Cattle, Sheep, Goats, or Swine), into the District of the Local Authority of the County of Chester FROM THE DISTRICT OF ANY OTHER LOCAL AUTHORITY IN ENGLAND OR WALES OR SCOT- LAND, shall (with the exception hereinafter mentioned) BE ABSOLUTELY PROHIBITED until this Order is revoked. 3. FAT ANIMALS intended for immediate Slaughter may be moved into the District of the Local Authority of this County upon the following conditions, that is to say— (a) On the Certificate of a duly qualified Veterinary Surgeon that such Animals are free from Disease. (b) That such Animals are marked by and at the ex- pense of the owner, consignee, or other person in charge of such Animals, as follows : CATTLE.—By the clipping of a broad arrow,about five inches long, on the left hind quarter of each of the Cattle. SHEEP AND SWINE.—By the painting or stamp- ing of the letter M about six inches long, on the left side of each of the Sheep and Swine with the following composition, namely :—Rosin, five parts : oil of turpentine, two parts; and blue or red ochre, one part; melted and used warm; or with some other adhesive composition of a blue or red colour. (e) That such Animals are moved along the nearest public road direct to some Slaughter-house within the District of this Authority, from which Slaughter- house they shall not be again removed, but shall be slaughtered there within a period of 48 hours, and shall be kept isolated from any other animals not intended to be slaughtered within such period. 4. Certificates of the Veterinary Surgeons relating to the Fat Animals moved into this District for Slaughter, must accompany the animals and be delivered within 24 hours at the Police Station of the County nearest the Slaughter-house to which they have been moved. REGINALD Parrs, Clerk of the Local Authority of the County of Chester. Chester, 19th March, 1892. N.B.—Licences for the movement of animals out of the district comprising the County of Chester, and also comprising the Boroughs of Birkenhead,Chester, Congle- ton, Crewe, Hyde, Macclesfield, Stalybridge, and Stock- port, can only be granted by an Inspector of the Board of Agriculture, or by a person appointed for the purpose by the Board. The foregoing Regulations do not restrict the move- ment of Animals by Railway through the District of the Local Authority of this County, without untrucking. Any Offence against the above Regulations ts deemed an °fence against the Act of 1878,which renders the Offender lable to a Penalty not exceeding Twenty Pounds.

WARRINGTOJ UNION.—R LISVING OFFICER. &c.. WANTED.—The Guardians require the services of a Relieving Officer for the No. 3 District of the Union. The person to be appointed must be healthy,active, and intelligent, competent to keep accounts and to comply with the duties as they are required to be fulfilleei by the Law and by the Con- solidated Orders. His whole time will be due, by law, to the duties. He will be required to appropriate such time to office attendance, visitation of the poor, payment of relief, &c.. according to regulations of the Guardians. He will also be required to reside at such part of his Distiict as they may approve. Salary £lOO per annum, payable quarterly.—Candi- dates must apply, in their own handwriting, by letter (with not more than three recent testimonials) endorsed" Relieving Officer" and to be sent to me on or before Thursday, March 31st. Selected candidates will be at liberty to attend before the Guardians at their Board meeting on Wednesday, April 6th. The person appointed will be required to enter into a bond for £lOO with an approved guarantee society. Canvas- sing the Guardians is strictly trohibitod, and will be deemed a disqualification. By order. JAMES C. SUTTON, Union Clerk. Dewsey Chambers, Warrington.

Messrs. Lawson's rope works, Dundee, were burnt yesterday. The damage is estimated at £8;,000. William McPherson hanged himself yesterday ini Paisley Prison. He wrote on the cell floor that he was weary of life. TERRIFI7 BOILER EXPLOSION. At half-past six yesterday morning a terrific explosion occurred at Messrs. D. and W. Taylor's Bridgewater Mill, Blackburn. The boiler house and mechanics' shop adjoining had their roofs blown off and the windows knocked out, the whole place being wrecked. Two men named Barton and Bradshaw, working in the place when the explosion occurred, were both shockingly scalded. Barton's injuries being very serious. The damage is very large.
